The capture Of a vicious Texas longhorn
by a man, barehanded, furnished the climax
Of a thrilling performance last night at the
first exhibition OF the Miller Bros.
-iOl Ranch Wild West show at Brighton
Beach.


Long" Lloyd Seeley Of Montana was
the cowman who turned the trick. Cutting
out from the herd a big black steer with
horns four feet wide, Seeley chased him
around the arena until his horse was run
ming neck and neck with the longhorn.
Then leaning over and seizing a big horn
in each hand, Seeley leaped from his saddle
and threw all his weight on the steers head.
The beast dragged him some distance
before he stopped. Then came irregular
Quo Vadis struggle in which Seeley won
by flooring the longhorn. Seeley limped
when he left the arena. .


Another feature Of the show was the round
ing up of the herd Of sixty Texas steers
and the roping and throwing Of certain
animals for. branding. There were also
an Indian buffalo hunt, the riding OF some
razor backed, rangy steers that bucked
devilishly and pitching horses and other
familiar Wild West stunts.

Madison. Wis. June 21-The public utilities
bill was passed by the Legislature to-day with
little opposition. except from municipal owner
ship advocates who objected to the provision
that municipality owned public utilities should
be conducted under the same style of books that
corporations forced 10 adopt.


The bill provides that all concerns. private or
public. supplying water, electric light or any
other such convenience to the people must be
operated under a set Of books which show the
allowance for depreciation and other such de-
tails. Municipal plants must make allowance
for tax paid by private concerns in making rates
for service. and such rates must be sufficient TO
continue the concern on a profit paying basis.


All the corporations included in the act ara
under the control of the railway commission.
and the bill includes every public utility except
electric railways. The bill gives the railway
commission power TO fix rates for all service by
public utility corporations. and all franchises
existent are made exclusive.

Los Angeles yesterday celebrated In
ioned manner, with speeches and music
in the parks and with the customary
ear-splitting racket, contributed alike
by young boys and old boys. some of
them young enough to fire their first
firecracker and some old enough to have
grandchildren of their own, but all boys
together.


The hubbub began, as usual. some-
what In advance of the calendar. In
fact. the great American eagle, copying
the habits of the mockingbird, began
screaming soon after sundown Wednes-
day night. BY breakfast time yester-
day morning he was already hoarse
BY noon he had burned off few tail
feathers, but night found him still in
celebrant mood, singed, tired, but
happy.


The day was hot and early in the
morning Senior Los Angeles, his wife
and the children packed great lunch
baskets and boarded cars for the beach.
Could a census have been taken yes
terday it would have shown the city
practically deserted and the beach
towns striving for metropolitan honors.


Desert City Early


The exodus began at an early hour
and continued all day. The cars were
packed, but the crowds were good ma
tured despite ifr discomfort, and there
were few compls'r 8. Where the cars
carried tens of thousands automobiles
and private vehicles bound for the
same destination added their quota to
the rapidly increasing throng. All the
main Travelled roads between here and
Ocean Park, Venice, Santa Monica and
Long Beach were crowded; and as
result there are in the city today sew
eral hundred new converts to the good
roads propaganda, for autos beach
bound found anything but easy going.


Arrived at the beach the crowds
thronged the strand, wandered along
the board walk patronized the refresh
ment booths and enjoyed themselves
generally. Those who were early
enough upon the scene to secure ac-
commodations in any of the bath
houses eagerly availed themselves of
the opportunity. Late corners were de-
MED this privilege, for the supply OF
dressing rooms and bathing suits ran
short early in the day.


Quiet Day in City


In town the day was rather quiet
The police rule prohibiting the explo-
sion of fireworks in the business dis
trict was generally obeyed and there
was little trouble.


The usual number of minor accidents
was reported at police headquarters.
but at late hour last night there had
been no fatalities. Other points in the
United States, however, were less for
tunate and from more than few cities
came news reports of fatal accidents,
casting their shadows over happy
homes from east to west and from
north to south.


There were fires, more than score
of them. before o'clock and this num-
ber was increased largely during the
night. The firemen probably were the
hardest worked men in town, with the
possible exception of street car crews.
None of the fires, however, resulted IN
any great amount of loss.


Ready at Hospital


Elaborate preparations had been
made at the receiving hospital to care
for the injured. The surgeons had la1d
in a stock of anti-tetanus serum, none
of which, however, was used. Many
cases of accidental burning were treated
in the homes of the victims, by their
family physicians and were never re-
ported to the police So far as is known,
however, none of these cases was sutfi-
ciently grave to cause apprehension or
permanent injury


The parks were thronged all day and
keep off the grass signs were disre-
garded with impunity. At Eastlake
park the New England society of South
ern California held it: celebration in
good old time fashion. Probably $500
members of the society attended the ex-
ercises and this number was swelled
largely by outsiders. All were made
welcome.


Judge Waldo M. York of the superior
court, president f the society, was in
charge of the arrangements for the
celebration and the program.

Buttons was a beautiful black cat. with

20" exclaimed Hilda, they're washing

CHICAGO, October 7.-Reports received
by the Tribune from ten of the Metho-
dist Episcopal conferences in Illinois and
neighboring states show that the question
of higher salary for the average minister
of that church has reached a crisis.


The generally expressed opinion is that
religious work soon will suffer for lack
of preachers unless salaries are raised.
In many of the conferences just held
there was an exodus of preachers from
the pulpit to enter business life.


The higher salaries movement was dis
cussed and advocated at practically all
the conferences.


Salaries have been advanced about 500
each during the last four years. but this
has not kept pace with
the increase In cost Of living-has failed
to stem the ministerial stampede into
business life.

The Population Of Manchester.
Out OF the 10000 population Of Man
chester land the newspapers Of the city

large proportion. and very few OF them
are children. The laws prohibiting child
forced throughout all New England. and

arrived aliens attempt to evade these laws.

ters. came In and took their places. Then

OAKLAND, March S.-Leaving West
Berkeley station at 7:4O o'clock to-
night the West Berkeley local train
for San Francisco dashed into an open
switch a short distance south OF the
station and crashed into another train
which had just taken the siding to let
the. outgoing train through. Only the
fact that the train had gained but little
headway before the collision prevented
serious accident. and as it was the
passengers were hurled from their
seats and the tenders of both loco
motives badly wrecked.


The crew in charge of the train
leaving the station declared that the
switch had been left open by the other
train crew after the train had taken
the siding, and this is probably true
Had it not been for the GOODNESS of
the engineer in charge of the local
much greater damage would have re-
suited from the collision. for when his
train ran into the open switch the
engineer stuck to his post, and setting
the brakes on the train, reversed his
engine, greatly lessening the effect Of
the shock.


The local train was running with
tender ahead, and this prevented
serious damage to the locomotive. al
though the tender itself was smashed
The train on the siding was also
standing with tender ahead, and this
also was considerably damaged.


C. H. Often. who lives at 1924 Uni
versity avenue, was one of the pas
sengers on the local train who was
hurled from his seat when the trains
met, and he declares that but for the
fact that his train was running slowly
at the time of the accident both would
have been wrecked. Although not
seriously injured Often was painfully
bruised. as were nearly all the others
on the train.

From the Mexican border to the koyu-

Nellie eastman is a picturesque character

kind all too soon.


Who among the old Cassiar miners but
will remember the memorable winter
when, with her little stock of goods, she
kept the camp alive, not only with the
provisions she sold and handed out to all
who were in need, but her presence and
ever optimistic spirit prevailed at all times
and paystreak of good feeling in camp

sled over thousands fof miles of Alaska
rivers and tundra. She has been in every
camp.sand when the news of the Innoko

Nellie eastman who was the hrst to say:
Boys, I'm off for the new excitements."
The old-timers say excitements, rot STAN
pedes.


During the forty years she has been
drifting around on the treacherous sea of
placer strikes, Nellie eastman has made.
given away and lost more money. per-
haps, than any miner in the north has
ever made out of Alaska diggings. If,
after she has been laid away. her name
does not go down in history embellished
by the richest of sentime ntS. deserving of

dead, good and honest effort are meaning
less and We must indeed also mourn the

boys took shelter in a roadside barn,
where they remained, cold and hungry,
throughout the entire night.


With the arrival of morning the
glamor Of their adventure had begun
to wane, and after partaking of a cold
breakfast the homesick lads set out
on foot for home. where they arrived
shortly after nightfan.


The lads had long planned their ad-
venture. They put their dimes to-
gether for a month after Christmas,
and with the joint savings bought
cheap shotgun and material for a tent,
with one or two minor articles that
hunters are supposed to need. They
made the tent themselves and, besides

brace of knives.

BELLINGHAM, Wash, Sept. 5-six
badly beaten Hindus are in the hospital
400 frightened and half naked Silkhs are
In the jail and corridors of the city hall
under guard, and somewhere between
Bellingham and the British Columbia line
are $50 natives OF India, beaten, hungry
and half clothed, making their way along
the Great Northern railway. bound for
Canadian territory and the protection
Of the British flag.


The long expected has occurred. and
drive out the Hindus'' was heard
throughout the city and along the water
front last night. The police were help
less and for five hours a mob of half a
thousand white men raided the mills
where the blacks were working, battered
down doors of lodging houses shetering
the foreigners, and, dragging the invad-
ers from their beds, with a beating
started them for the city limits with
orders to keep on going.


The trouble started at and Holly
streets last night, a district of Indian
lodging houses The houses were cleaned
out and the denizens started on their
tramp for the Canadian line. The mob
then swept down to the water front and
mill after mill was visited, the white
employees Joining the mob, and every
Hindu was hustled outside.


Here the police suggested that the un-
desirables be taken to the Jail. This was
greeted with delight, and the foreigners
were hustled along. From this time on
very few were beaten and the blood
thirsty ones of the mob seemingly were
satisfied.


Continue for Hours


The mob kept up its work along the
water front until early this morning.
when Larsops mill was visited and a
hundred Hindus brought in there.


Four women were found this morning
among the city buildings.


There is quiet today, but there is a
strong undercurrent of opinion which
apparently approves the action of the
mob and 1t may be found impossible to
prosecute the leaders.


Racial feeling has played but a small
part In the affair. The Indians have sup
planted white labor. The invaders have
become bold and insolent, many instances
of women being pushed into the gutter or
insulted on street cars being reported.


The Hindus are all British subjects and
their case is being placed before the Brit
ish authorities.


Following a special session of the city
council this morning Mayor Black took
charge of the situation. Fifty armed
specials were sworn In and the mayor
declares as many more will be If neces-
sary to give the blacks protection.


Jobs have been offered the Hindus again
by mill men and protection guaranteed
but the Hindus have been so thoroughly
frightened that they are drawing their
pay under police protection and are dis
posed to leave for Vancouver during the
day


Mob spirit is still rampant and 1t Is
said further, attacks will be made tonight
If any of the foreigners remain. The city
and county authorities, however say
they will be able to cope with any
emergency.

miles distant. one of the largest in the
country, will close down owing to trouble

NEWPORT. May s.-The Octopus broke
the worlds record to-day by making a
speed Of more than ten knots under water.


The best time heretofore made was eight
and q half knots by one OF the submarines
Of the British navy.


The Octopus made three high speed runs
this morning with Capt. Mark and other
members Of the Naval Board on board.
She Rlided through the water with apparent
ease and covered the first mile at the rate
Of lois knots. This was her maximum
speed, while her average was ten knots
plus. which was only a fraction less than
she made last week while running semi
submerged.


After the high speed runs three runs
were made at reduced speed to standardize
her rropellers. Subsequently she was
put through mannuvres, which proved
successful. She made three rapid dives
at an angle OF about 8 degrees, and Game
up from a depth Of thirty feet In a fraction
under forty seconds.


A feature Of the tests to-day was the
use for the first time OF the submarine
bell. with which the Octopus is equipped.
Another bell and receiving instrument
were attached to the tender Starting and
communication was kept up all the tins
the submarine was under water.


The Lake, which was to have begun her
submerged trials to-day. sprung q leak in
her torpedo tubes, and it was decided TO
postpone her trials until the damage can

LETHBRIDGE. Alberta. December 81
Because they believed that a prominent
citizen had been murdered in Chinese
restaurant LOO men raided and wrecked
the oriental quarter late Christmas night
Restaurants and laundries were smashed
and doors, windows and entire fronts OF
buildings were reduced to splinters. The
regular police of the town were powerless
and brigade of mounted police had to
be called out to quell the riot.


story was circulated that Harry
Smith. a well-known cattle rancher, had
been fatally wounded in the restaurant
Neither Smith nor any one else had been
hit. but the police were misled and two
orientals were arrested, charged with the
murder.


Mounted Police Arrive.


An indignant mob gathered opposite the
restaurant and there was talk of lynch
ing. Suddenly some one threw rock
which smashed window. In a moment
the crowd was beyond control. Bricks
and stones were hurled. and when the
doors had been broken in the tables and
chairs and dishes inside were smashed
The Columbia and Alberta restaurants
were literally wrecked. Later a$detach-
ment of mounted police appeared and
the crowd scattered.


Hundreds of the rioters merely shifted
the scene of the pillaging. Three blocks
away, opposite the Arlington Hotel. they
cleaned out another Chinese restaurant
and severely handled two orientals who
were caught within.


Mayor Galbraith and Magistrate Town
send both addressed the mob and urged
It to disperse, and, as all possible damage
had been done, it obeyed.

defile four miles from Winslow. Eighteen

of the men was hurt.

den Gate avenue yesterday afternoon

escaped serious injuries.


The collision was the most peculiar
that has been recorded in the many
street car accidents that have happened
ir Los Angeles and vicinity.


The car was running fast. The wagon
was being driven slowly, close to the
rails. Although the motorman applied
the brakes when he saw the collision
was inevitable the front steps of the car
mounted the hub of a rear wheel of
the wagon and, passing on, mounted
the hub of the front wheel, where it
stuck. The driver turned the mules
attached to the wagon sharply at right
angles from the car and they strained
with all their might, wrenching the
wheel from under the car steps. The
car settled back on the track with a
jolt that broke the glass and splintered
much of the framework.

air by succession of explosions and

the dry dock. Scores on board the
lena jumped overheard onto the stone

The first shock of the explosion was

fore and aft 1t was followed instantly
by other shocks. The crew rushed
wildly about the dock. The men for
ward clambered over the bulwarks and
jumped down, some of them into the
dock and others to the stone quay,
many being fatally hurt.


The hundreds of men below deck
were enshrouded in smoke, and while
they groped their way toward the eX-
its they became the prey of suffocating
fumes which caused many of them to
fall unconscious.


Shells and charges of explosives in
the magazines continued to explode,
and masses OF metal were nurleu lHtc
the air and fell about the docks and
arsenal. These flying missiles demol-
ished the torpedo shed, the engine
works and the pump house near by,
and constituted most serious menace
to the lives of those who made their
way toward the battleship to begin the
work of rescue. The lena was afiame
from bursting projectiles. and the fire
prevented approach.


1t is declared that for thirty minutes
the authorities were unable to discover
the keys with which to open the lock
ers to flood the dry dock and submerge
the ship, but when they did finally
open the locks the water rushed in on
the lena and the explosions came to
an end.


Amidst masses of dense smoke the
search for the dead and wounded be-
gan. The lower decks of the lena were
Uttered with fragments of shattered
and torn bodies. while the surrounding
water was dotted with human frag-
ments.

The delegation of Los Angeles
Chinese who were sent to San Francisco
for deportation reached San Francisco
Saturday and will sail for China to-
day. With Yee Lung, the young mis-
sion student who was ordered deported
two weeks ago by the federal court,
will go his white wife, formerly Emma
Culver of Duarte, who has refused to
abandon him.


Mrs. Yee Lung was married to her
Chinese husband at Albuquerque, the
union being brought about by her aunt,
who was convinced that the marriage
was advisable, and who has since per-
suaded her that it is her duty to go
with her husband to China. After their
marriage they returned to Los Angeles,
where Yee Lung had been charged by

ering of local bears steadily drove quo

rather than practical effect here. OPP
orators on the bourse are closely watch

speculation.

The shipment Of turkeys. chickens snd
other fowls from river points to the deal
ers here for the Thanksgiving market has
as yet been light. but 1t is expected that
the steamers arriving here tomorrow
morning will bring up many hundred
pounds Of the Thanksgiving bird that the
country people along the river have been
raising for year for this market. A con-
siderable number of the fowls will be
shipped dressed. but the larger part Of
them will come here alive and will be
killed and dressed by the local dealers.
Potomac raised turkeys are generally in
demand at holiday seasons. as they are
always fresh and in good order. The
steamboat men on the boats running to
the lower river anticipa-e handling large
quantities of holly and other greens dur
ing the next day or two. but the ship
ments will be light compared with those
that will come from down the river during
Christmas time.

unconscious.

to the aid of the Hoffmans. They carried
them to the automobile and made them
comfortable in the big rear seat, Miss
Howard aieing them. Meanwhile James
McKe,way, the chauffeur, went on hunt

to his home. The Frenchmen offered the
machine as an ambulance, and while 1t
was carrying the injured husband and
wife to the doctors house they walked
alongside and at, the house helped carry

Geneva, Sept. 2S.-An extraordinary mo-

end of the Lake Of Geneva last night.


The car belonged to n Claire, a
wealthy Frenchman. who, with his chauf-
feur, was driving four friends 10 Mon
treux by the road which runs along be-
tween the south Of the lake and the rail
way.


At Bouveret the road crosses the rail-
way, recrossing against Just above the
town. OF this fact the chauffeur was
evidently unaware. At any rate the ear.
la large and powerful one. and proceeding
at great speed in the darkness, after hav-
ing safely negotiated the first crossing.
dashed headlong into the closed gates Of
the second crossing.


The impact was terrific The gates
gave way like paper. and the car sped
across the railway. As the gates were
crashed through. however. a piece Of the
flying debris struck the chauffeur and
stunned him. causing him 10 entirely lose
his cCntrol over the car.


Thus. with no hand on its steering
wheel, and with no slaekening OF pace.
the car continued its career across coun-
try straight for the lake.


The few hundred yards which separate
the railway from the water were covered
in minute or two and the next moment
1t had jumped the sixty-foot bank into
the water


Fortunately. there were several specta-
tors OF the disaster, and they promptly
rendered help, or ell the occupants Of the
car must have been drowned. As II was
when they were brought to land It was
found that four Of them were seriously

not expected to recover. The car is still

LONDON, May 1.-THE Duchess of
Marlborough, who was Consuelo Van
derbilt, made her first appearance in
society since her separation from the
duke on Wednesday night. Lady Dick
son Poynder gave a ball for the Duke
and Duchess of Connaught at Chester
field gardens and there the American
duchess made her re-entry, which prob
ably had been planned with Lady
Poynder, long her chosen friend and
strongest adherent


The Duchess of Marlborough entered
the ball room just after the royal quad
rifle had been danced. Her presence
caused sensation; conversation was
almost hushed as the guests directed
their attention to her.


The Duke and Duchess of Connaught,
Mrs. "Jack' Leslie and Lady Poynder
were seated in a curtained alcove which
commanded a fine view of the ball
room. At the Duchess of Connaught's
bidding Lady Poynder arose, advanced
to meet the Duchess Of Marlborough,
greeted her with extreme cordiality
and manifest pleasure and led her to
the royalties, who asked her to be
seated.


During this ordeal the duchess
seemed rather shy and self-conscious.
But she looked very pretty and plainly
was very much pleased.


True to her reputation of having per-
feet taste in dress she was the best
gowned woman in the room. Her dress
of turquoise blue panne velvet was
very becoming; she wore crown of
diamonds with great egg-shaped tur-
Quoise; her necklet was double row
of turquoises and diamonds.


Had she ever doubted her friends
fealty she would have had every reason
to be gratified by the attentions every
one paid hel. Princess Patrick and
Prince Arthur of Connaught greeted
her warmly. She danced with Prince
Arthur, but pleading fatigue refused
most invitations to dance. For she
had Travelled from Paris only that
morning.


Miss Jean Reid and Miss Ridgely
Carter had an animated conversation
with the duchess whom Earl Crewe
took to supper and who withdrew soon
after their royal highnesses did.


Visit to America Put OF


The Duchess of Marlborough has
changed her plans and has abandoned
her visit to America, for the present,
at least. She has rented until autumn
a small country house at Nottingham,
near Brighton. Her two sons are with
her and she intends to pass much time
there.


Lord Ivor Churchill, her younger boy,
has not yet recovered his strength,
after his severe illness. The children
will visit their father periodically, or
the duke will go to see them at Rot
tingdean when their mother is absent.
She intends to take them for the Whit
suntide holiday to visit their friends,
the young Dickson Royndus, at their
country house at Hartman, Berkshire.


But, while she is leading this pas
toral existence with her sons the duch-
ess evidently intends not to neglect
her friends, but to entertain them at
Sunderland house, her splendid city
residence. For six weeks a number Of
French and Italian artists, brought
over especially for the purpose, have
been completing the decorations in the
ball room in Sunderland house. A
temporary stairway has been built
from the sidewalk to a window in the
ball room, so that the workingmen can
carry in paints and plaster without
tramping through the halls. Aside
from entertaining, the ball room must
be complete, should the duchess wish
to sublet Sunderland house.


The Duke of Marlborough is stopping
at the Coburg hotel in Mayfair, but Is
looking for a suitable fiat for the sea-
son. He dined with the party Win
ston Churchill invited to meet the
colonial premiers.


Blenheim palace is closed practically,
the establishment has been reduced as
far as possible and all unremunerative
outlay on the estate has been cut off.

Prof. Irving Fisher of Yale, after ex-

very we'll as individuals without meat.
Prosperous Americans who lead sedentaiy

way to Greece, were valiant trenchermen.
In later days the Englishmen-"fivem meal,

ruled an area sixty times as great as their
own chill island home.

owners found charging excessive ferry
rates in the flooded districts.


In Springfield and vicinity more than

Blanchard river, which had reached

towns depending on them. Marietta

Marie Fassnauer. Tyrolese woman, tow

the topInost plume of which was a good

In 1869 and 1870 Miss Anna H. Swan the
Nova Scotia giantess. caused considerable
sensation. Miss Swan seemed destined
from the cradle to be woman of abnor-
NAL dimensions. for though her father, q
Scottish immigrant. was barely five feet six
Inches high and her mother was half foot
shorter still Miss Anna reached six feet at
the age Of eleven. ard at fifteen was the

had. too. some histrionic ability as was
proved when she appeared as Lady Mac
beth in New York. and before going to
England she made triumphal tour Of the
United States.


In her prime Miss Swan was but a few
inches short of eight feet and she found

Bates. the Kentucky giant. who was actual

Robert Hales. the Norfolk giant, who

half century ago, was member of
very remarkable family. which included
some women Of extraordinary stature. His
father. farmer. six feet six inches
high, and although his mother was but a
paltry six feet, 1t is said that >she had an
ancestor in the sixteenth century who stood
four inches over eight feet.

daughters but one and one-half inches less.

was little over seven and one-half feet
high and measured sixty-four inches and

chest. respectively. while the tallest Of the

build.

NEW YORK, April 25.-Although the
public suffered Inconvenience last night
on account of the queerest strike this
city has seen for many.a day, that of
the lamplighters, the brunt of the trou-
Die was borne by the police


Good sized sections of the five bor-
oughs, especially the Bronx, the upper
part of Manhattan and the outlying
parts of Queens, were in darkness until
late, save for the light cast by three
quarters moon.


Early in the night, when the more
remote populace suddenly became
aware that the customary illumination
was not forthcoming, complaints began
to pour in upon police headquarters
and Commissioner Bingham ordered
that the police render all the assistance
possible.


Police Climb Posts


Much discontinue resulted. Some of
the patrolmen climbed the lamp posts
and used matches, a process which re-
quired numerous matches as the night
was rather breezy.


Others who had more forethought
took along poles and tapers. But un-
familiarity with the work resulted in
the ruination of numerous mantles. To
cap the climax strikers put out some
of the lights where some of the police
beats are four and five miles long and
word came by telephone to police head
quarters that unless help was vouch-
safed it would be daylight before all
the lamps had been attended to. This
necessitated calling out police reserves
to help light up.


The strikers union numbers about 400
men. These men are employees of the
Welsbach Lighting company, which
has contract to light streets where
there are no electric lights. They are
mainly Italians. They are striking for
recognition of the union.

MILAN, December 21-About fifty years
ago the then Prince Della Pescara mar
ried girl of extremely humble birth. and
Immediately afterward declared before
the tribunal that he had had a son by
her before the wedding. The boy was at
once recognized as legitimate. Suisse
quently the prince died. and his son in
herited the title and his fathers fortune,
estimated at S3,OOO,OG0. Some time after
her husbands death the princes widow
married again. after which his relatives
appealed to the courts, alleging that the
present prince is not the son of his re-
puted mother. The courts ordered that
the widow should undergo an examination
by specialists, who have now unanimously
affirmed that she has in reality never
given birth to a child. Thus Prince Della
Pescara loses his title, and his father S
relatives are now pursuing their case with
the object of depriving him also of his
millions.

NEW YORK, April 4.-Fire Chief Edward
Croker, Deputy Chief Guerin and thirty
in a fire in five-story building at $50
Maiden Lane just before dawn today.


All were hurt more or less, and four men
were badly injured and would have been
smothered under the falling ruins had not
their comrades dug them out, throwing
aside burning timbers and hot bricks with
bare hands. The badly injured men were all
members of hook and ladder company
No. Is.


The fire started in the house occupied by
William H. Sheel, dealer in varnishes and
gums. This house is in block of old build
ings where a fire has always been consid-
cred dangerous. All about it inflammable
goods are stored.


When the fire was discovered it had
eaten it's way through the roof, and the
block bounded by Maiden Lane, Fletcher,
South and Front streets was threatened.


Forced to Retreat.


When hook and ladder company No. Ii
arrived the house was broken into and the
men made their way up the ladders to the
fourth floor. The building was so hot they
were forced to retreat to the street


Then came engine company No. 4. The
firemen from the engine entered the lower
floor, when there came a back draught like
the bursting of many cannon. The walls
of the upper rooms fell and the roof
dropped to the fifth floor. The front walls
buried the firemen on the sidewalk, and at
the same time the doors of the building
were closed n the men from. engine No 4
hemming them in the burning building.


These men got out with difficulty, and as
they emerged they saw every fire horse
dash Off, frightened by the explosion and
the falling walls.


The firemen allowed the horses to 60

Four Men Buried.


The four men buried under the walls were
quickly dug out. Many Of their comrades
were bleeding from cut heads and bruised
bodies, and commanding them were Croker
and Guerin, both with bleeding heads, hav-
ing been struck by falling brick


The four men rescued, the work of put
ting out the fire was begun in earnest.
Croker would not let his men enter the
building, and they were ordered to fight il
from all sides. The fireboat New York
came to their aid, but the fire spread to
No. 157. and then to No. 161 Maiden Lane.
Before 1t was conquered $50,0OO damage to
property had been done.

Ground was broken yesterday for the
new plant of the City Gas company be-
tween Tenth and Twelfth street, on Santa
Fe avenue.


Operations were begun with smoke-the
only smoke which will mark the history
of the new enterprise, the officials say


1t was necessary to set fire to accumu-

fertilizer, carpet beating and other in
dustrial establishments.


ArEaed with shovels and rakes, forces

sump holes, ignited the oil and then
watched sharply for sparks and spreading
flames.


The minute the fire got too far out OF
reach piles of earth were thrown on the
flames to put them out.


In few hours all the surface oil pools
had been consumed and the work OF
plowing and excavating was started.


Lines of hose had also been laid from
nearby plugs, hose company No. 8 was or
duty, and the Densmore-Staffler refinery
people had their private hose lines out
and their employees on outside duty until
the snmp holes had been obliterated.


In order that the railroad ties would
not be burned, the spur track of the Santa
Fe company which leads into the City
Gas company's grounds was covered with
earth.


Over this track in the next few days
sixty carloads of materials will be dumped
for future use, the City company having
ordered steel piping and structural ma
terials months ahead, so that building OPP
erations would not be delayed when the
permits had been obtained


MANY of the directors and stoclholders
of the company, who number over fifty
were on hand to watch the first earth
turned for the enterprise which vii
eventually represent an investment Of
millions.


As many men and teams as can be
crowded on the grounds. which cover
nearly five acres, will be employed. Il

presence of mind of 6-year-old Zelma
Pierce saved the life of her 3-year-old
baby sister Zada, this afternoon.


The two little girls are the daughters
of C. M. Pierce, the Balloon route man.
They were playing doll house on the
float on the lagoon at the foot of the
boat landing.


Romping about too near the edge, little
Zada fell into eight feet of water.


As she fell the baby uttered cry.


Her sister saw her predicament and
promptly dropped fiat on the platform
with her arm stretched over the water.
AS Zada's head rose above the surface
Zelma grasped the golden cprls and as
tenderly as possible drawing her little
sister to the edge of the float, Zelma
pulled her up until her arms rested on
the boards.


Then with strong, vigorous tug she
brought her little sister safely to the
landing.


Beyond a thorough drenching and
fright the baby was none the worse for
her involuntary plunge.


Not a grown person was near when
the child fell into the water, and had
it not been for Zelma's presence of mind
the baby would have drowned.

For me terrestrial mountains rise;


For thee celestial rivers run;
My steps are meath familiar skies,


But thine in realms beyond the sun
This peaceful scene, that does not change,
This smiling vale, SO fair to see,
Those lonely plains. that mountain range
Z So glorious-all were known to thee.
For many a year, in shade or shine.


When life was gay when life was drear,
Thy friendly hand was clasped in mine
Thy form was oft beside me here.
Now. though sought through every land,
I should not feel. in any place,
The pressure Of thy loving hand,


Nor hear thy voice. nor see thy face.
So friendship fades, so love departs;


So living joy becomes a name
Shrin'd in the depth of breaking hearts,
And yet the world remains the same.
The roses bloom. the fields are green,


The branches wave, the streamlets flow
For Nature, ruffled or serene,


Is deaf and blind to human woe,
Thy mind to Beauty was subdued,
In Beauty's service thou vert blest--
Stern warrior in the bitter feud


That would not let thy spirit rest!
The feud that wakes angelic rage.


The war IN which so many tire,
The deadly strife that Art must wage


With mean intent and low desire.
Sleep sweetly, noble heart and true!


The tempest of thy life is Ger;
Nor baffled hope, nor pang OF rue.


Nor any grief can wound thee more!
Sleep sweetly. in that haIIow'd dell.


Far off, beside the solemn sea.
Where tears and prayers WILL constant, tell
The love that lives to mourn for thee.
There wild flowers, emblems OF thy soul,
Around thy tomb will bud and blow,
While Oceans melancholy roll


VIII chant thy requiem, soft and low.
There oft the pilgrims musing gaze


VIII linger on the votive stone
That mutely tells to future days


Thy power and charm, forever flown
And there, in golden time to come,


When all the clamor OF our day
Has sunk to silence, and the hum
OF vain detraction died away,
Fame's Angel hovring DER thy rest,
His amaranthne bough will wave,
Procaiming-Here lies Glorys guest.
Here Genius sleeps in Mansfield's grave!


William Winter, in New York Tribune.

PORT JERVIS, N. Y, April 49,
Boys living along the Delaware river
between Mast Hope and Tuston have
been having fine sport at herring fish
ing from holes in the river where they
had been imprisoned by the ice freez-
ing solid around them.


A big hole was discovered on Fri
day and the ice chopped around it.
The fish were so plentiful that they
made the water foam within. The
open air seemed to revive them. They
were hungry, too, and from the num-
ber of dead fish on the surface it was
evident they had become cannibals and
fed on one another.


Samuel Jones, years old, fell in the
hole, and before he was rescued the
fish, many of them pickerel, had torn
his trousers almost from his legs in
their savage frenzy for food.


Some of the pickerel taken from this
hole weighed five pounds each, while
many of the cells were of tremendous
length, averaging six pounds apiece.

ture, fought valiantly, but finally sank

cans expelled their rivals from the chapel,
but the victory was dearly bought. All the
holy vessels and lamps were broken and
the altar cloths were stained with blood.

ed an inquiry into the case.

SURAT, Bombay. Dec. 27-After two
days of futile efforts to elect a president

afternoon in a fight.


The congress was of special interest this
year owing to the agitation for home rule.
When the delegates assembled the mod
crate and Indian extremists at once
locked horns on this issue, and the meet
ing was adjourned amid much distorder


When they reassembled today their
anger broke loose again and the platform,
from which modera tion and constitutional
action had been advised, was rushed by
the extremists in body, who loudly de-
manded the speedy establishment of COM
plete home rule.


Chairs were broken in the scrimmage
and table legs and other pieces of shat
tered furniture were used by the dele
gates as bludgeons. Many delegates sus-
tanned serious injuries before the police
finally cleared the hall.

The unusually chilly spring of this year re-
calls other unreasonable seasons" ofthe past.
The year of 1916, the so-called 'year without
a summer" seems to have made the record in
this direction. In that year there was freezing
weather every month, and nothing but the
most hardy crops could be matured. The win
ter of that year was not remarkable, and the
month of April began with rather warm
weather, but grew colder as the month advan-
ced, and ended with much snow and ice all
over New England and the Middle States.
May was repetition of April, with ice half an
inch thick and corn entirely frozen. June af-
forded no relief. but had several visitations of
ice and snow, with almost every green thing
killed. There was nearly foot of snow in
Vermont, and quite snowfall also as far south
as Massachusetts. Even July had times of
frost and ice and still water froze over on sew
eral occasions. Corn which had been replant-
ed and secured new start was killed back
again, except in very sheltered and particularly
favorable localities.
headline: A Year without a summer.

SACRAMENTO, March 24-The news
from down river points received by the
Union this morning was far from en-
couraging. The idea abroad Satur-
day that the worst was passed in the
island districts was not not borne out
by developments.


Saturday night levees crumbled and
islands rich as the tabled gardens of
the Indies were inundated while the
people We're yet battling to save them.


Before noon today the telephone from
Courtland and Rio Vista had an
nounced the breaking of the levee of
Brannon island and that the flood that
poured in swept over the back levee Of
Andrus islnd and soon made of it an
inland sea.


Saturday night it was hoped that
Brannon and Andrus islands would be
saved and the announcement that the
Sherman island levees were high and
strong was received with satisfaction.
| Today little hope was had of holding
the Sherman island levees. Rio Vista
reported that the levee of Sherman is
land could keep out no more water and
that the river was rising, Nor was that
the worst.


Weather Observer Scarr stated upon
receipt of the news that the water at
that point would continue to rise. The
prospect for saving the big island in
the extreme southern part of Sacra-
mento county looked gloomy.


Further Disasters


On top of these disasters came word
from knights Landing, twenty-five
miles up the river, that Reclamation
District No. 10S, situated on the east
side of the Sacramento river, south of
Colusa, and extending thence south to
a point nearly opposite knights Land
ing, was being submerged rapidly
that late Saturday afternoon it's front
levee had gone out in at least one place
and that it was impossible to repair
the break. The district contains 75,-
600 acres of the richest land in the vail
ley, and it's levees collapsed in the big
flood in the early spring of 1904.


Reports from Courtland, thirty-five
miles down the river, were that there
was little change in the situation from
Saturday night. The Randall island
and Pierson district front levees were
still holding and there were hopes that
these would be saved. The Southern

THE growth of the population in this coun-


L try is speedily exterminating the wolves,
bears, coyotes, etc, which were such an an
noying and expensive pest few years ago.
Every State in the Union has at one time or
another offered bounties for the skins of such
animals. According to Government report,
incomplete returns show that two million four
hundred thousand dollars has been expended
annually in this manner. Six months after
the prairie dog and squirrel bounty law was
enacted in Montana in 1887, the treasury was
exhausted.


The great fault of such laws lay in the fact
that they afforded too much opportunity for
defrauding the Government In 1905 bounties
were paid on wolves and coyotes in the two
Dakotas, Montana, Wyoming and Iowa. The
rate, however, varied from dollar and half
in South Dakota to five dollars in Iowa, with
the result that most of the animals shot in
South Dakota were carried to Iowa for re-
demption, and those captured in North Dakota
were usually transported to Montana, where

SAN RAFAEL, Oct. 3.-Two

ternoon. The Marin company sent

ply. F. T. Howard, who put his water

ment of the county, and deal for the

OO1i llc Mai III COAlpdHy mas an

ing situation of Corte MADEIRA and

DANVILLE, Pa, July 12.-Death, sudden
and violent, came to Miss Agnes Hilda Gar
ger show girl, when she fell from
swiftly moving automobile on a country
road near this place at an early hour yes

she was riding, after picking up his injured
companion, and while she was breathing
her last, dashed for Danville at top speed
in search of the nearest medical assistance.
only to find on his arrival here that Miss
Garger was dead in his arms.


Miss Garger was playing here with a
carnival company. She was about twenty
1--WE years of age and most attractive. Mon
day night, after the performance, she, with
MIR. Owen in one car, and another member
of the carnival troupe, Miss Agnes McVey,
and Harry Cromwell, in another left for
the Oak Tree Hotel, a country roadhouse

ing. The party stayed at the Oak Tree
for several hours and left the hotel on the
return trip home.


Coming into Danville from the Oak Tree

was taking the grade at a good clip, when

when Owen recovered from the jolt he
found his companion missing. Backing his
car to the waterway he found Miss Gar
ger lying PROSTATE on the road.


The girl was still breathing. and Owen
placed her in the auto and with one arm
grasping the dying girl and the other on

with DEATH Before half of the distance be-

TIME story of Teddy Bear, major dome
of the nursery, guest of honor al
| Il bridge parties and owner of jeweled
| collars is not generally known to his


little playfellows and grown-up admirers.


Teddy's humble origin is in striking
contrast to his brilliant and world-re-
nowned career that has been crowded
with conquests quite enough to turn his
head But, like all truly great people,
his manner is modest and unassuming.
Inc first of his race was born In pic
turesaue village in Germany some hVe
years ago, his foster mother being
fiaxen-haired little girl, Fraulein Schmidt
who was very, very poor. One Christmas
eve fraulein's mother was disconsolate;
she hadn't enough money even to buy
little rosy-cheeked doll for Augusta, who
would surely expect such a gift from
Kris Kringle, but fortunately Frau
Schmidt possessed an inventive mind.


Rag babies Augusta had in plenty, but
a little bear made of brown flannel would
be surprise at least even If his eyes
were shoe buttons and the soles of his
feet made from scrap leather.


With native ingenuity Frau Schmidt
soon cut pattern of little bear from
brown flannel, sewed the pieces together
and filled him with bran -four A piece
of black cloth made presentable nose,
and altogether this creature was happy
looking specimen of his TRIBE.


On Christmas morning, when Augusta
awoke she found a queer little brown
creature in sitting posture under her
miniature Christmas tree that was decked
with birds and bright paper garlands her
mother had made. Her joy knew no
bounds, and Immediately she christened
him Teddy" prize of her nursery of rag
puppets.


Of course, Teddy had to go to school.
but he must be warmly clad for such
frosty weather. Frau Schmidt came to
the rescue and fitted Teddy with suitable
farments. These were knitted trousers,
a little coat and a Tam o'Shanter.


Naturally his advent at the village
school caused considerable excitement,
for nobodys doll could compare with this
wonderful Teddy bear, who went the
rounds of his admiring audience, resting
first on Gretchens arm then on johann
mas, and so on.


Soon the village children flocked to
Frau Schmidt's house to have her make
them Teddy bears just like Augustus,
they bringing varied materials with which
to make this new playfellow Soon, how
ever the thrifty frau realized that manu-
featuring Teddy bears was occupying too
much of her time and she concluded to
charge a very little for her services.


Being a toy making village, orders now
came to Frau Schmidt from factories not
only for Teddy bears made from f1annels,
but fur cloths, and these in turn were
dressed in the quaintest garb some in ma
tive costume, others typical of various oc-
equations.


There were wee little boy bears, middle
sized bears and big fellows almost the
size of live ones. These were shipped to
various countries, principally to America,
and everybody here is familiar with the
enthusiastic and lasting approval which
has been rendered to Teddy Bear.


Frau Schmidt no longer makes Teddy
bears, for her income is now a substantial
one, and the little girl for whom they
were made has graduated into knitting
class, but the original Teddy is among
her most priced possessions.

SAN JOSE, Aug. 26.-A boat contain
ing Miss Josephine Murphy. a school
teacher of this city. and Miss Kate Bel
lew, daughter of wealthy Milpitas
rancher, capsized in Coyote creek this
afternoon. Miss Murphy was drowned,
but Miss Bellew managed to swim
ashore


Miss Murphy was the guest of Miss
Bellew today at the Be1lew ranch.
which IS situated along the creek Dur
ing a stroll by the banks OF the stream
after luncheon they discovered an old
boat moored in the brush. They
clambered aboard and padded about
In the creek. which at this point is 40
feet wide and 15 feet deep.


Suddenly the young women noticed
that the boat was rapidly filling with
water and they started to turn it
around to row for the shore. They
were not much frightened, as both
could swim. While they were turning
the craft tipped over. 1t is thought



that Miss Murphy must have been
stunned. for she sank at once


Miss Bellew made. her way to the
bank successfully. Her screams at
tracted nearby residents to the spot
and they dragged the hole with. long
boat hook for Miss Murphy. They did
not bring the body to the surface until
several minutes had elapsed Several
hours were spent in trying to resusci-
tate her, but all efforts were unavailing.
Miss Murphy was graduate of the
Hopkins institute of art, San Francisco.
and taught drawing and painting in
the Sunol Hester school In this city for
several years. She also spent two
years at painting with the artist, Rollo
Peters.

There was a strangely lucky accident
in the Lackawanna Railroads tunnel
through Bergen Fill. just west Of Hoboken,

was as bad as II felt. He went home when

bones were broken.

NEW YORK, January 1O.-Almoet within


rifle fire of the lamp posts Of New York


streets, yet SO far from shelter and aid that


they might have been modern Crusoes,


three men lay freezing on the barren rocks


Of Berrian's Island, in Little He'll Gate yes


terday. When, after five hours upon the


water and wind-swept reef, rescuers finally


came and saved them, the castaways were


half dead from cold and exhaustion. In a


short time all would have persisted of ex-
posture.


The three victims are Edward Kankau-
suer Of 1918 Avenue A, Charles Stretmut-
ter, his neighbor, and George Woerehing of
zoos LIST avenue. Kankausuer bought
thrty-f foot naphtha launch from a man at
10th street and the Harlem river a few
days ago, and yesterday, with his two
friends, he set out from the Morrisania
Yacht Club house on South Brother Is
land in a ten-foot skin to tow his purchase
back.


Desperate Pull Against Wind.


They hitched a hawser to the launch and


with two pairs of oars started the long two


and-a-half-mile pull against wind and tide


to the clubhouse Entering Little He'll Gate


on Lawrence Point, there came a blow Of
sudden wind that reeled both skiff and
launch hard over on their sides and shipped
a lot of water. After that every foot
gained was struggle. The tide swept out
faster, the breeze turned to a half gale and
though they all took turns at the oars and
the bailing can they could make no head
way toward the island.


While still off Lawrence Island the
launch rolled in the trough of the sea- and
the hawser parted with a snap that nearly
capsized the skiff ahead. Promptly the
naphtha boat was hurled against the island


reefs and the three men We're SO exhausted
that they had not strength to pull her off.
Instead they started in their row boat
trying to beat their way to South Brother
Island without their tow. But the wind
and sea kept rising, the little craft took in


more water than they could BAIL and finally
was swept over near the rocks that grid
Berrians deserted island off Mount Morris.
1t was case of swimming ashore
twenty feet of land. Kankausuer the
strongest swimmer and the least exhausted
of the three, got his companions ashore
after terrific struggle. 1t was then IL 80
O'Clock.


Only One Dry Match.
Weak from their battle with the waves
| their clothes drenched and freezing to their
| bodies, the three men up and down the
| little island suffering terribly for two hours
Then Stretmutter found match box in
his coat pocket and the last match proved
dry. With drift wood they kinded a fire
and warmed themselves about it while it
lasted Two Of them removed their coats
HolSteu THEM on Tree branches and waved
for hours before the signal was seen by any
of the many passing tugs.


Finally, when the castaways were nearly
frozen again and about ready to throw
themselves upon the rocks to await death
Capt. Kelgins of the New York, New Haven
and Hartford tug, passing up the East
river footed his whistle to show that he
had seen the signals and would send aid
His tug drew too deeply to approach the
island, but he steamed over to the Port
Morris side and notified the police.
From pier A roundsman and two police


men of the harbor squad started out to the
rescue. They were Roundsman Wittlaufer
| Heaiey, and they went in little police
launch.


Rescuers Lose Oars.
All this time they could see the three
castaways who cried out to them to hurry


or it would be too late. There were no


more matches and only the proximity of the
life savers spurred them in their struggle to
fight off the benumbing cod. The police
hurried, but halfway in from the launch
their oars broke, leaving them helpless.
But with his broken oar for a paddle
Roundsman WHITAKER managed to reach
boathouse near Steinway creek, a mile
| away from the marooned men.


Here new oars were found and the DO
licemen returned again to the rescue.
The three men were almost unconscious.
Arrived at the New York side they were
hurried to Lebanon Hospital, where treat
ment restored them in few hours and
they were finally able to go home.

The Herald is anxious that every boy
and girl in Los Angeles should enjoy
the beautiful trip around the Balloon
route. To this end The Herald has made
arrangements with c. M. Pierce, manager
of the Balloon route excursions, by which
every boy and girl will have the chance
to make this trip free.


Any bright boy or girl who has never
enjoyed the beauties of the seventy-mile
run in comfortable observation cars, with
jolly guides to point out places of interest,
should not miss this exceptional oppor-
tunity. Twenty-eight miles of this in
comparable trip are along the ocean
front, and stops are made at the various
beaches, giving time to see the chief
points of interest.


The cars start from the corner Of
Fourth and Hill streets every morning at
$40 o'clock From that point they pass
through the business section of the town
and out past the historic old Spanish
plaza with it's ancient chapel, through
Chinatown, past Sonoratown and out by
the oil feds.


Through the center of beautiful Holly
wood, Los Angeles most aristocratic
suburb, through the picturesque towns
of Sherman, Sawtelle, Santa Monica the
excursionists are conducted.


At Sherman the car stops and the Los
Angeles Pacific company's shops, at Saw
telle a side trip is made to the National
Soldiers home, where 3400 veterans are
enrolled.


Free Attractions offered


The route of travel on the ocean front
lies through the beach towns of Santa
Monica, Ocean Park, Venice, Playa del
Rey. Moonstone Beach and Redondo.,


At Santa Monica the camera obscura
is one of the free attractions provided
for the excursionists.


Ocean Park with its beautiful bunga-
lows, great auditorium and bath house.
Venice of America with it's canals resem-
bling old Venice LII Italy and it's count
less other attractions; Moonstone Beach,
where moonstones are found; Redondo
with its shipping scene, provide variety
of entertainment that appeals to the
sightseer.


Accompanying the excursion is a cour-
teous guide, who explains all points of
interest throughout the entire trip. c.
M. Pierce is the manager of this now
famous excursion, which gives any one
the opportunity of seeing the city, noun
tains and sea all day for dollar.


The Herald proposes to put this beauti-
full trip within the reach of every boy
and girl in Los Angeles. Here is your
chance.


Any boy or girl securing three prepaid
65 cents each. for one month
to the Los Angeles Herald will be given
one of these round trip tickets over the
Balloon route excursion. For blanks and
further information call at Herald office.


Excursions leave daily from S16 West
Fourth street.

An evening stroll around Ballarat, Ben
digo, or any other Australian golden center
has an excitement peculiar to itself You
never can tell when you may drop down an
abandoned shaft into the bowels Of the
earth. During the f1fties and sixties-the
period of the great ''rushes thousands of
these shafts were sunk, varying in depth
from 30 feet to 500 feet. Some of them have
been filled up. but the great majority still
yawn for unwary pedestrians. The latest
Australian papers record three cases of peo-
pie falling down these shafts. They were
all rescued alive, one after five days i'm
prisonment and starvation. Accidents of
this sort are seldom fatal. The accumulat-
ed mud and water at the bottom of the
shaft break the fall. The special providence
that watches over drunken persons is also
a frequent life preserver.

SAN FRANCISCO, Dec. 4.-Peter Ster-
ling justified the favoritism shown him
in the betting for the fourth race, the
Berkeley handicap, at Oakland today, by
making the five horses opposed to him
ook, cheap and winning as Jockey More
land pleased. Sterling was taken along
under pace furnished by Dollie Dollars,
and when the real going was reached
simply breezed along to win by two and
a half lengths.


The first rainfall of the season was
recorded today and after the first race
the track had a sloppy appearance. While
fast time will now be cut out, the sprinkle
will be for the best as many horses rae
ing here were suffering because of the
too hard going OF the past three weeks.


Sereneity was the longest priced win
ner of the day. some of the books laying
as good as ten to one against her
chances. Peter Sterling. Blondy and
Heather Scott were the winning favorites,
a second choice and a well-played third
choice taking the other events.

SAN FRANCISCO, March About 1900
men and 300 teams turned out yesterday
and made a big success of the first public
street cleaning record. More was done
in ten hours by volunteers than had been
done in the ten months since the fire. Bust
ness men shoveled dirt side by side with
men in overalls who work every day at
cleaning brick.


BugIers from the Preside sounded the
call to work at o'clock. The city had
been districted and under good managers
the work of sweeping the streets and cart
ing away the dirt went along lively. Be
fore noon 1t was clear that the wagons
could not keep pace with the cleaners, and
when work ended at night there were hum
dreds of loads Of dirt which will have to be
removed.


The street in front Of police headquarters
was cleaned expeditiously by prisoners who
were arrested Saturday night for drunken
ness. When they had swept the street
clean they were allowed to go. Along Mont
gomery street, formerly one of the worst In
the city for dirt. financiers. brokers and
real estate men turned out with their full
office force of clerks and soon had the
thoroughfare well cleaned.


Thirty eating stations were established in
various parts of the burned district and
these were attended by prominent women
who had volunteered to look after feeding
the workers. Even cigars were handed out
to all who worked. Take 1t all in all 1t was
unique experience in city cleaning, and
it's democracy recalled the days Of the great
calamity.

DARBY, Pa, Aug. "A two months
old kitten saved Dorothy and Eobert
Clutch, aged and.5 years, from being
bitten by a snake this morning, which
came wriggling down the trunk of a
hundred-year old tree in the yard of
their home, 934 Main street. The chill
dren were playing in the yard when
they saw the snake, which was about
four feet long, come gliding down the
tree. Not knowing their danger, the
children ran over to the serpent, which
was about three feet from the ground,
and were about to pick it up in their
hands when the little kitten seing the
moving object on the tree trunk, clam
bered up after it and pulled it to the
ground.


There the snake wrapped itself around
the kitten, which promptly lay on it's
back and clawed vigorously at it's en-
emy. The children rushed into the
house, shouting that the kitty was
playing with a big worm,' but nothing
was thought of it until several min
utes later, when they came in again
and eXcitedly said that the big worm
was choking "kittv' to death.


Investigation showed that the cat was
holding it's own, and had the reptile
clawed and bitten, but the make was
drawing its coils more closely around
the brave little pet and would have
chicken it to death within few min
utes.


Armed with clothes props and brooms
the cftildren's mother and grandmother
attacked the snake and after five min
utes compelled it to relinquish its hold
on the kitten, which had to be held
from continuing the attack, while the
snake crawled rapidly away.


The kitten was badly stung on the
right foreleg, which soon swelled to
three times it's natural size. 1t may
have to be killed. Three years ago a
snake slightly longer fell from a tree in
the front yard of the residence of Rich
ard Purdy, next door. but escaped.

BY Associated Press.


ST. PETERSBURG, Sept. 1.-For the
second time since Red Sunday, January
49, Emperor Nicholas today entered the
citadel to attend the conservation of
church to the memory of his grandfather,
Alexander the Second. who was assass-
mated in March, 1881, on the spot where
the edifice was raised. The date OF the
trip coincident with the conspiracy trial
just closed here, mainly was designed to
raise the loyalty of the army and the
people. 1t was complete surprise and
no untoward incident occurred.


The police neglected no precautions to
insure the safety of the emperor and
even went so far as to thoroughly search
the city and inspect the passports Of sus-
picious- individuals. Gendarmes were sta
toned In every window facing the rer1te
over which the imperial family passed
and owners of houses were forbidden to
open windows under pain of fine.
. Bridge and river traffic was entirely
suspended; the bank of the Neva were
lined with marine guides, and torpedo
boats patrolled the river The imperial
party arrived from Peterhof unan-
.nounced, not single salute being fired
during their whole stay.


The emperor was in excellent spirit,
but the empress had the same careworn,
said look that has been remarked so
often.


The emperor wore simple uniform
with a dark blue tunic. The empress was
gowned in white silk and wore a white
ostrich feather in her hat and a string Of
diamonds Both their majesties remained
standing throughout the entire ceremony,
which lasted three and quarter hours.
After the ceremony the imperial party
left for a cruise on the gulf Of Finland.

summer home OF Albert c. Burrage of Boston
the we'll known 1nancier and copper mine owner
Burrage. their four children. Mrs. Burrage's
sister, Miss Sally Haskell. and six servants, man.
aged to escape from the burning building with
what clothing they could lay their hands on
The loss is estimated at upward of $4,000.


To the heroism and presence of mind of Miss
Haskell is attributed the safety of the other
twelve persons who were at the estate The
fire, apparently caused by an overheated fur
mace. broke out when all the members of the
household were in bed Miss Haskell awak-
ened by smoke and the cracking of flames

awakened every one in it. All escaped without
injury but the only things saved were such
scanty clothing as they could snatch in their
hurried departure

was valued at $4,000 It stood about two miles
from the centre of the village and was richly
furnished The furnishings were estimated to
be worth more than $4,000 and ten trunks
filed with expensive clothing that Mrs. Burrage
had just brought back from Europe also were
destroyed The family had been at The Needles
for only eight days


The town has fire fighting apparatus and
il was impossible to check the fire that was rag
ing through the house almost before II was dis
covered. The stable and garage were saved by
neighbors, who formed bucket brigades.

A sea covered with oranges is one
of the unusual attractions near Ven-
tura, Cal, at the mouth of the Santa
Clara river. Thousands upon thou
sands of oranges floating on the
oceans surface, many of them strew-
ing the beach, give an indescribably
beautiful golden hue to the sea-


There are wonder for some time as
to how the oranges got into the sea.
The belief was general that they came
from washed out orchards in the east
end of the county, owing to the high,
storm waters in the river This is not
the case, however. The oranges were
deliberately thrown into the Sespe
creek from the Sespe bridge, 25 miles
back from the coast From the Sespe
they found their way back into the
Santa Clara river and thence into the
sea.


The oranges are from the great
packing houses in the Sespe country.
They are known as culls, but most
Of them are good, or were when
dumped off the bridge. 1t is claimed
that only the best oranges can be
shipped and sold.

sweeping the northern part of the pier

| from end to end, and the tremendous
| seas which washed over the Berlin from,
bow to stern quickly battered her to

at the mercy OF the wind and waves
Huge rollers struck her and carried off
the deck gear and swept some of the
passengers into the churning waters

A further brilliant idea came to Carter
next morning that after all he and White
Man s-Trouble had been raising difficulties
about the rivers navigation that were quite
unnecessary. There was a village of
tives close at their door who were river
farers. What was more likely than that
there were many men there who could pilot
canoe through a chain of creeks till at
last they heard tie great Atlantic surf
roaring on a river par?


White Man s-Trouble shook his head
when he heard the suggestion. Dem BUSH
men savvy nothing" said he contempt
uously.


Upon experiment it proved that he was
right The villagers had acquired the habit
of fishing on the reaches which ran two
miles up stream and two miles down; they
had adopted the customs of their forefath-
ers: no one of them had ever padded be-
yond these limits. They were an incurious
people.


Their canoes were small and narrow and
unweldy. They were dug out from cotton
wood trees with fire, and dubbed into vague
shape with native AIDES, and through sheer
idleness and incapacty the builders had
rarely selected straight timber. Even ex-
pert polers and paddlers could not propel
those miserable craft in straight course
One thing only were these fishers good at,
and that was baling. But in this they had
abundant practice, for all the canoes were
sun-cracked, and leaked like baskets


Il wish" said Carter, for a great raft
that will carry twelve tons of the shiny
stones which fall from the mountain.


They did not know what raft was,
neither did they appreciate the size of
ton. but Carter demonstrated to them, and
White Man s-Trouble kept them from for
getting The Krooboy had found chiquot,
and, from having felt chiquots across all
parts of his own person many time, was
well qualified to WELD such a baton of
authority. Carter picked out suitable cot
ton woods, and the Krooboy apportioned
out the cutters and stayed beside them till
their work was done.


They handspiked the logs down to the
water, again having to be instructed in
this most elementary piece of mechanics,
laid cross-pieces at right angles and dashed
all tightly together with lanes. Then
when they had built up the interstces be-
tween the logs with large pieces of tin
stone. they carried down the smaller
in baskets till the logs were sunk to three
quarters draught


Next they built house the raft and
covered 1t with thatch, and in part of the
house they piled great store of dried fish
as provision for the voyage. And all the
while the ju-ju organ behind them doomed
out at intervals its dismal boo-paa-b umm,
bumm- paa-boo.

A carriage containing mourners at
the funeral of Mrs Annie Fitzpatrick
was struck by "a McAIlister-stree car
at 1915 o'clock yesterday afternoon
and almost demolished. The horses
were rolled over and over along the
track for a distance of forty feet be-
fore the car was stopped, the driver
was pitched from his seat and. while
the occupants of the vehicle were not
seriously hurt, they were hysterical
from fright. A large crowd gathered
around the carriage and the car and
became so threatening that riot call
was turned in.


The funeral procession was passing
along Buchanan street when the car,
No. 73S. rushed toward the crossing
with great speed. Witnesses of the
accident declared that the motorman
made no effort to stop after he saw
the carriages filing past ahead. A
woman and a child stood on the corner
signaling for the car to stop for them,
but the motorman paid no attention.
The car caught the carriage while 1t
was squarely across the track, and,
with a crash of splintering wood and
amid the shrieks of women and the
cries of men, showed it forty feet along
the pavement The horses reared and
plunged, fell down and were dragged
by the harness. Spectators rushed for
the wrecked vehicle TO pull from the
debris what they supposed would be
senseless forms, but by miracle the
occupants were not injured beyond a
few scratches and bruises.


Inside the carriage were Daniel
Fitzpatrick. whose wife's dead body
lay in the hearse ahead; Lena Fitzpat-
rick. his niece, and Annie and Lille
Saunders. They were assisted to a
nearby store. where they were given
medical attention, and while this was
going on a serious situation was devel-
oping in the neighborhood of the car.


People living along McAllister street
have long complained of the failure of
the cars to stop when signaled, and
when they saw what had occurred they
hurried to the scene.z Numerous threats
were made.


When the accident occurred the fun
eral procession was on the way to ST.
Michaefs Church, Ocean View, where
the services were to be held. After
another carriage was secured for the
mourners the procession moved slowly
onward again.


Flynf, the driver. was injured inter-
nally and was taken to the City Hos
pital.

NEW YORK, October IAN unidentified

have have had on had seen taken Her money


The wounds from which she must have

this point.


There was a body wound high up near

From the wound in the breast, which

a knife blow, there were trac-S of blood,
apparently fresh. These, however, were
the only traces upon the body. The
clothing and hands of the young woman
We're entirely free from blood stains.


Indications pointed to the fact that the
young woman had met her death only a
short time before her body was found.


The woman was about thirty years old
and of medium height. She was dressed
entirely in black, with black shirt waist,
black skirt and black shoes and stock
ings. Her clothing was of good material,

a mammoth black bear and three cubs,
which were alternating there.


Weeks and his son attacked the bears
and after a struggle succeeded in killing
two of the cubs. BY this time the mother
bear had escaped from the nest. She ap-
peared slightly dazed from her long i'm
prisonment, but realized her danger and
started into the woods. She was followed
by the third cub, which was not injured by
the men, and the latter did not chase the
fugitives.


The carcasses weighed about one hundred
pounds each and the cubs were apparently
about ten months old. The men stated
that the mother bear stood nearly eight feet
in height when erect. and that she must
weigh between four hundred and five hun
dred pounds.

SAN FRANCISCO, Cal. January 5.-The
fact that four life rats from the Pacific
mail steamer City of Panama came ashore
yesterday at Waddells Beach, twelve miles
north of Santa Cruz led to assumption that
the Panama liner had been wrecked. But
investiga ton today showed pretty clearly
that no other wreckage had come ashore
between Santa Cruz and Pescadero The
officials of the Pacific Mail Company. as
well as marine experts of San Francisco
all unite in the opinion that a heavy sea
washed off the life RATS that came ashore
from the upper deck of the City of Panama.
but that the mail steamer herself was un-
injured.


This theory is based on the fact that the
City of Panama was spoken to on New
Year day about noon by the Standard Oil
tank steamer Maverick, from New York
fully fifty miles below the point where the
life RATS came ashore The Maverick ex-
changed holiday greetings with the City of
Panama and no mention was made of any
accident on board of the liner. The weather
was fine and the City of Panama was max
ing good time. The fact that bareback and
water were found on the life RATS does not
show that the RATS were launched. Since
the disaster to the steamer WalIa Walla on
the Oregon coast, all life RATS and life
boats have been provisioned. The law also
requires that the lashngs must be freed
and then tied again and the theory is the
RATS were not secured.

PITTSBURG, June pas one result of a
trifiing joke two men fought here Saturday
the worst duel in or out of the code-the
duel with white-hot iron bars. They were
Louis Yurick and Adam Buick former
cavalrymen and experts in fence. They
fought in the mills of the Carnegie Steel
Company, where all work stopped as the
other men rushed to watch the battle. but
not to interfere where the points of white
hot iron were in play.


Stout as were the two contesting rolling
mill men. the burns and the effort of swing
ing the heavy bars-for this was broad
sword combat-told on them and they sank
exhausted after five minutes, SO their fell
lows were able then to rush in and take
away the sizzling bars.


After the nights work Saturday Yurick
threw himself down on bench in front
of his furnace and was soon fast asleep.
Buick took Yurick's shoes and hid them.
When Yurick awoke he was in a bad
humor. He accused Buick of having taken
his shoes and Buick admitted it. Yurick
instantly seized cold bar from the floor
and started after the joker. Buick seized
another and defended himself, blow for
blow. Yurick became Infatuated as a result
of blows and. lea ping to the furnace pulled
out white.hot bar.


I Before he could attack Buick the latter
also pulled one of the bars out of the fur
mace and rushed on Yurick. The original
assailant, now on the defensive turned
viciously and swung the eight-foot bar in
circle about him, Buick had to fall ba ok
TO avoid him and the crowd of workmen
that had been drawn by the combat fell
back, too. With the white-hot iron circling
him. it seemed like counting death for
every one concerned to attempt to seize him.
The crowd left ring for the combatants
and Buick, advancing with his bar, forced
Yurick into direct combat. In a second
they were handling the bars like two-hand-
ed Japanese swords


Each time the bars came together there
was shower of sparks and each time one
OF the bars touched the opposing fencer
there was an Odor of burned flesh For
fully five minutes the two men fenced. The
bars slowly cooled as the mems strength
waned. but were still redhot. when the
two finally fell from exhaustion.


Each man had many severe scars when
the battle ended. A patrol wagon was hur-
riedly called and both men were taken to
the Jail hospital.

gowns of chiffon, and gowns of lace;
walls draped in American flags. the ma
tionaI emblem. and navy ensigns were the

Admirals and ensigns, generals and sec

Meanwhile the line Of general guests, con

FEW people know that the number of hairs
in the human head varies largely according
to color. Taking four heads of human hair of
different colors, but of equal weight, it has been
found that the number of hairs to the head
varies as follows: Red, ninety thousand;
black, one hundred and three thousand brown,
one hundred and nine thousand; blond, one
hundred and forty thousand. Red hair is
usually the coarsest.

lows: Red haired people, thirty; black, sixty

brown three hundred and thirty-eight; and
dark brown, eight hundred and seven.

inch in width.

ist.

men were taken from the water they
had been carried far down the stream
and were exhausted.

The needed improvements to the Cap
uol that have been in progress for several
years have continued during the last fiscal
year.


Mahogany revolving doors have been
placed at five of the principal entrances
to the basement story and at the east ro-
tunda entrance. The utility of these doors
was fully demonstrated during the past
winter. especially at the north and west
entrances, where much difficulty was eN-
perienced in keeping the ordinary doors
closed during hard winter storms. Pro-
vision has been made for installing re-
volving doors at the remaining entrances
to the basement story and also at the en-
frances to the principal story. Fifteen
pairs of mahogany doors have been
placed at committee and other rooms in
the place of the pine doors put up when
the building was first occupied.


'In the Senate and House restaurant
kitchens radical changes have been made.
The floors have been reconstructed of con-
crete and tile. new sanitary plumbing has
been installed, thing has been placed on
the side walls. large permanent refrger-
ators of the most modern type have been
built, and new portable refrigerators.
cooking ranges, other necessary furniture.
and large exhaust fan have been added.
These Kitchens are now as complete and
sanitary as any In the country.


Additions have been made to the por-
ton Of the auxiliary draft of chimneys
over the Supreme Court section of the
Capitol.


Last year there were removed from the
walls of the rotunda the several coats of
paint which had been put on the sand
stone, and the rotunda section is now re-
stored to its original appearance. During
the past year the same work was done i'm
Statuary Hall. which was the old Hall of
Representatives.. The old stairway lead
ing from the basement and principal
stories has been restored and now admits
the visitor to the gallery of the hall. The
same restoration has been made to the
stone work in the corridor entrance to the
Supreme Court and in the crypt, and the
forty columns of the crypt now show the
original beauty of this masterful work.


Painting of the Dome.


The dome. which had not been painted
for several years. has been thoroughly
gone over. Joints and openings have been
carefully covered with proper material.
and the whole has been painted with spe-
cially prepared paint, which it is believed
will add very much to it's resistance to the
elements well as to its appearance.
Repairs to ceilings and porticoes have
also been made.


THE exterior central portion of the
Capitol has again been painted as before
In order to preserve the sandstone OF
which 1t is constructed.


In nine of the terrace committee rooms
the old wooden floors have been replaced
by floors of concrete. which are not only
more durable. but sanitary. The sashes
and frames of the windows throuhout the
building have been painted. During this
year, as for several years past, progress
has been made in the substitution of
more modern type or plumbing. new
toilet for public use has been installed in
one of the terrace rooms in the Senate
wing. Repairs to roofs, guttering and
skylights have been made. Several mar
BILE hearths have been set in committee
rooms. and marble thresholds have been
laid in the Senate lobby. Seventy-five
committee and other rooms have been
painted OF decorated. corridors have been
painted and repairs have been made to
the frescoing. During the year sXty-siN
important and 10 minor repairs have
been executed throughout the building.


AT engine house No. 3 and al the Sem
ate and House stables necessary repairs
