STOCKTON, March 1S.-The streams
in the vicinity of Stockton are rising.
The San Joaquin is coming up fast,
but is not at dangerous stage. Re
ports from the mountains tonight are
that the storm has been very heavy
along the watersheds of the Calaveras,
Stanislaus and Tuolumne rivers. and
much higher water is looked for to-
morrow. The flood waters of the
Stanislaus and Tuolumne rivers arose
seven feet today. Reports from Sonora
are that the rainfall today was the
heaviest of the winter. All of that
water will reach the San Joaquin River
south of Stockton probably tomorrow
night. None of the streams here are
dangerously high, but they cannot
carry much more water. and there is
a prospect for a higher stage tomor-
row. 1t is raining hard here tonight.


The American River Electric Com
pany's plant near Placerville. which
generates electricity used in Stockton
for operating the Central California
Street Railroad lines and for illumi-
mating part of the city. was closed
down today by the great flood that
came down the American River and at
o'clock this evening the service was
cut off here. The plant was located
high above any possible danger, it
was thought, but the water is over
the switchboard in the power house
and the food is unprecedented. Stock
ton has another electric system, the
old one owned by the Stockton Gas
and Electric Company. which is not
affected by the storm. and only the Gus
toners of the American River company
are disturbed at this time.

SCRANTON, Pa, March 2-Fourteen
men are lowering near death in Taylor
Hospital and twelve others suffered slight
burns through a terrific explosion Of gas
that swept through a portion of the Clark
vein of the Holden mine Of the Delaware,
Lackawanna and Western Company at
North Taylor this afternoon.


Whether or not thirty other miners at
work in the affected section escaped was
in doubt up to 10 o'clock tonight, when
Mine Inspector David Williams felt safe in
saying they were all out of the mine and
alive. This statement he made only after
it was possible for searching parties to
make tour of the affected parts of the
mine and who returned with the report
that they could find men in the workings
who had been reported missing. Still this
news was not reassuring to hundreds who
still gathered about the shafts head for
the doubt and fears of the afternoon and
evening were not removed, and they felt
certain that there were yet others whose
lifeless bodies would be found later.


Severely Injured.


Among the seriously injured are:


William Williams, miner, of Taylor.


Thomas Williams, his son, miner.


Daniel Evans, door tender.


VIM. Beavans, runner.


Andrew Ranski, iaporer, of Old Forge


Frank Ransld, Andrews brother, miner.


Daniel ]. Evans, miner.


John Hill, miner.


The great force of the explosion was felt
on the barn road that leads from the main
gangway to the mule barn. This was
fully q half mile from the foot of the shaft.
The roadway was strewn with the debris
of battered doors and brattice work, which
so obstructed the air courses that for some
hours it was impossible for the rescusing
forces to penetrate into the dense after
damp.


Caused Panic.


The first news of the explosion caused
panic in Taylor, and it's seriousness spread
into Hyde Park and Mineoka, where lived
many of the men working at the mine.
There was great apprehension as to their
fate. Hundreds hurried to the mine and
special train sent from Scranton with AS
sistant Superintendent Tobey. Washeres
Superintendent Smith, District Superintend-
ent Evans, Mine Inspector Williams and
the fire bosses and foremen of the Dia-
mond, Bellevue and Dodge mines on board.
They reached the Holden mine within a
half hour and found that four of the burned
men were then in the emergency hospital
at the foot of the shaft receiving the first
aid of the mine forces. These men were
| soon hoisted and hurried away to the Tay-
lor Hospital. Then others were brought out
until fourteen had been carried to the hos
pital and twelve others were sent to their
homes.


Some of the worst burned were devoid of
any clothing when the rescuers found their
blistered and blackened forms, the ex-
blossoms force having been so great as
to tear ne clothing completely from them.

THAkI, the olive colored canvas cloth worn
N by soldiers in hot climates, owes its pres
ent use to lucky accident, is the case with
many inventions. This cotton stuff has been
worn in India by British troops for many
years. Its tint was greenish brown; but it
always faded when it was washed with SOAP


A business man from Manchester, while
travelling in India, CHANGED to enter into
conversation with an English officer, who
remarked carelessly that the first manufac-
turer who could produce a cotton drill that
would not fade would make his fortune


The young Englishman never forgot this
hint. He came home, found skilful DYER
and with him began the search for an olive
dye which, when used on cotton cloth, would
not yield to soap or soda. They spent years
in these experiments, all of which proved
fruitless.


One day they found among several scraps
of dyed cloth one which retained its color
under the most severe tests The puzzling
fact was that it had been cut from the same
piece of cloth and subjected to the same
processes as the other scraps, all of which
faded. The two experimenters were greatly
perplexed and for months tried in vain to
solve the riddle. The one little fragment of
khaki was the only one which kept its color
against all attacks.


By chance day they found that the dye
in which this scrap had been dipped had
remained for time in metal dish of peculiar
kind. The secret was found. The metal of
the dish, in combination with the chemicals
of the dye, had furnished the one thing
needful. They tried the experiment with
other pieces. The dye held, and their fortunes
were made.

C. Schroeder. first officer OF the
schooner John G. North. had a thrill
ing experience during that vessels re-
cent trip down the coast.


He fell overheard. and as he fell he
grabbed the log line. and for two
hours held onto the cord while the
ship sped swiftly onward.


Schroeder was buneted about by the
seething pillows, and dashed here and
there until he was hauled safely on
board again.


The accident took place on New
Years day. when the schooner was off
Cape Blanco, when she ran into
terrible hurricane. which nearly threw
the vessel onto her beam ends.
Schroeder was trying to cross the deck.
when wave struck the craft and
swept him over the stern. AS he
plunged into the sea he grabbed the
log line. He shouted for help, but
the fury of the gale drowned his cries.


The captain and crew were so busily
engaged in trying TO right the vessel
that the plight of Schroeder was not
noticed, and two hours elapsed before
they began to look for him.


Meanwhile the storm had somewhat
abated and the vessel had been prop
erly trimmed. Search for the missing
mate began and a faint cry was heard
over the stern. Captain Nelson, rush
ing back, was astonished to see
Schroeder trailing on behind the ship.
clinging to the log line.


The schooner was hove to and
Schroeder hauled on deck. He was al
most exhaused, but after few hours
rest was able to resume his duties.
When he arrived here yesterday he APP
peared to be none the worse for his
dreadful experience.


The storm found by the schooner
lasted about ten hours, and Captain
Nelson says 1t was the worst he ever
experienced on this coast.


During the gale the deck load OF
lumber was more or less shifted


The North was eight days making
the run from Cosmopolis to this port.


She brought 400 900 feet of lumber.

LONDON, August 31.-The stock ex-
change started the week full of promise
for moderate boom and revival, but fin
ished dull, with prices considerably below
the best for the week. The feature of the
six days trading was Secretary Cortel-
yous announcement regarding deposits in
New York banks, which considerably eased
tile monetary situation everywhere and
dispersed the fears Of further rise in the
London bank rate, and this in turn caused
a general buying movement. Consols and
frst-class British securities advanced
steadily until the week end, when the buy
ing, which appeared to be largely profess
sionai, slackened with general profit-taking
and movement ensued which caused a
sharp reaction from the best prices of the
week. although the final rates were much
higher than Friday of last week.


Foreign bonds shared in the upward
movement, the clearer monetary situation
reviving confidence in Paris and Berlin, and
support from these cities came more freely.


Americans were supported on the better
monetary outlook. but business throughout
ing to fears of cuts in railroad dividends
and the absence of a decided lead from
Wall street. Later the announcement of
the Erie dividend and reports that impor-
tant financial interests intended to support
the market caused better feelings, but fall
ed to stimulate activity. The market closed
quiet and firm, with net gains from 81
to 81.


Money has been easily obtainable
throughout the week at about 21a per cent.
Secretary Corte!you's announcement had a
reassurng effect on the money market, and
weakened discounts considerably. This per-
mitted the placing of American trade bills
here at easier rates. The weaker discounts
caused adverse movements from the for
eign exchanges London, making pos
sible continental competition for the $3,-
100000 in gold available Monday.

BY Associated Press.


MILWAUKEE,. Dec. SO.-Hugo Kelly Of
Chicago and Billy Papke of Spring VAL
ley, ILL.,, fought ten fierce rounds to
draw before the Badger A. @. tonight.


Both fighters started in hammer and
tongs fashion at the first tap Of the gong,
using right and left with frightful effect
Kelly knocked Papke down, the Spring
Valley boy taking advantage of the
count.


The first round was easily Kellys The
second round ended with honors even,
Kelly having the first half and Papke
evening up In the last half. In the third
round Papke drew blood from Kelly's
right eye and Kelly in turn jabbed
Papke's face, also drawing blood the
round ending with an even break.


The fourth round was easily Paqke's
he having fioored Kelly with vicious
right to the body, following this up with
rights and lefts to the face with good
effect and drawing blood freely.


The fifth round was fast and furious for
the first half, both fighters easing up to-
ward the end, Kelly seeming to have the
better of the round


Both men bored in with rights and
lefts to the head and body in the sixth,
Kelly uppercutting with good effect
Papke slipped to the floor in this round
but recovered without losing any ground
Honors were even.


The seventh round was Papke's Kelly
being well winded at the end.


In the eighth Kelly did considerable
clinching and seemed very weary, but at
this point the honors were standoff.


The fight in the ninth looked very much
like decision for Papke, who had Kelly
wobbly from fusillade of rights and
lefts and uppercuts to the body and head,
the gong alone saving the Chicago man.


In the last round Kelly came up strong
and evened up any advantage scored by
Papke up to that time. Kelly used right
and left with good effect, keeping up a
hot pace until the gong sounded, leaving
nothing for the referee to do but to de-
clare the bout draw.


The decision was well received.

ITO the ordinary law abiding citizen the


l. range wars seem anomalous and strangely
at variance with American civilization. They
can't understand how it happens that these
bloody, vindictive, and prolonged conflicts
waged between rival interests of unlimited
wealth and vast political influence over lands
to which neither has the shadow of claim.
The sheepmen assert, with some show of reason,
that they have as much right to make of
the vacant public lands as have the cattle
men. But the cattlemen allege that whereas
cattle will Craze upon the same lands year
after year without doing them any injury,
the sheep eat off the grass down to the
hard-baked soil, pull out the roots, and then
with their sharp hoofs trample anything that
may be left into atoms that never can sprout
up again.


PROFESSIONALLY sheep are close grazers; but
it is worthy of notice that in New Mexico and
Arizona there sheep ranges that have been
pastured continuously for more than three
hundred years. and that have more sheep on
them and better pasture than ever before in
the memory of men. 1t is apparent, therefore,
that sheep are far from being SO destructive as
the champions of the cattle interests would
have the public believe. The further assertion
that no genuine cowboy hesitates to make and
swear to,-that cattle will not Craze in COM
pany with sheep, nor even upon lands where
sheep have recently been pastured, must be
dismissed as gross and inexcuSable libel upon
the good sense Of the cows. Anyone who visits
the ranges of Texas, New Mexico, Arizona,
Colorado, Wyoming, Montana, Idaho, or any
other of the great stock raising common
wealths, may millions of sheep and cattle
browsing together in perfect amity and good
fellowship. 1t is evident, therefore, that the
wars of the range are purely of mans making;
and that there is no deep seated enmity or race
prejudice between the four footed representa-
tives of the two great branches of the Western
live stock industry.

For the last two weeks Leopold
Batres has been excavating one of the
small artificial hills to the southeast
OF the Pyramid of the Sun. This is
one of the tumuli that form the row of
the Street of the Dead. Here have
been discovered a number of rooms.
which are apparently a part of an an
clent temple, with rooms and patios.
Below these stairways lead to a large
room some thirty feet in length. APP
parently there are other rooms on this
level connected with one another.

this buried city the houses were two
stories had been destroyed by fire,
but the lower remained untouched, and
upon them there still remains the red
paint which was the characteristic color

kings. Beside the human skeleton was

red. In addition to these there were

kets representing heroes who lived
years ago. Many spiral shells were
also encountered which had holes
drilled through them, showing that
they had been used as beads. They

Many copper, bronze, chichehuite and

fully polished and of extraordinary
size.-Mexican Herald.

important highway bills and killed two others. in
accordance with the decision OF the highway CON

policy in this matter decided upon.


The more important bill passed. introduced by
Senator Cobb provides for a graduated system Of
aid for local road Improvement in towns

dollar for dollar to the poorest towns and
gradually decreasing amount TO richer towns. IN
proportion to road mileage, until the present rate
of 80 cents the dollar is reached. The other bill
passed, also introduced by Senator Cobb provides
for a bond issue in harmony with the general
amendments to the HigbieArmstrong law.

West bill. laying upon the state the entire Of

Special to The Herald.


NEW YORK, June ia simple little
kiss, imprinted upon the lips of pretty
typewriter in one of the downtown Office
buildings one day last week, brought
several fire engines and hook and ladder
companies racing to the scene of pos
sible conflagration, hurried out the
police reserves, blocknded Nassau ctreet
for half an hour and caused several
thousand persons to congregate.


Tenants of the Office building in ques-
tion have noticed of late a Irritation be-
tween the handsome young letter car
rier who delivers the mail and the
pretty typewriter. At the office in
which she is employed the letter carrier
devoted far more time to picking out
correspondence for the firm than was
absolutely necessary.


The postman was swinging along the
corridor the other day, but his heart
beating more quickly than usual, as he
neared the Office where his sweetheart
is employed. Just then the door opened
and she came out. The couple walked
along a few steps together. chatting
gayly. The corridor was deserted, and
the gallant letter carrier decided to
embrace the opportunity and the girl at
the same time. He succeeded in kissing
her, but the suddenness of the affair
startled the girl and she broke away
from his encircling arm. In so doing
she upset small ladder, which fell
against the fire alarm box, smashing the
glass and pressing the electric button in
full accordance with the printed rules.


The girl fled to her office and the post
man disappeared around corner of the
corridor and began delivering mail with
flendish rapidity. When the firemen ar
rived they saw the broken alarm and
| the prostrate ladder and promptly
summed up the situation as a false
alarm. They didn't know how the lad
der happened to fall. but blamed the
usual skylarking boys. But the girl
knows and the postman knows. So does

TIFLIS. Trans-Caucae,a, December Ia
A band of sixty robbers attacked and de-
rallied the mail train running between
Tifis and Baku last night near the sta
ton of Salakhu.


The train was carrying a large sum of
money. The train guard repulsed the ban
dts after a fight in which many passen-
gers and soldiers were wounded. The ban
dts finally retreated, leaving four dead
behind them.


The attack was daringly conceived and
carried out. Thirty yards of track on a
down grade had been torn up and the
train running at full speed plunged it's
way over the ties. Both, locomotives and
most of the cars were ditched. The rob-
bers, who were in hiding nearby, imme-
diately came out ,and advanced on the
train guard and passengers. They threw
eight bombs and opened heavy fire on
the confused travellers.


The train guard rallied quickly and re-
turned this fire from behind the mass of
wreckage. They held their ground te-
naciously until the robbers were driven off.
carrying off their wounded. hospital
train has brought a number of the
wounded passengers and guards into Tiff
lis. Troops are in pursuit of the robbers.

At Wangamumu bay, on the northeast
coast Of New Zealand, whales are caught
in big steel nets. The nets are made of
three-Quarter-inch wire rope in six-feet
mesh. and have barrel buoys along the
edges to hold them close to the surface. A
whale cruising along the shore strikes the
net and gets his head through a mesh, and
instead Of backing out he rushes forward
and entangles himself in the wire ropes
He may carry the net away from Its an
chorage with the momentum of his rush,
but the buoys impede him, and instead Of
heading out to sea and taking the net with
him the whale thrashes about furiously and
soon gets the wire ropes round about his
fins and fiukes. The animal thrashes
around until worn out, then the boats of the
fishermen creep in upon him and the har-
poon and lance are used. When the whalers
give chase in the old-fashioned way now
adays power launches are used instead Of
rowboats. At Wangamumu al the parts
of the whale are utilized, the bones and
refuse being converted into fertilizers.
headline: Whale Nets.

The loves and friendships of indi-
viduals partake of the frail character
of human life, and are brief and un-
certain. The experience of human
life may be shortly summed up: A
little loving and a good deal of sor-
rowing; some bright hopes and many
bitter disappointments; some gor-
geous Thursdays when the skies are
bright and the heavens blue, when
Providence, bending over us in bless
ings, glads the heart almost to mad
ness; many dismal Fridays, when the
smoke of torment beclouds the mind
and undying sorrows gnaw upon the
heart; some high ambitions and many
Waterloo defeats, until the heart be-
comes like charnel house filled with
dead affections, embalmed in holy
but sorrowful memories; and then
the chord is loosed, the golden bowl
is broken, the individual life-a cloud,
vapor, passes away.-Matthew Hale
Carpenter.

most interesting feature OF the political
events in Massachusetts was the fact
that both The Republican and the Demo
cratic platform declared with almost
equal force for tariff revision, says the
Buffalo Express. The Democrats went
no farther than to demand a gradual
revision, which should not unduly inter-
fere with established industries and
which would bring rates to a point where
they will merely cover the difference in
the cost of manufacture here and abroad.
That is substantially what Secretary
Taft advocates. The Republicans urged
a special session of Congress 10 remove
duties which are needed neither for reve-
nue. nor protection. and make such modi-
fications as experience may have shown
/ 10 be necessary. Massachusetts has long
been stronghold OF protection and the
fact that both parties now agree in de-
manding tariff revision has significance
which Congress cannot well afford TO
overlook.

NEW YORK. December 26.-Philip
Mundy, who runs a saloon at 354 Metro
politan avenue. Williamsburg. is dying in
the Eastern District Hospital in Brook
Ign as the result of pistol duel last night
with James Jacarusso, who runs a saloon
just opposite Mundy's place.


Mundy set out fine turkey lunch yes
terday and succeeded in getting all the
Christmas day patronage of the vicinity.
Jacarusso saood outside hir place gloom
lily watching his customers flocking into
Mundy's. When evening came he walked
across the street, heaved a cobblestone
through Mundy's brightly lit front window
and began to curse Mundy at the top of
his voice. Mundy seized a pistol which
lay handy behind his bar and ran out 40
see what was the matter.


Jacarusso, from the dark street. opened
fire on Mundy the moment he appeared in
the open door of the brightly illuminated
saloon. Mundy attempted to reply. but he
could hardly see his opponent and his
shots went wild. After several shots had
been exchanged Mundy went down with a
ball through the lower right lung and
liver.


Jacarusso escaped.

American ship Atlas dropped anchor here
yesterday, 275 days out from Baltimore,
ending trip made tragic by collision
OF Cape Horn, attended by the sinking of
another vessel. the drowning of the fated
crafts captain and the captains wife,
mutiny on its decks and death among its
crew.


On June 6 at O'clock pm. the Atlas
struck the Norwegian bark Viking, Capt.
Peterson. bound from Hamburg to CAL
lao. Both were badly damaged by the
contact, but the bark Jared worse. In
the terror of the night thirteen of the
crew of the Norwegian bark boarded the
American ship, crawling over tangled
shrouds and dangling booms. but Capt.
Peterson and his wife were not among
those who made the dangerous transfer
1t was too dark to render aid, though the
Atlas stood by during the night. and next
morning the Viking had disappeared. The
captain and his wife are believed to have
persisted.


The Atlas put into Rio Janeiro for re-
pairs leaking badly. On the way to this
port mutiny took place among the
crew over some trouble with the mate,
but 1t was soon ouelled. ,

flooded district early today, eight persons.
all children but three, lost their lives by
jumping from the windows of their homes
into the waters of the flood and drowning
before they could be rescued. The names ::

Allen Bretries aged nine years


Simon Allis. aged two years.

Thomas Badsay, aged five years.

Surrounding the pottery is a colony of
Syrians. The explosion occurred about 1
o'clock this morning. and was followed i'm
mediately by fire, which enveloped the en-
tire plant in few minutes and threatened
adjoining property. Fearing death in the
flames, the frenzied foreigners leaped from

the eight named are known to have gone

FLORENCE, N. j., February 2S.-Elght

o'clock, without scarcely minutes rest

of Miss Barbara Barr. popular young
woman of this place and member OF the
Baptist Church choir. Miss Barr was
visiting at the home of a friend Tuesday
afternoon and during the drift OF con-
yersation some one made witty remark
which brought laughter among those pres
emf. After a few minutes Miss Barr found
it was impossible to stop laughing, and
each minute her Mysteries grew more V1o-
lent until fatal results were feared.


Her laughter could be heard for block
and neighbors wondered what 1t all meant.
All kinds of local remedies were tried, such
as throwing water in the young woman's
face and eandeavoring to make her angry,
but without success. Drs. Thatcher and
Baird were summoned and conveyed the
exhausted and semi-conscious young wom-
an to her home.


Until 10 o'clock Tuesday night she con-
tinued to laugh and the physicians were
more than puzzled. Miss Barr grew weaker
every minute. Finally, still laughing, she
sank into a doze and the spell finally grad
ually passed away. When she awoke she
was in an extremely weakened condition.

NEW ORLEANS, La, June 8.-The turf
war between the two merry-go-rounds
which have been running full blast since
the shut down of the two big race tracks
and the subsequent decentralization from
free gates and all sorts of gambling. has
already become an issue In the state cam
paign. Col. Theodore 8. Wilkinson Of
Plaquemine, candidate for governor. in his
first campaign speech at Alexandria, dis
cussed the race track evils in Louisiana,
and declared unequivocally for a state rae
ing commission to regulate the sport in
Louisiana. He declared that racing had run
mad in New Orleans and that the present
decentralization from all-year-round racing
summer and winter, including Sundays, and
threatened night racing, had gone beyond
the limit, and must be curbed. He declared
that the youth of New Orleans were being
led astray, and that the state must take a
hand else all racing would be killed In this
state The position Of Col. Wilkinson has
met with general favor.

BRIDGEPORT, Conn, June 22-Topsy. a
huge elephant, one of the herd of the men,
agerie of Ringing Bros./ circus which
showed here Thursday, threw nearly one
thousand persons into a panic by breaking
from the fastenings and charging into the
menagerie tent. The elephant had been Ill
tempered for several days and was chained
outside the menagerie tent a short distance
from the ether twenty-eight elephants in
the herd. Suddenly it gave vent to shrill
trumpetings, and the other beasts an
swered the cries from the menagerie tent
the big elephant broke from its fastenings
and dashed madly for the tent. Tearing
through the canvas walls, it dashed into the
open space by the cages. sending the spec
tators fleeing in panic Animal trainers and
other attaches at once surrounded the beast
and quickly subdued it, while others kept
the remainder of the herd quiet. Topsy
was then led outside and securely shackled.

for safety

lingering sickness the younger Of the

bank account having been depleted from
defraying the expenses of the weeks OF
medicine and doctors" visits, she was
obliged to contract debt at the under
takers. After that she paid small
monthly installment until the bill was half
settled, when one day there came through
the mail a receipt for the remainder. The
receipt was accompanied by a badly writ
ten and blotted note from scrub-woman
in large uptown hotel. who knew of
the trouble, knew the family and the cir
cumstances, and in her note explained
that she had no family nor near relatives

herself, and that she wanted to use this
surplus money for the little mother who
needed all that she could make extra to
support the remaining child. AS scrub
women receive only fifty or seventy five
cents a day, one will readily appreciate
the spirit which moved one kind soul to
help another in distress.

yet recorded.


For thirty-nine days this animal re-
mained in deserted granary completely
surrounded by water. and had nothing to
eat but wheat and the mice that inhab-
tied the building.


No one knew of the dogs presence in
the building, and his discovery and sub
sequent rescue from starvation were
merely by chance.


Two boys bent on pleasure were rowing
over the flooded lake bottom and when
near the, deserted granary heard the
yelping of dog which seemed to be
confined within. They made an investiga-
tion and discovered the emaciated animal.


Despite earnest coaxing and entreaties
they could not make the beast move, and
further advances on their part was met
with snarls and the showing of teeth.
He was taken off in the boat.

the jingle Of bells in the engine room

the Newark's passengers again showed

Special Cable to The Herald.


BERLIN. Aug. 1L-Thousands of per-
sons in the central Prussian provinces
have been suddenly seized with an acute
form of religious mania.


Detailed kilograms from Cassel state
that the outburst, which is manifesting
itself in all kinds of astonishing forms,
was started by two fanatics, who pro-
claimed themselves divine emissares,
specially sent by heaven to lead the in
habitants of the adjoining provinces to
salvation.


Their principal lieutenants are two
Swedish women, whose oratory exercises
a strange fascination over the populace.
Extraordinary scenes take place at meet
ings held nightly in Cassel and many sur
rounding towns and villages. The par
Elephants at these meetings emit inarticu-
late shrieks, throw themselves on the
ground roll on the floor, fling their arms
and legs wildly about beat their heads
against the wooden benches, and amazing
confessions of sin then pour from their
lips. After this they declare they see
visions of heaven, hell and other worlds.


Sometimes all those present at meet
ing PROSTATE themselves simultaneously
on the floor and groan in unison, with
wild gestures. Suddenly man springs up
and graphically describes some strange
vision which he sees before his eyes.


Loud shouts of "Hallelujah" greet the
speaker, and when the vision has been
described men and women arise from the
ground, embrace one another with ecstatic
fervor, and dance with many amazing
movements, all through the night till sun
rise.


Amazing Scenes


A spectator of one of these meetings
states that there were over 200 people
II ,,a1 OH oil oil "
intoxicated with religious ecstasy. He
says: II heard wild cries, loud confess
sions of sin, uncanny shrieks, groans and
other unearthly noises. l saw distorted
faces, men and women gesticulating like
lunatics.


81 saw them sink to the ground and
kick out in all directions. Suddenly
young man sprang up and uttered sounds
which the chairman described as being
the result of divine vision. No sooner
had the chairman uttered these words
than a great shout of triumph rose from
the assembly. They all looked as if hyp-
Noticed"


At another meeting, after a hymn had
been sung, a young man sprang to the
platform threw himself about with
extraordinary vigor, made indescribable
grimaces, and then shouted incoherently.
One of the founders of the movement in
formed the congregation that the youth
was divinely inspired and that his antics
and noises were a divine revelation. The
worshipers clapped their hands, knelt
down, gesticulated, shrieked, groaned and
groveled in the dust.


Several worshipers shouted, I'VE see
the blood of our Savior" Women en-
braced one another, saying, 1--WE. have
seen our Savior himself"


Strange Frenzy


The preacher then offered up the fol-
lowing prayer: 20 Lord let every one
here kneel down. Whoever refuses to
kneel, let him be thrown from our midst"
One man remained standing, whereupon
there were wild cries of out with him!
Out with Beelzebub!


When the unbelever left the hall the
worshpers shouted: 1.-The devil has now
gone The evil one has left our midst


At a meeting at Gross Almerode young
man Invested himself of his collar and
cuffs, declaring that he desired to re-
nounce luxury. Young women tore off
their hats, wells, ribbons, laces and other
finery for the same reason.


Night after night hundreds of deluded
enthusiasts are attending meetings of this
kind where eccentric doctrines are sys-
tematically preached by fanatical relig-
ious maniacs.


The congregations are principally com
posed of peasants from the agricultural
districts, but the intelligent classes of the
urban population are also strongly repre-
scented at the meetings.


Large numbers of peasants are pouring
in from the provinces of Upper Hesse and
Lower Hesse in the hope of seeing signs

misguided movement

Becoming respondent because of con-
tinued Illness Mrs. Pearl Chapman, TWEEN
ty-s.x years of age, wife of G. w. Chap
man Of Jersey City, committed suicide last
night by cutting her throat with a razor
She had come here to be with her sister.
Mrs James w. Bauby. 2S35 10Th street
northwest, thinking the change would ben
eft her and that her nervousness might
be cured. but the relief did not come, and
last night the sick woman ended her suf-
ferings in the manner stated. Mrs. Mary
Rolls, mother of the deceased; Charles
Rolls, her brother, and Mrs. Bauby were in
the home of Mrs. Bauby last night when
the deed was committed.


1t is stated that Mrs. Chapman's nerv-
BUSINESS had become acute to alarm
her relatives, but she said nothing to any
OF them yesterday which would indicate
that she contemplated ending her life. Her
condition yesterday, it is said, did not
seem worse than it had been during pre-
cedng days, and members of the family
were shocked when they went to her room
and found what she had done. Mrs. Chap
man went to the room of her brOther-in-
law about : o'clock and got possession of
his razor. She then went to her own room
on the first floor and cut her throat. in
ficting terrible cash. Blood streamed
from the wound and weakened the young
woman to such an extent that she soon
fell upon the floor.


Noise Attracts Attention.


The noise attracted the attention of her
mother. sister and brother. Mrs. Bauby
was the first member of the family to
reach the room, and she discovered her
dying sister lying upon the floor with blood
streaming from the wound, while near her
was the razor she had used. Mrs Rolls
and her son followed Mrs. Bauby to the
room. AS soon they fully realized what
had happened they sent a messenger to
the office of DR.. A. ]. Carrico, 2S17 18th
street northwest. The physician responded
and remained with the wounded woman
until the arrival of the ambulance from
the Emergency Hospital.


Mrs. Chapman was hurried to the hos
pital, DR.. Sutton, who was in charge of
the ambulance. attending her while the
vehicle was the way to the institution.
When the hospital was reached the sur
geons found there was no hope for the
wounded woman. Her death occurred
before 10 O'Clock.


Coroner hewitt gave the necessary death
certificate, and relatives were notified OF
her death. Her body was removed from
the hospital this morning and prepared for
burial. Mr. Chapman was notified of the
suicide, and he came here from Jersey City
to make arrangements for the funeral.

CHICAGO, April 20.-A dispatch to
the Tribune from Escanaba, Mich.
says:


Caught in a mass of coal, Frank
Erickson, laborer was carried head
foremost Thursday through a chute at
the Refs Coal company's dock, and
after being entombed under twenty
five tons of coal for nearly twenty
four hours, was rescued alive yester-
day.


Although bruised from head to foot
and sustaining internal injuries, hopes
for his recovery are entertained.


Erickson's disappearance was not
discovered until late Thursday night
and crews dragged the bay throughout
the night, thinking that he had been
drowned. Yesterday, when a car of
coal was being dumped at the rail-
road yards a feeble shout was heard
from the outside.


The car was quickly emptied and
Erickson found alive and conscious
He said that he had heard men pass
ing near him throughout the night and
had shouted repeatedly, but could not
make himself heard.

Fighting and struggling for her
freedom and occasionally swearing at
her guards, Miss Lucy Van Meter, a
talented young artist, yesterday was
taken before the insanity commission
in department two of the superior
court and there adjudged insane.


The young woman lost her mind in
the pursuit of her art.


Miss Van Meters mother, Mrs.
Fannie Van Meter of Twelfth street,
testified that her daughter had been
good girl all her life, that she had
never even heard language of ques-
tionable character, and yet as soon as
she became crazed her one thought re-
verted to the language of the streets


Miss Van Meter is 20 years of age
and a native of Illinois. She began
painting when she was little girl and
simply gave up her life for the sake
of art Throughout Missouri, Nebraska
and Illinois in the various places she
has lived with her parents, her work
had been continued and some of her
clever sketches of mountain scenery
are now gracing fashionable eastern
homes.


Paints in Bistering Sun


For several years she restricted her
work to portrait painting and then she
decided to come west The oils and
water colors of the great American
desert lured her. She had seen such
paintings on exhibit and her one ambi-
tion was to paint the desert, to trans
NIT the marvellous hues of morn and
eve to canvas, and she came west with
her father and mother to live. The
father settled at Macy, Ariz., and the
girl went to the desert. Day after day
the horrible heat beat down upon her
head and she became nervous. Her
people attempted to persuade her to
give up her work, but she refused to
listen to them. She painted and
painted the sun blistered the varnish
on the easel and beat down on her
head, but her brush was untiring.


One day several months ago she
walked into her mothers room and
stood there looking at her parent.
Then, without a word, she fell to the
floor as though she had been shot.
For fourteen days and nights Miss Van
Meter remained unconscious. On the
fifteenth day when she awoke from her
sleep of paralysis she failed to recog-
niZe her people.


Operation Is Fruitless
Her mother and brother brought her
to Los Angeles on Christmas day in
the hope that she might gain strength
here. She was taken to a hospital and
since that time the girls mother has
been her constant attendant.


Several days ago an operation was
| performed in a last forlorn hope of
bringing back to sanity the wandering
mind Of the girl, but the operation
proved fruitless.


| Yesterday when Miss Van Meter ap-
peared in court she~s brought some
scraps of drawing paper with her. She
would place some object before her and
carefully measure the dimensions with
her eye as though preparing to begin
some drawing, and then she would
laugh, and her long slender fingers
would crush the paper.


The examination was short one and
the girl was declared insane. AS she
sat there, waiting to be taken back to
the county hospital before her trip to
the asylum, she sang in a sweet, clear
voice the refrain Of mo, Never Alone"
then without another word she accom-
panied the guards on what will prob
ably be her last journey, for her case
is considered nearly hopeless.

darkness Thursday night stones were
throw at a fast passenger train on the
Pennsylvania railroad as it was passing
through the Brushton district. The stones
crashed through the car windows, injuring
four persons seriously and creating a panic
among the passengers. Following acct
dents to four of the railroads most i'm
portant passenger trains within the last

road officials much anxiety. The four per-
sons injured were F. w. Clark and wife of
Pittsburg, Miss Grace Woodward of Cleve-
land and Miss Catherine Smith of Brad
dock. The injured were taken from the
train at Williamsburg and brought back to
the city. They were all badly cut about the
face and head by flying glass. Efforts to
catch the men who have been wrecking

trains were redoubled yesterday. Railroad

BERKELEY. March 10.-Miss Eliza
beth Blossom has left with her aunt,
Mrs. r. Pew, for the Orient. where she
will meet her hance, Newton Booth
Knox. Their marriage will take place
at Yokohama Miss Blossom and her

Those who wished Miss Blossom a

pier could not but recall the experience
which Miss Blossom underwent few
months ago. when her friends feared
that her life would. be forfeit to the
risk she took IN making a midnight
expedition through the town. clad in a
thin dress. and exposed to the cold
mists of the night, while her body was
then weakened by fever.


Miss Blossom. while suffering from

the window OF her bedroom and made
her way along the roof and down the
pillars of the porch to the ground. all

absence not being noted until the nurse
who was supposed to have her in Gus
tody awoke and discovered that the girl
had fed. The alarm was sounded, the
police were called out and the hills
were searched. but the girl was not
found She was given up for dead, sup
posedly having died from cold in the
hills 1t was not until thirty-six hours
after her escape that the police learned
OF her presence in a private family.
where she had gone after tramping
through the town The girl gave no
name to the family and they could not
learn her address Few supposed the
frafl girl would recover from this sx-
perience, but she passed through IL

sen for the whole force TO turn out and

great plot against the Car having been

complied with. The detectives who were
accessible were hurried off in all direc-

who were off duty.

chiefs to doubt its accuracy. He reflected
that there were more than 1000 Russians
in the city, and concluded that there must
be mistake somewhere. He telephoned
10 the first officer, who fastened to head
quarters, and found that Truelsen had
gone suddenly mad. The order was can
celed in time to save the liberties Of the
Russians.

Bert Simmons, aged eighteen years.

blown to atoms. The concussion shook
down the plaster in the ceiling of the

worshipers hurriedly left the church to
join the crowd seeking the scene Of the
explosion.

NEW YORK, January 21.-The Clyde
Lines crack steamship Comanche, which
should have been here Saturday, arrived
yesterday with a tale of collision at sea.


A bark ran into the steamer last Friday
evening, tore away some thirty feet of the
port rail- smashed one of the lifeboats and
made a hole in the plating just forward of
amidships. Then the bark backed off in
the fog and went her way without leaving
Capt Watson her name and address. She
left about fifteen feet of her jibboom on
board the. Comanche.


The Comanche was steaming slowly at
the time, blowing her whistle at intervals
because the weather was thick, and keep
ing a sharp lookout. Capt. Watson was on
the bridge when the shadowy form of the
sailing vessel popped out of the fog. She
was SO close aboard When she was first seen
and, was coming so fast that the Conan
che's quartermaster didn't have time to put
his wheel over before the bark's jibboom
was tearing its way along the port side.
Her bowsprit punched a hole In the Co.
manche about fifteen feet above the water
line.


A verbat tim report of the conversation
between Capt. Watson and the skipper of
the bark was not obtainable yesterday,
but it was said that the fog seemed thicker
while they were talking. When the bark
had disappeared the steamer stopped and
hung about, thinking she might be of as
sistance, but there was no call for aid,
and after an hour or She steamed ahead.
But the ten passengers will have something
to tell about the rest Of their lives.

Navy defeated today its ''landlubber

ury Beekman. occupied a box on the south

Each Side Cheers the Other.


The West Point cadets who came to
Philadelphia to cheer their team were
the first to march upon the field, headed
by their band. They formed into six COM
panies, facing the south stand, after
which they marched to section In the
center of the stand.


The midshipmen followed few minutes
later and formed into twelve companies,
facing the north stand, but instead OF
marching to the section allotted to them
they quick-stepped it at the signal of
whistle, and, standing at attention, gave
vent to their enthusiasm with their Ia
nous siren yell.


To match the naval siren yell the West
Point cadets on the other side introduced



yell Each side cheered the other, and
together cheered for the Red and Blue of
the University of Pennsylvania.


A big gray mule, covered with the gray,
black and yellow Of the army, In the ca
pacity of mascot. ambled in front of the
Army stand, and goat was mascot for
the Navy. The latter animal wore navy
blue blanket with yellow letters on 1t,
and his horns were decorated with
steamers The West Point contingency
also had bear cub, sent from Detroit,
but bruin did not like the publicity. and
his keepers had difficulty in holding him
in the open.


From the time the game started until
the last whistle blew there was one con-
tinual round of cheering and singing. and
when the Navy came out victorious pam
demonium broke loose. The cadets threw
away flags, emblems and colored stream
ers. and rushed upon the field to bear
away their team.


Navy Goal Never Threatened.


Though the score looks close, the West
Point team never seriously threatened
the Annapolis goal. the Midshipmen play
ing all around their opponents at nearly
every stage of the contest. The result
was a great surprise to the Army. for
with a heavier team. more experience
and better seasons record than the
Navy, the cadets from up the Hudson
could see nothing but victory. But after
the first few scrimmages it was seen that
the Navy was very strong, and the way
the Midshipmen tore up the Cadets line
and raced around their ends took the
Army boys off their feet. The Army
plainly the run But IKE good
soldiers, they came back and fought the
sailors hard. 1t was no use. however,
for ii was Nays day.


From a scientific viewpoint the game
will not go down in history as first
class contest. True. 1t was hard fought
from beginning to end. but it was marred
by much fumbling and other misplays.
The new style pays. particularly the for
ward pass, were failures nearly every
time they were tried. The loss of dis
lance through players failing to catch the
forward passes more than made up for
the ground gained. Nevertheless. the
game was spectacular. Neither side ap-
peared to have the strength to pene-
trate its opponents line successfully, and
end running.


Only Score in First Half.


The only score of the game was made
in the first half. which was full of action
from the kickoff to the timekeeper's
whistle. The Midshipmen twice had the
ball within striking distance and each
time failed to follow up their advantage,
but finally. after punting duel. an Army
man fumbled and q Midshipman fell on
the pigskin on the Army's 25-yard line.
Left Halfback Douglass. who played a
wonderful game for the Navy. went
through the West Point line for 10 yards.
A forward pass helped some. and another
line play put the ball yards from the
Cadets goal


The Army braced, but the Navy was not
to be denied. Selecting Douglass to make
the try. the midshipmen dug their feet
into the ground. and with a mighty plunge
forward carried Douglass with them with
what proved to be the winning score.
Lange kicked the goal.


During the remainder of the half the
Navy several times got within twenty
yards of the Army goal. but each time it
lost the ball either through fumbling or a
poor forward pass. Lange, the Navy
quarterback. tried a field goal, but it was
blocked.


Second Half Rather Listless.


The second half was more or less list
less. play frequently being stopped to en-
able the trainers to fix up their injured
men Each team constantly punted. with
the hope of recovering the ball on FUN
bles in its opponents territory. This fire.
quentlS happened.


The star of the game was Capt. Doug
lass His punting was uniformly good and
his tackling sure. But it was running
with the ball where he showed best He

The United States revenue cutter service
training ship Itasca. which was re-
modelled from the United States naval
cadet training ship Bancroft, sailed
yesterday from Baltimore on an ex-

two months. and during which several for
eign ports will be visited. The Itasca has
aboard the first and second classes of rev.
enue service cadets. and under the COM
mand of Capt. Reynolds. she will first visit
New York. and then she will make a stop
at New London. From the latter port she
will shape her course across the Atlantic.
and after stopping at the Western Islands

Fillefranche will next be visited by the
cadets and the ship will start from there

made at the Bermudas and other ports in

of next September.

view of making her the practice ship for
cadet engineers of the Naval Academy, an
idea that was abandoned. and the vessel
was sent to foreign service She proved
herself capable vessel, but becoming too
small for the demands upon her was trans
ferred to the revenue cutter service.

in the vessel to fit her for the duties of the
cadets.

1893. On her trial trip. after being general
ly overhauled at Newport News. she made
a speed of 1928 knots per hour, better time
than she made when first built. While at
the shipyard two new water-tube boilers
were installed, engines taken down and
parts renewed. an entire new electrical out
fit. including searchlight. was installed and
sanitary system was placed in first-class
condition. New forecastle. main and poop
decks were laid and new piiothouse and
galley were among the changes.


New fore and main masts. the former
rugged as a topsail schooner for aloft prac
tice. new standing rigging, bilge keel to
minimize rolling combine new features
added.

wrecked. She was seriously injured and

Mrs Goucher had driven her husband to

which she recently captured several rib

to have been hitched up with a wrong bit,
but exhibited no temper until the young
horsewoman started alone on the trip to
her home. about three miles outside Moores-
town. Then Brownie became nervous.


When the runabout struck tree the
brave woman was thrown headlong into a
ditch while the horse kicked itself free
and continued on its wild run. Mrs.
Goucher was carried unconscious to farm
house and it was several hours before the
physicians would allow Mrs. Goucher to be
removed to her house. Both her collar
bones are fractured and 1t is feared that

can be pulled off at high tide. Warnell
and his helper, Albert Thornton, missed
the light on the government break
water last night, and Thornton, who
was on watch, was first awakened to
the sense of their danger by seeing the
red light on the Salt Lake tracks at
Ostend. He awakened Warnell, but
they were inside the breakers and their
engines could not make headway out
to sea. Thornton threw two anchors
overheard, but they did not hold.

PHILADELPHIA. February 21.-Spike
Robson, the little English lightweight fight
er. rudely shattered Tommy Murphy's
championship aspirations last night in six
round fight at the National Athletic Club.
The English boy was much the cleverer and
outpointed the New Yorker in every round.


The fight was fast throughout. In the
first three rounds the Harlemite fought hard
and the advantage gained by his opponent
was slight. In the fourth Robson began to
show his superiority and landed many sting
ing blows without receiving one in return.
Murphy began to show signs of fatigue in
the fifth and when his blows landed they
had little no effect, while the English
man apparently grew stronger, for he fol-
lowed his opponent around the ring, send
ing in rights and lefts, both swings and
jabs.


In the last round Robson started after
Tommy like an enraged tiger. He landed
blow after blow on Murphy's jaw, but none
Of them had in 1T force enough to put the
sturdy Murphy out His face was cut and
bruised. Blood was streaming from three
different places, but he could see and heed
and would not give up. though he was in
an almost helpless condition.


Although Robson was the virtual winner
the fight proved that Murphy is one of the
toughest lightweight fighters in the ring
today.


More than four thousand persons. many
of whom were New Workers, saw the fight

BUTTE, Mont. March 27.-Having
adjusted all differencets with the labor
unions the newspapers of Butte and
Anaconda will resume publication at
once.


The Inter Mountain Evening News
will appear tomorrow afternoon and
the Butte Miner and Anaconda Stan
dard Friday morning. Three year con-
tracts have been signed by the COM
mittees from the typographical union,
the pressmens, the stereotypers and
mailerS unions.


The suspension, which lasted for six
weeks, was precipitated by the press
mems union demanding an increased
scale of wages for its members.


The demand was refused by the pub
fishers and suspension followed. The
printers refused to go to work after
having been advised that they would
return to work at the old scale, five
dollars day for day work and $3.50
for night work, or not at all.


The printers refused to recede from
the prevailing scale of $3.50 for day
work and $500 for night work and a
lockout resulted. The printers then
made a determined fight but lost by
being commanded to return to work by
the international Typographical union.

The capture was effected by Deputy

picioned by the desperadoes, the Off

The confederate veterans are having the

swarm toward Seven Pines. to Cold Ifar-
Dor, to Dutch Gap, to Petersburg, Yellow

them, and they point out just where their
commands stood when the battles were on,
where officers fen and where the charge
was hottest.


Though the city has been crowded for

worth note. True many of the old men
have fallen by the yside-fatiEue some
times. and sometimes it was from too much
eating and drinking. But il good
natured crowd The police pulled the

PASADENA. Jan. If. Screaming
with terror and pain, rushing madly
about i'm the back yard while her
clothes fed the flames that were famed
by the breeze her flight created, Mrs.
Carrie Tiernan, aged 81 years and a
widow, nearly perished this morning
from the burns she received. Had she
not been caught and held by a neigh
Dor the distracted woman would have
ran on and on till the flames had suffo-
Gated her and burned her body to a
crisp. She was hysterical when several
of the neighbors grabbed her and
wrapped blankets about her to smother
the blaze. Others poured water on the
blankets and saturated them. Wet soda
was applied to the deep burns on the
back and limbs, but the flesh peeled
away.


1t was while she was preparing her
breakfast over a gasoline stove that
Mrs. Tiernan's clothes caught fire, and
becoming hysterical nearly ended her
life in her flight.


1t was cold. There was no fuel in
the house and Mrs. Tiernan is a
woman of limited means who could not
afford coal famine prices. Crouching
over the blue flame of the gasoline cook
stove she sought to warm herself. The
blaze communicated to her clothes and
before the fire had been completely ex-
tinguished the whole body except the
feet was burned and charred. The hair
was completely burned from the head
and only where the shoes protected the
feet and Smothered the flames was
there any break in the single burn that
covered the entire body.


Moaning on a cot in the Pasadena
hospital Mrs. Tiernan fingers between
life and death, and while the physicians
watch over her there are no relatives
near to comfort. Between her means
the aged woman told her medical at
tendants that she had no relatives eX-
cept two stepdaughterS, and these are
somewhere in the east-where she does
not know.


Woman Lived Alone


For several years Mrs. Tiernan occu-
pied alone a cottage on the back por-
tion of the lot at 237 North Pasadena
avenue. Benjamin O'Connell occupies
the house on the lot fronting the street.
When Mrs. Tiernan discovered her
clothes were aflame she rushed about
the back yard and then dashed into the
O'Connell home. Mr.. O'Connell was
eating his morning meal and when the
frantic, flameclad woman rushed into
the dining room he made an effort to
catch her. The effort was futile, so
swift was her flight about the house.


Some employees of the Pacific Trans
fer company were engaged in removing
some furniture from the house next
door. They saw the woman rush into
the O'Connel home with blazing gar
ments. Fastening over the back yard
fence they aided Mr.. O'Connell in catch
ing her and eXtinguishing the blaze.


Physicians at the hospital state that
there is very slight hope for the
Woman's recovery.

''You shall not go to that place." de-
clared the mother of White and Blackie
one day when her .petted darlings were

unknown. There are terrible creatures
in that forest, and they eat up little

dangers that abound there"

CAMBRIDGE, Mass, November 23.-
Harvard square was bustling with activity
and brilliant with the red and the blue
when the first of the army of 10000 peo-
pie, all eager for todays foot ball game
between Harvard and Yale, reached Cam
bridge. The old college buildings in the
and the stores in Harvard square were
gaily decorated with both colors Across
the river rose the gray walls of the
stadium. the scene of the days contest.


Additional temporary stands had been
erected at the open end, along the side
lines and on top of the great structure.
The turf was well rolled and entirely free
from frost. but yesterdays moist weather
had made it a tri1e slippery.


Harvard Confident.


Despite the swarm of Yale enthusiasts,
all sanguine of victory, the undergrad
yates of Harvard were still confident,
Notwithstanding Yale's undoubted strength
and the recent Crimson defeats Still
there was very little betting on the game,
and what wagers were made were almost
entirely on the matter of the size of the
score, or on Harvard's chances of cross
Ing YaeS goal line.


Reports from the quarters where the
two teams had spent the night were that
all the players were in excellent shape.
The day was typical of perfect Indian
summer. The players. however. would
perhaps have been better satisfied if the
atmosphere were more frosty and bracing.


Before leaving Auburndale for the
stadium today the Yale coaches held a
conference. and it was reported later that
they had decided to put Dunbar at center
in place of Congdon, who was injured in
the Princeton game.


In the first half Yale scored a touch
down. Score: Yale, 6; Harvard, O.

COPENHAGEN, June SIT behooves
theatrical companies performing in
Russian dominions to bestow anxious
care on their makeups. A Danish COM
pany, which has just returned from
Finland, found this out to their cost.


After the first performance the actor.
Bewer, who acted the part of the am
bassador, was summoned by Governor
General Gebard, who addressed him in
Russian. Bewer, who had seen the
governor general in the audience,
thought he was complimenting him and
received the remarks bowling and smil-
ing.


His smiles however, suddenly stopped
when the interpreter translating the
utterances into Danish, revealed the
fact that the governor general had fined
Bewer $1,000 because his makeup too
nearly resembled the governor him
self, who, like Bewer, is extremely fat.
The levying of the fine was accom-
panied by a peremptory direction that
Bewer citer his makeup before appear
ing in the character again.

NEW YORK. December 2s-Happy that
her children, for whom she had sacrificed
everything. even the last scraps of food,
had at last found friends, Mrs. Phyllis
Frisco died at a Brooklyn hospital OF
starvation.


Mrs. Prisco's husband has been dead
some months. and with four little ones,
the eldest four years. the youngest four
months old, to care for she labored day
and night until she was taken Ill. Her
pride prevented her from asking for aid,
so she saved what bits of food she could
obtain for her little ones while she grad
ually grew weaker and weaker from the
lack of food. The last bits of crusts went
for the children's Christmas dinner, and
the next morning neighbors heard the
crying OF hte little ones in the unfur-
nished room in which the mother and
children lived. They entered and found
Mrs Frisco dying and the children weak
from the lack of food and from the cold.


Children Cared For.


The police removed the mother to a
hospital and the Children's Society took
care of the little ones. When the physi-
clans found that all hope for the mother
was gone the little ones were sent for
and Mrs. Frisco was assured that they
would be cared for.


They were happy again, for they had
had plenty Of food and toys Rosie and
Katherine cooed over pretty dolls. Sans
eyes glistened at a furry horse and Baby
Angeline clutched in her chubby hands a
woolly lamb. Their troubles were forgot
ten in their new-found happiness, and as
they played with their treasures on the
floor beside the hospital cot the tired
woman realized that their sufferings were
over. And as she watched them playing
there the mother smile faded out Of her
eyes-the mothers heart was stilled and
the mothers sacrifice was complete.

Small wonder that the soul of the girl who
watched felt one instant's regret that she was
never again to know the exhilaration of the
fray A half smile of tenderness parted her
lips as she thought that there in the air above
her were her friends and companions in arms
grim old Fighting" Bevins with his prayerful
oaths, good natured Brockton whose kindli-
ness she knew, and studious little Jenkins
whose imperturbability equaled his steadfast
bravery.


Guy, understanding and respecting the
storm of feeling which must be hers at sight
of this pageantry of which she had been such
vital part watched her in silence. Almost at
their feet squatted Fort Hancock, whose guns
were to below for the last time. 1t too, like
its fellow forts, was of the dying. Like them
its bastions would be abandoned and the men
within driven to ways of peace. Fortress and
ship, garrison and crew, would be no more.
Crumbling, untenanted walls left records of
a nations defense, and rotting uniforms rele-
gated to garrets, would be all that were left
armies reorganiZed and reduced to a police
force only, and sailors become fishermen or
passing their lives in other occupations and
reminiscing of the sea; swords rusting in scab-
bards and guns corroding in embrasures,-
nothing more!


The last salute had doomed out Lower and
lower flew the radioplanes, till they were close
above the outgoing ships. The ports of the
peacemakers opened, and from them fell gar
lands of flowers, which f1uttered down through
the air unfortunately upon the doomed
craft and the waves themselves,-a tribute of
peace from the living and wreaths for the
dying gladiators of war.


Hand in hand Norma and Guy stood upon
the headland beneath the gray beacon lights
that would welcome strange travellers from
foreign ports no more. Into the darkening
skies of the east the fleets of the nations were
speeding to dissolution and death. The long
steady swell of the free and unburdened sea
came monotonously hammering at their feet
In silence they watched the relics of cruel war
sail out saw their huls disappear, saw the
trails of smoke diverge as each squadron sought
its own course, and then looked into each
others eyes, reading therein nothing but
promise of love and serenity. Their troubles
had vanished as had those fleets of the sea-
and life with all its possibilities of accomplish
ment and contentment was before them. They
turned from the great silent ocean and walked
into the mysterious benedictory glow of the
sunset toward their home.

letics hattled through twenty-four innings.

for water, which meant life TO them,
on the Arizona desert on Friday one
prospector was wounded and the owner
of the waterhole, with its slender and
insufficient supply of water in that bar
rem region priceless, was killed.


After two weeks prospecting for
gold on the desert, two young brothers,
William and Lynn Desplain, nearly
perishing from thirst, came upon a
waterhole known as Bears wells,
twenty five miles from Salome, Ariz.
An old man named Jones had taken
possession of the waterhole and for
bade the prospectors filling their empty
kegs. Refusing TO obey, they continued
to replenish their supplies from the
hole. Jones seized his rifle and opened
fire upon them and they replied


When the shooting ceased Jones was
dead and William Desplain badly
wounded

and washed away.


Near Elkins a cloudburst occurred and
the streets of the town were flooded.


At Washington Pa, this afternoon, the
Hazel, Atlas Glass companies plants were
put out of business by floods from over
flowing streams, causing a loss of $780,
900. Street car traffic was crippled and
houses were washed away.


Bridges and buildings continue to float
down the river and the situation on the
Baltimore & Ohio and Western Maryland
is chaotic. The damage to highways will
reach several hundred thousand dollars.

Deputy Sheriff Rufus H. Vincent brought

burgh and Henry Wagner. two young
white men. who escaped from the Marlboro
Jail during the night of March last. The
men were located at Hamilton. small
village on the Hartford road in Baltimore
county. where they were working for a
dairyman Speanburgh was going under
the name of Harry Webster and Wagner
was known as Harry Williams. The for
mer was charged with burglary at Heu-
rich's farm last Christmas day and Wag-
ner was charged with burglary committed
at Capitol Heights. The men escaped from
jail while the jailer was at supper. They
tried to persuade other prisoners to &C
company them, but were unsuccessful
Speanburgh had been serving a sentence
in the jail at Towson and was released
Sunday evening.

washed out culvert while going at high

ditch No one was injured.

afternoon passengers and mail were
transferred and brought to town.

night accompanied heavy rain, which is
the first fall of any consequence within
the last year and a half

clear across the desert from Mecca to
Yuma, and train No, 10 was held at I'M
perial junction for twenty four hours.

text:
LONDON, February 9.-Titled women, clad
in silk and velvet, women with university
degrees, girl graduates in caps and gowns,
women artists, members of the .Lyceum and
other women's clubs, temperance advocates
and women textile workers, gathered from
all parts of the country this afternoon and
marched in procession through the rain and
muddy streets of London in support of the
movement in favor of women suffrage The
participants in the procession were mar
shaled at Hyde Park and with bands and
banners marched through Picadilly, Regent
street and Pail Mall to Trafalgar square
and Exeter Hall, where a public meeting
was held.


The speakers demanded the early atten-
ton of parliament to the bill providing for
the enfranchisement of women. The dem
onstration included such we'll ,nown per-
sons as Lady Frances Balfour, sister of the
ex-premier; Lady Maud Parry and other
titled women Mrs. Fawcett, widow of the
former postmaster general, and most of the
leaders of the more important suffrage
societies, who are utterly opposed to the
militant methods of the so-called "suffrag-
ettes," who recently were carried out of the
house of commons by policemen and COM
mitted to prison for disturbing the peace.


There were several thousand women in the
procession, which was half mile long.

Orlando *. Fitzsimmons of ill-fame in
connection with the notorious Cumulative
Credit company which operated from
palatial offices in Los Angeles and San
Francisco until it was exposed by The
Herald, must serve his six months SEN
tence in the local county jail for having
violated the laws against using the United
States mails for the purpose of boosting
a lottery scheme


Judge Olin Wellborn, in the United
States district court, yesterday filed the
remittitur following the refusal of the
United States circuit court of appeals to
sustain Fitzsimmons appeal and the sen-
tence went into immediate effect. The
prisoner 'also paid fine of $3.50, and mis-
associates John w. Neighbors and Dalton
Arnett, were let off easily with the pay
ment of like sum, without imprison-
ment


Fitzsimmons worked his lottery graft
for long time with apparent success.
and his offices in the Mason building
looked like the headquarters of big cor
poration. But l.: Il. Valentine, who was
United States district attorney at the
time, finally accumulated enough evidence
to obtain his indictment before the grand
jury, and he was convicted October O.
1905. Ever since that time Fitzsimmuns
has put up hard legal fight for freedom
but his attorneys, Walter e. Bacon and
Burrel ID. Neighbours, were unable to
clear him.


The Cumulative Credit scheme was
worked on the idea of each subscriber
putting in about S1OO per month, and then
drawings were held whereby the lucky
subscriber got $3.50. The company de-
pended on the delinquency of the poorer
subscribers and the catching of fresh
dupes in large numbers to keep the farce
up. Many people of small means suffered
when the inevitable break came.

STEPHEN WEIR. wealthy young American,
~ who was First Secretary of the American Lega-
ton at Constantinople, was watching the Sultan 8
procession to the mosque when his attention was
attracted to beautiful girl in of the Sultan's
carriages, who displayed card containing the
words, Il want you to help mel" He was en-
raptured with the girl and was on the point of
rushing to her, when his companion, Mrs. Grace
Blake, an American friend, drew him back, with an
exclamation at his dangerous imprudence.


Two days prior to this, Rhasneh, lovely young
Turkish woman, was told by her father, Takshan
Pasha, high Government official that she must
prepare to marry Haleb Bey, Turkish society
devotee. Her mother had been an American, and
she was brought up with some disregard for Oriental
bigotry, she had filled her mind with modern
romances She was in despair; for she had longed
for marriage with love- which she did not have for
Haleb Bey.


She dreamed that night of being saved from
death by handsome young foreigner; and in the
morning was astounded to see the same foreigner
rowing on the Bosporus beneath her window She
Immediately fell wildly in love with him, and that
forenoon displayed her card with its peculiar word
ing. to him when he was watching the parade:


Chrysanthy Mavrocorthato, of Greek family of
liberal tendencies. promised to help Rhasneh in her
love affair, and that night at her garden party dis
played elaborate life size portrait of the Turkish
girl to Weir. The latter found the next day that
it had been Rhasneh herself who posed in the
frame.


Chrysanthy eloped with her tutor, and was dis
inherited.

Some of the kindred spirits who gather

the war in South Africa. The Briton had
never before visited this country, but he
had evidently heard much of the wonders
to be found here, and If the stories told by
the arriving passengers are true they found
greater wonders for him than even the
usual newcomer hears.


When the vessel was nearing Sandy Hook

sort of a place Sandy Hook was and who
lived there.


why Sandy Hook isn't land" he was
told. Its merely the place where the
big hook comes out to meet incoming
steamers."


This led the captain to ask other ques-
tons. He was told that the latest Yankee
invention was hook for towing big ves-
sells into New York harbor. 1t was ex-
planned to him that a big hook was sent
out on a powerful tug to grasp vessels and
bring them into port. For this reason the
place where the hook met steamers was
called Sandy Hook.


The captains friends further declared with
their hands on their hearts that late on
Saturday night, when the Amerika was
nearing the Hook, the captain went on deck
and remained there until nearly o'clock
in the morning, explaining that he did
not wish to miss the sight Of the Hook
coming out to meet the Amerika.


The captain had vanished before report
ers could tell him what the other fellows
were saying about him, but the other fell
lows said that was his modesty.

steamship Como were arrested by
policemen and immigration guards this
afternoon at the Greenwich dock in an
attempt to escape from the vessel and
were taken to the harbor station and
from there across the bay to Alameda
county Jail. A complaint charging
them with being illegally in the United
States will be sworn out tomorrow

han, Chinese inspector in charge.

The wholesale graduation of foot ball
stars that will affect Yale, Harvard and
Princeton has caused widespread specu-
lation as to where these teams are to
get material to fill the gaps that will
be left. Harvard graduates nine of the
men who played against Yale; Yale loses
eight of those who played against Har-
ward and Princeton, and Princeton loses
seven of her eleven. Pennsylvania and
Cornell also suffer losses. The most seri-
Gus difficulty that confronts Yale and
Harvard is to find quarterback. as each
loses its quarterback. Tad Jones and
Dimes graduate from, Yale and Newhall
and Starr from Harvard.

Durango, Colo-Three children OF
Samuel Cook, Julia, fourteen; Rose,
eleven, and Sallie, five years old, were
literally trapped and drowned in a hor-
rible fashion Wednesday afternoon.
The three children were returning from
school and were walking through an
arroya, when above them they saw a
wall of water ten feet high coming
down from cloudburst in the foothills.


Julia, the eldest, believing that she
saw chance for shelter, made heroic
effort to save her sisters, and, regard
less of her own danger, dragged her
two sisters up the hill to a cave, where
she believed they would be safe from
the flood.


But the volume of water in the flood
was more than she had calculated and
in spite of her efforts to find safe
place the water climbed up to where
the three little ones had sought safety
and they were all drowned. The cave
was completely filed with the water
and then the cave fell in, burying the
bodies.


The girls were missed from home
shortly after the time they should have
returned and a searching party at once
sought them out The hats of the chill
dren showed where they had been and
the search followed.

SOUTH NORWALK, March 20-James
Cooms of Darien was arraigned in the po-
lice court here yesterday on the unusual
charge of painting his baby green on Sum-
day Cooms was on parade Saturday
night and was still going some on Sunday
morning when he marched home with pot
of paint. His wife was asleep and while
she slumbered he painted his young hope
full green and then left the house to re-
sumo his celebration.


Mrs. Cooms was shocked when she awoke
and saw her infant had turned green over
night. When she learned what had hap
pened she became very angry The child
had licked off some of the green paint,
which failed to agree with 1t. Mrs. Cooms
had her patriotic spouse arrested and APP
peared in person to make the charge. He
was fined 81 and sent to Jail for thirty days.

CHICAGO, December 24.-Four masked
men entered thefsaloon Of William Wright
last night and obtained 800 in money.
eight gold watches and four revolvers.


The watches and currency were secured
from fifteen patrons of the saloon. The
men were playing cards when the visitors,
each presenting revolver. entered. The
players were persuaded to drop their game
for moment and line up at the bar,
where two Of the quartet accepted their
contributions while the others stood at
present arms.


After the ceremony one of the collectors
went behind the bar and Invested the cash
register Of $40. Then the four left the
saloon and escaped.

Bound from Port Elizabeth to Hali-

consumed before aid came.


Distress signals were run up to the
masthead, and the hungry seamen lined
along the vessels rails, straining their
eyes in search of the horizon for signs
of relief. and frantically waved their
arms for help when any ship, real or
imag aginary, came into range of vision.


Early that morning the Snowflake's
lookout saw the distress signals and
reported that the bark seemed to be
shipping heavy seas. He could see the
sailors waving their arms, and the Brit
ish tanker was soon run alongside. A
boat loaded with water and provisions,
on order of Captain Kell, was lowered
and the cargo transferred to the bark.


Their distress relieved, the bark's
crew thought the supplies sufficient to
see them through, and their voyage was
resumed. The ships met in latitude
1905. longitude 50.17.

BUFFALO Feb. 13.-Blind almost all
her life and forced to earn her own liv-
ing by sewing rags, Miss Eliza Cosle-
man, now SO years old, has mastered
the art of threading needle to such
perfection that her blindness does not
bother her in the least. She threads
the needle with her tongue.


Miss Cosleman lives within a few
miles of Buffalo, and recently gave a
little exhibition for some visitors. She
took the needle in her left hand, rolling
the thread in her right, while she rolled
or put a point on the thread with the
free fingers of her right hand. She
then placed the needle on her tongue
and. as she explained. found the eye, so
that when she put the thread in her
mouth with her right hand she could
pass 1t through the opening of the
needle.


She threaded an ordinary needle the
first attempt and readily detected the
difference when one with an eye too
small for the thread was handed her.

physiological effe cts of odors, and
German physician enters new field

belief that strong perfumes have an
Intoxicating and benumbing action.
His experiments were made by plac-
ing frogs under glass bells with
sponges saturated with the essences.
AS in chloroform poisoning, brief ex-
citement is followed by partial or COM
plete paralysis, and the many odors
tried seemed to differ only in rapidity

est. Camphor, peppermint, lavender

turpentine, elder flower, ylang-ylang,
asafoetida, carbon disulphide, mustard
and nicotine were rapid and energetic.
Instantaneous action was noted in
some cases. Jumping about moment
or two In lively way, the frog would
very soon stop, close his eyes and rub
his nose, while breathing and heart
action became slow and he freely per-
spired. Continued little longer, the
cdor caused convulsive breathing, roll
ing Of the eyes, and gradual stoppage
of the heart.

text:
BEFORE the days of books, parchments be-
- came SO costly that economical scholars
erased more or less perfectly what had been
written, and used them a second time. In
this manner some highly interesting and valua-
BILE manuscripts have been lost to the world.
But in many cases the ancient characters are
still family visible. Twice used manu-
scripts are called palimpsests, and many mod
ern scholars have strained their eyes in the
effort to decipher the original writing.


Of late years photography has been success
fully applied in Germany for this work. The
color of the faded ink of the older writing on
palimpsest is yellow. Aphotograph of such
manuscript was made through yellow screen.
The result was negative on which the old writ
ing was barely discernible, being little darker
than the background, while the later black
writing was found to appear distinctly as white
letters.


Next an ordinary negative on bromide
plate was made, and from this was produced
a transparent positive on which both writings
appeared dark and about equally distinct.
Then the transparency was superimposed on
the first negative so that the dark letters of
the later writing covered the light letters,
representing the same writing in the negative.
They were thus eliminated, being indistinguish-
ably merged with the general dark background
produced by the combination of positive and
negative. But the earlier characters since
they were dark in both cases, appeared in the
combination intensely black and distinct.
headline: Ingenious Use of Photography

breakers which rolled in along the beach last
night tore away 100 feet of sheet piling from
each of the two jettes being built at the
mouth of the San Gabriel river by the Los
Angeles Dock ana Terminal company. The
sheet piling only recently put The

Manager c. j. Curtis of the Dock and Ter
minal company said this morning that he felt
much gratifed that the jetties, in their unfn-
ished condition, stood the severe test well
they did.


Throughout last night and all of today the
tide has been unusually high. Huge combers
have rolled in upon the beach in quick sue
cession.


Bathers in the surf have hugged the shore
closely. There were no accidents in the water


today, however. An attempt made to
keep the lifeboat out this morning, but part
of the time the breakers were so high that
the life savers in the station the beach
were unable to see the guard out in the boat.
