Henry a. Frazier, a newspaper man who
lives on Heller avenue, rescued Los Angeles
woman and her three small children from a
dangerous tide riP off the foot of Hermosa
avenue last night. While on his way home
going along the bluff, Frazier the little
party bathing in the surf. Suddenly huge
breaker swept over them, throwing them off
their feet, and the undertow carried them sea-
ward.


One end of long rope he was carrying
Frazier tied around palm tree on the bluff
Ringing the othel end over the edge of the
cliff, he slid rapidly down. then rolled aud
jumped the rest of the way down the hill 10
the base of the hill. Plunging into the water,
he seized the three children and carried them
ahsore. The woman by this time had re-
gained her footing and reached the sand safely.
Several amusing incidents occurred this morn
ing and afternoon along the beach, when wom-
en- and children lying asleep or nearly so upon
the sand in places normally high and dry
we're completely immersed by tricky tides
which crept up about them


From until clock this afternoon the tides
grew to their highest and the beach was
thronged with sightseers.

breakers four miles east of the pier last
evening and was only kept from going
ashore by the crew throwing out the
anchor.

assistance from Capt. Art Paschall of the

trouble. The machinery was repaired and

BOSTON, July 15-With eight OF her
officers and crew dead and thirteen 9TH
ers either dying or suffering from terri
BILE burns received in an explosion OF
powder in the after superimposed tur-
ret, the battleship Georgia steamed
slowly up Boston harbor from the target
practice grounds in Cape Cod bay late
tonight and landed the dead and injured
men at Charlestown navy yard.
With the arrival of the Georgia there
became known the details of the most
terrible naval accident that has ever
taken place along the coast of New
England.


The accident occurred shortly before
noon today while the Georgia's crew
were at target practice off Barnstable,
in Cape Cod bay.


In some manner, as yet unexplained,
two bags of powder became ignited and
in the terrible flash that followed the
entire turret crew, consisting of three
officers and eighteen men, were engulfed
in fire and received horrible burns, one
officer and five men dying before the
ship reached port.


The victims of the accident are:


Dead:


GOLDTHWAITE, FAULKNER, mid
shipman, Kentucky.


THACKER, w. j.. turret captain, Will
mington, Del.


BURKE, w, j., seaman. Quincy. Mass.
HAMlLION, aGBORGE H., ordinary
seaman, South Framingham, Mass.


MILLER, GEORGE E., ordinary sea-
man, Brooklyn, N. Y.

Newport, r. 1.


PAIR, WILLIAM, Brooklyn.


GOODRICH. LIEUT.. CASPER, Brook
lyn, N. Y; burned fatally.


Seriously injured:


Cruise, James t. midshipman, Ne
braska; hands and face burned, very Sc
riousIy.

second class, North Adams, Mass; back.
chest, arms and face burned.

class New York; face and hands
burned.


Taglund, Orley, chief yeoman, Rich
ford, Mimi; arms. back and face burned
Walsh, Ed. j., seaman, Lynn, Mass;
chest and face burned fatally.

York; face, arms and chest burned; pos
sibly fatal.


Eich. Charles L., ordinary seaman,
Frankfort. Ind. face, arms and hands
burned.


Fone. John A.. ordinary seaman, South
wick, Mass; two-thirds of body burned.
Gilbert. Harold L.. ordinary seaman.
Southwick, Mass; two-thirds of body
burned.


Maleck, John c.. ordinary seaman,
Cleveland, Ohio; arms and face burned


Meese, Louis o., ordinary seaman, Be
rea, Ohio; arms, face and chest burned


Rosenberger, Samuel L., ordinary sea-
man, arms and face burned.


Thomas, James P, ordinary seaman
Brooklyn. N. Y; face and arms, chest and
back burned.


Other men received minor injuries.
Their names were not given out and they
were not taken off the ship.


The explosion occurred after the super
imposed turret where the men under
command of Lieut.. Casper Goodrich. son
of Rear Admiral Goodrich commandant
of the New York navy yard, and Midship-
men Faulkner Goldthwaite and James T.
Cruise were operating the S-inch guns


Ammunition ExpIodes


The guns in the forward turrets had
finished eight rounds of practice and the
guns of the after turret had fired one
round.


Two cases, as the big 100 pounds of
powder are called, had just been sent up
through the ammunition hoists and were
in the arms of the loader, whose name
was withheld by the ships officers


The loader stood at the breech of one of
the S-inch guns, ready to insert the
charge.


AT this instant the turret was seen to
be smoking and two men who stood near



indicating that the charge had ignited
and was smoldering.


The loader discovered the spot at the
same instant and threw himself forward
on his face at the same time shouting a
warning to his turret mates.


The other men who had seen the smoke
were Eich and Hansell. and they also
threw themselves on the floor of the tur-
ret.


Before the other men in the turret
could understand what caused the load
er's cry of warning there was a binding
flash as the burning powder exploded.


Flames, smoke and nauseous gases filed
the little superstructure, where more
than dozen men were confined.


AS the powder was not confined there
was no report, nor did the vessel suffer
any injury, but every nook and corner
of the turret was filed with flames.


Loader Badly Burned


The loader. who was of course nearest
the powder, was terribly burned, as was
every other man in the turret, with the
exception of Eich and Hansell, who, all
though scorched, escaped with injuries
much less severe than the others.


Blinded by the smoke and flames,
choked by the acrid, penetrating, gaseous
fumes, and maddened by the pain, the
men screamed in agony.


Some staggered blindly about the lad
der to the hatchway in the top of the
turret, while others crept along the tur-
ret floor, begging piteously for assistance.
Lieutenant Goodrich and Seaman MaleS
became crazed staggered up the iron lad
der to the top of the turret. and threw
themselves headlong into the sea. in
despairing effort to choose death by
drowning in preference to the death by
slow fire.


When the smoke of the burning powder
had cleared away the shipmates of the
unfortunate men rushed to their assist
ance, and tenderly the suffering sailors
were lifted out of the fire blackened tur-
ret and quickly conveyed to the ships
hospital where their burns were dressed
by the surgeon

text:
Fighting and struggling for her
freedom and occasionally swearing at
her guards, Miss Lucy Van Meter, a
talented young artist, yesterday was
taken before the insanity commission
in department two of the superior
court and there adjudged insane.


The young woman lost her mind in
the pursuit of her art.


Miss Van Meters mother, Mrs.
Fannie Van Meter of Twelfth street,
testified that her daughter had been
good girl all her life, that she had
never even heard language of ques-
tionable character and yet as soon as
she became crazed her one thought re-
Verted to the language of the streets.


Miss Van Meter is 20 years of age
and n native of Illinois She began
painting when she was little girl and
simply gave UP her life for the sake
of art. Throughout Missouri, Nebraska
and Illinois in the various places she
has lived with her parents, her work
had been continued and some of her
clever sketches of mountain scenery
are now gracing fashionable eastern
homes.


Paints in Blisterine Sun


For several years she restricted her
work to portrait painting and then she
decided to come west. The oils and
water colors of the great American
desert lured her. She had seen such
paintings on exhibit and her one ambi-
ton was to paint the desert, to trans
NIT the marvellous hues of morn and
eve to canvas, and she came west with
her father and mother to live. The
father settled at Macy, Ariz., and the
girl went to the desert. Day after day
the horrible heat beat down upon her
head and she became nervous. Her
people attempted to persuade her to
give up her work, but she refused to
listen to them. She painted and
painted, the sun blistered the varnish
on the easel and beat down on her
head, but her brush was untiring.


One day several months ago she
walked into her mothers room and
stood there looking at her parent.
Then, without a word, she fell to the
floor as though she had been shot.
For fourteen days and nights Miss Van
Meter remained unconscious. On the
fifteenth day when she awoke from her
sleep of paralysis she failed to recog-
nize her people.


Operation Is FruitIess


Her mother and brother brought her
to Los Angeles on Christmas day in
the hope that she might gain strength
here. She was taken to a hospital and





been her constant attendant.
Several days ago an operation was
performed in last forlorn hope of
bringing back to sanity the wandering
mind Of the girl, but the operation
proved fruitless.


Yesterday when Miss Van Meter ap-
peared in court She brought some
scraps of drawing paper with her. She
would place some object before her and
carefully measure the dimensions with
her eye as though preparing to begin
some drawing, and then she would
laugh, and her long slender fingers
would crush the paper.


The examination was a short one and
the girl was declared insane. AS she
sat there, waiting to be taken back to
the county hospital before her trip to
the asylum, she sang in a sweet, clear
voice the refrain of mo, Never Alone"
then without another word she accom-
panied the guards on what will prob
ably be her last journey, for her case
is considered nearly hopeless.

PROVIDENCE, r. l.. February 23.-Tfn-

mediately after the collision Capt. McVay

that time out.

evidence

heard any inquiries made as to the where

passengers.

PASADENA, March 15.--"We, the

Frank M. Washburn, came to his death
by nitric acid poisoning, administered
with suicidal intent" Thus closed the
last chapter in the life of one of the
Crown city's most prominent jewelers..
He had struggled long and wearily
against misfortune after misfortune,
and the overwhelming blow came at
last, crushing out what little hope in
life there remained. He had been a
devoted follower of church work and
a devoted father to the wife and chill
dren who survive him.

not until the autopsy surgeon this
morning discovered that the stomach
had been eaten away by the fatal
poisoning that the suicide theory was
advanced, believed and acted upon by

HUGaTOwN, Dec. 14.--After sue
cessfully riding out a. succession OF
gales which she encountered all the
way across the Atlantic in which she
lost her lifeboats, the American
schooner Thomas W. Lawson was cap
sized in Broad sound, Scilly islands
where the captain took shelter from
the fiertl storm raging along the Eng
lish coast last night.


OF the crew of eighteen, including
Pilot Hicks. who boarded the vessel
from the life savers, boat during the
night, only three were rescued. These
were Captain G. w. Dow of Melrose,
Mass. Edward L. Rowe, the engineer,
of Wiscasset, Me-, and George Alien
of Bramford, England.


The schooner left Philadelphia NO
vember Is for London with a cargo OF
oil. She had hard battle with the
seas all the way across, and when she
entered Broad sound her captain, know
ing the dangers Of the coast, threw OUT
his anchors.


Later. in answer to his signals of dis
tress, the life savers put out two boats
and found the Lawson anchored In a
dangerous position off Gunner's rock.
The seas were running high and the
gale was increasing and the life savers
found that their efforts. at rescue We're
useless, One of the boats returned for
a tug and the other was compelled to
put bac-s to shere because of the ex-
hausted condition of the men. During
the absence the Thomas w. Lawson
turned turtle.


Heroic Rescues Effected


Allen, one of the rescued men, Is not
expected to live, and Captain Dow Is
suffering from a broken arm. HIS
rescue was effected only through al
most superhuman efforts of the life
savers and the gallantry of Frederick
Hicks, son of Pilot Hicks, who accom-
panied them on their second trip in the
hope OF Finding his father.


Late this afternoon after long
search Captain Dow and Engineer Rowe
were found alive in. the HelwetheN
rocks, to which they clung for more
than fifteen hours, the tremendous
waves preventing their making land
ing Young Hicks plunged into the
boiling seas and swan ashore, carry
ing a life line by means of which Allen
and the captain were hauled back to
the boat. The engineer, who was prac-
tically uninjured, was then pulled
ashore.


After assisting Captain Dow. Hicks
was able to reach the boat unaided, but
the effort exhausted him and the life
savers ordered him to remain quiet to-
night.


Captain Dow told the life savers that
when he found his ship was doomed he
the engineer and the pilot lashed them
selves to the Inizzen rigging. When
the masts fell the captain and the pilot
managed to get clear. They jumped to
the deck, but were washed overheard,
being carried by the currents to the
rocks, where they were found. Pilot
Hicks however seemed to be entan-
gled in the rigging and was lost.

escape but was later arrested and taken back

town than be was taken from the officers and

ment prevailed in the town and other troubles
were feared. but fortunately nothing further
occurred to disturb the peace of the town.

So certain was the father that the child
was free from danger, he left the build
ing to do some work on the outside.
While absent there was sharp, loud
noise inside the building and rushing back
the father found his son lying ifeless on
the floor near the large switchboard.
Elmer Chase, the father, operator at the
station, lifted the lifeless form of his
child and dashed upstairs to the apart
ments of himself and wife. Physicians
were hurriedly called but found the little
fellow had been instantly killed by the
terrible shock.

station the baby crawled through the
iron fence, toddled over to the switch-
board and, attracted by the bright brass
bands and polished knobs, reached forth
his hands to examine them. AS soon as
the brass connections were touched a
short circuit was formed, and thousands
of volts of electricity were thrown into
the little body. Death was instantaneous

srated with grief over the boys death.

heard nothing more until the doors were

OMAHA, Sept 6.-The Rocky Mountain
Limited on the Rock Island road was
raided this morning just before daylight
near Murdoch. Neb.., by three masked
men,


The robbers went through the chair car,
robbing every passenger of their pocket
books and purses covered the train crew
with revolvers and escaped by leaping
from the train.


The robbers were passengers on the
train. Shortly after leaving Murdoch the
men arose in their seats, their faces COW
cred with Masks and with revolvers in
each hand surveyed the passengers.


Then the leader ordered everybody to
keep still and not make resistance else
they would be shot. Two men went down
the aisles with hats in hand, while the
third kept the passengers covered. All
passengers were ordered to throw pocket
books into the hats, and this was done.


The conductor appeared in the car with
a pistol in his hand, but was promptly
covered with four guns and forced to
drop his revolver.


After getting all the money in the car
the robbers jumped from the train while
1t had slowed down for a grade. An at
tempt was made to enter the sleeping car.
but the door was locked.


The pursuit is being prosecuted vigor.
ously with bloodhounds.

FOR instance, canoe express was descending the
= Mackenzie River; the canoe smashed in ice
jam, and the packeteers were drowned. A few weeks
later passing Indians caught sight of stick bobbing
on the surface of the stream. Though the water
deep and the current running at the rate of three
miles hour the stick remained in the place
So the Indians padded over to investigate. They
found that to the floating stick fastened long
thong, which on being pulled up brought the missing
packet to light.


Again. while making camp the Athabasca
River the packeteers had slung the packet in tree
the usual place for it while in camp. During the
night their fire spread and burned up the whole
equipment except the tree, which, being green, re-
ceived little more than a scorching. The packet vas
unframed.


On Great Slave Lake during fierce storm
the packeeers became separated from their dogs and
were frozen to death. But the packet recovered


In one autumn two packeteers journeying from
Georges River post to Ungava post drew up their
canoe on sandy beach, and camped beneath a
high, overhangng bank. During the night the bank
gave way and buried them as they slept. When the
ice formed, the trader at Ungava sent out two men
to search for the missing packet They found the
canoe on the beach, and, from the appearance of
the bank, conjectured what had happened. Next
spring the landslide dug into, and the packeteers
found both lying under the blanket, their
heads resting upon the packet.

Bertha Jane Routt of Long Beach, 10
years of age, who had frequently told
her younger sister, Mile, that she
would kill herself if she had any quar-
rel with her lover, fulfilled her promise
last night when her sweetheart came
to Los Angeles against her wishes.


The girl drank nearly half pint of
carbolic acid and the three physicians
VINO were summoned at once pro-
nounced her case hopeless. She died
at o'clock, forty-flve minutes after
drinking the poison.


Bertha Jane Routt was the daugh-
ter of Edman Routt, a brick con-
tractor living at 1345 Railway street,
Long Beach,


For five months she had been the
sweetheart of Sydney Crosby, a brick
layer, 21 years of age, whose home is
on East Sixth street, Long Beach.


Two weeks ago the girls father or
dered Crosby to discontinue his fire.
quent visits, claiming that the late
hours his daughter was keeping would
prove disastrous to her health.


Rather than lose the pleasure of her
sweetheart's visits the girl decided to
leave home, and with her sister secured
a room at the little home of Mr.. and
Mrs. A. Lewis, 249 East Fifth street.
Prior to this time Bertha had been
working several months as a domestic
in Seventh street residence. This
place she held after moving to the
Lewis home.


Here young Crosby continued his Wis
it's, according to Mrs. Lewis, every
night. Several times the elder sister
told the younger one that If anything
went wrong between her and Crosby
she would do something desperate and
hinted at self destruction. Her sister,
however, did not take these threats
seriously.


Bids Sweetheart Good BY


Last night about o'clock Crosby called
and after a short conversation said
that he had to go to Los Angeles and
that he was to meet party there on
business at o'clock. Bertha begged
him not to go, saying that she was
lonesome and that she believed he was
going to Los Angeles to see another
girl. Crosby was firm, however and
soon started for the street to catch
car bound for Los Angeles. The
Routt girl followed him to the street,
having, in accordance with his instruc-
tions, placed O shawl about her shoul-
ders. With tears in her eyes she bade
him good by. Then she returned to her
room, whore her sister lay almost
asleep. A moment after. lying down
upon the bed she began to tremble
violently and her sister was aroused.
The girl complained that she had a
terrible headache, then fell back on the
bed, motionless. Thus she lay, uncon-
scious, until death ensued.


A number of neighbors We're at her
bedside when the end came. The ia
ther arrived a few moments later. 1t
was hard for him. for but four weeks
ago his little son died of spinal menin-
gifts. The girls mother died many
years ago, but her father had remar-
ried.


A pint bottle. half full of carbolic
acid, was found hidden among the bed
clothing.


The body was taken to Cleveland &
Harris morgue and the coroner noti-
fed.

Marie, pronounced her cargo to be contra
band and sank her The cruiser was even
tually interned at Batavia, Island of Java,

ough belief in the soundness and honesty of

My Dear Mr.. Cortelyou: 1 congratulate you
upon the admirable way in which you have
handled the present crisis. congratulate also

men who in this crisis have acted with such
wisdom and public spirit BY their action they
did invaluab BILE service in checking the panic,
which. beginning a matter of speculation.

business No one who considers calmly can
question that the underlying conditions which
make up our financial and industrial wellbeing

dealing and speculative enterprise are merely

men in question has been of the utmost conse-
quence and has secured opportunity for the
calm consideration which must inevitably pro-

tons. Faithfully yours.


THEODORE ROOSEVELT.

CHICAGO, ILL.,, March 1.-The town will
be full of ball tossers tonight and tomor-
row for the clans of both Chance and Can
tillon will be assembling. Cubs will flock
in from all directions and so will the Sena-
tors. Chances men will hover round the
Masonic Temple and Cantillon's tribe will
frequent the Log Cabin. There will net be
much fraternizing, as the players of these
two teams are less acquainted than is the
rule In big league society. The Cubs have
never met most of the Senators.


Joe Tinker, the great shortstop Of the
Chicago Cubs, will not be with the team
on the trip to New Orleans and may not
get into the play before May !, or even
later. The lightning infielder has been
stricken with appendicitis and was taken to
the Monroe Street Hospital today for a
hurried operation. Tinkers condition while
serious is not believed dangerous, as no
time was lost when the disease was located.

two other officers were attracted by the
sound of firearms and when they made
their appearance Delgado turned his
weapon on them. Hosick drew his re-
volver and shot the Mexican, one bullet
entering the abdomen and another the
left side.


The man was taken to the receiving
hospital, where an operation was per-
formed and he was later sent to ths
county hospital. The body is at Pierce
Brothers undertaking rooms. An inquest
will probably be held today.

MARION, o., Aug. 5.-After being
buried under twenty-five tons of hay for
a week without food or water, during
which time bloodhound and hundreds
of searchers passed within few feet of
her Miss N A. Black, a Pittsburg school
teacher who last Monday evening left
local sanitarium, was found yesterday.
She probably will recover.


She was discovered near the old hay
barn where all trace of her was lost
Tuesday.


Miss Black says she took a stroll into
the country and when dusk was falling
started home. 1t was chilly and she was
but thinly clad. She entered a barn, got
inside the hay and fell asleep. Tuesday
morning the owner of the barn began
filling the barn with new hay and by
night it was full to the rafters.


Yesterday, almost crazed by thirst, the
young woman burrowed out of the barn,
but was SO weak she fell where she was
found.

Partisan women are holding Indignation

nual rush of Americans for clothes is

A large audience greeted Mr.. Dwight Ell
mendorf. the traveloguist. when he stepped
upon the stage at the National Theater
yesterday afternoon. His discourse yes
terday was on Norway and it's wonderful
fjords.


Supplemental to the lecture, Mr.. Elmen-
harbor, the starting point on the journey
to Norway.


From Hamburg the audience was trans
ported quickly to Christiania, where the
first glimpses of Norwegian life were given
in motion pictures. The wonderful geo.
logical formations known as fjords (fiords)
are the striking characteristics of Norways
scenery. Despite the fact that bright,
clear day Is an exception in that faraway
northland, the views were reproduced on
the canvas with fidelity to the natural
conditions. Many deep ravines between
mountains, whose precipitous rocky sides
stretch skyward from 500 to 5000 feet
high, extend back from the coast for
eighty or one hundred miles and are very
often fully two miles deep. The width
varies, some places being so narrow that
no ocean steamer can enter them, notwith-
standing the fact that the water Is often
400 feet deep when the ocean bed just
outside the ford is only 400 or 500 feet
deep.


Bergen, Macs. Trondhjem and Digger
mullen were visited, and many of the strik-
ing characteristics of Norwegian life and
the fish industry were shown. Chief among
the views We're those showing the corona
ton of King Haakon, and In a motion
picture the audience got several glimpses
of the king and his little son.


Next week Mr.. Elmendorf will close his
series of lectures with the Land of the
Midnight SUM- This season has been Mr.

San Juan Del Sur.-Word has been
received here from President Zelaya
of Nicaragua, in Namasiquo, Hondu.
ras, declaring that the bloodiest battle
in the history of Central America
costing 500 lives, has been fought and
won in that place.


The struggle lasted three days, be-
ginning on March 17th The Nicara-
guam army of invasion, intrenched in
Namasiquo, was suddenly confronted
by the combined forces of the Hon.
durans and the Salvadorans. the latter
having taken the field as the ally of
| Honduras.


1t was the flower of the Salvadoran
army, together with the best troops
President Bonilla of Honduras could
| master. The allied forces suddenly
threw themselves upon the city
shortly before dawn on the 18th. Then
followed incessant firing for seventy
two hours.


President Zelaya in person CON-
manded the Nicaraguan troops. The
first onslaught of the combined forces
was repulsed. but the Salvadorans and
Hondurans renewed the attack. The
firing grew heavier and again the al
lied troops were repulsed. This hap
pened again and again, the Nicara-
guans always being successful in
keeping the enemy at bay.


After three days of unsuccessful at
tacks, the allied army withdrew.


At first it was believed that once
more the assault would be ordered,
but soon it was seen that the COM
bined forces had retired for good.


When he Nicaraguans left their de-
fenses they found 500 dead and 300
wounded Hondurans and Salvadorans
on the field. The Nicaraguans lost
300 killed and about the same number
wounded. All the bodies of the dead
were buried.


Many Hondurans were taken prison
ers, including General Martinez, who
was wounded, together with other Off
GERS.

PORTSMOUTH, England, Aug. 9-The
200 ships of war constituting Great Brit
aims fleet paraded before King Edward
and Queen Alexandra today on the So
lent, and incidentally furnished mag
nificent pageant for the opening OF the
annual Cowes regatta week.


Spread out in seven long lines between
the Isle of Wight and the Hampshire
shore, this splendid array of vessels,
great and small, formed a floating steel
city with population of $1,000 officers
and men.


Never before have so many British
men-of-war been seen together under the
control of single admiral. From the
battleship Dreadnaught down to the
smallest submarine every vessel was
decked from stem to stern with flags.
The crews were assembled on deck, and
as the king and queen, on board the
royal yacht Victoria and Albert, passed
down the lines each ships company gave
a rousng cheer.


For eleven miles up and down the king
and queen steamed between steel walls


This gathering of warships forms the
recently organized home guard section
of the British navy, and the government
and the admiralty are so proud of the
assemblage that they departed from the
usual rule about the visitors, and threw
the entire fleet open to the critical in
spection of the public. Dotted through
the lines were no fewer than six fiagships,
headed by the Dreadnaught. The splen-
did naval panorama was completed by
scores of pleasure yachts clustered off the
Uncovered walls of the Royal Yacht
squadron'S castle at Cowes.


Hosts of pleasure launches and excur-'
sionists' steamers loaded with thousands
of the general public, each with it's band
of music playing, helped to enliven the
unusually attractive scene. The weather,
which was gloomy early in the morning,
cleared UP before the departure of the
king from Portsmouth.

Special to The Herald.


RIVERSIDE, May 5.-This city threw
itself wide open to the incoming Shrin-
ers today, and every temple that passed
through tasted it's boundless hospital
ity The consequence was that the
first stop in the noted southland of
California will long be remembered
by those who had just crossed the
burning sands and reached this oasis
with their tongues hanging out and
their camels footsore and weary.


The receptions here began as soon as
the special trains reached the several
railroad stations. In each depot COM
mittees had thousands of bouquets and
mountains Of oranges, and the trains
were boarded as soon as they stopped,
while Californias glorious blossoms
and golden fruit were passed about In
the greatest abundance. Then lines
were formed in every case and the
Shriners, headed by bands, were es-
corted to Riverside's pride and boast,
the beautiful Glenwood Mission inn,
where Mine Host Frank A. Miller did
the honors Autos and tallyhos were
at the visitors disposal and they were
taken for hasty tours of che city, but
the Mission inn was the spot to which
all clung, and all day it was thronged.


Algeria Warmly Welcomed


The first temple to reach here today
was Algeria, from Montana. 1t was
headed by the famous B. & M. mill
tary band Of fifty players, in fine uni
form, with two drum majors, one
seven feet tall, the other four feet
short.


This great band headed the Algeria
procession, and all marched to the
Mission inn Immediately upon their ar
rival, about 9 o'clock. The party was
greeted there by the sweet sounds OF
the chimes from the campanile, and
by the glad hand from Proprietor Mil
ler, his wife and his excellent staff.
The band formed in the beautiful
lobby and gave an elaborate sacred
concert, while the Shriners and their
wives inspected the hotel and went
into raptures over it's quaint and ar
tistic details The party had break
tasted on it's train, but the two hours
spent here were all too short for the
visit.


At noon, Cyprus temple, from Albany.
with several others, came in and
marched to the Mission inn for lunch
con. This had been ordered the day
before, and Mr. Miller had provided a
spread that made the Shriners sit up
as they had not done in many a day.


Hundreds Banqueted


Several hundred of them partook OF
the Glenwoods famous and typical hos
pitality, and like their predecessors,
became 50 absorbed in it's beauties
that they could scarcely be prevailed
upon to take the drives provided. All
were laden with armfuls of flowers and
pockets full of oranges, and the post
office receipts were largely increased
by their lavish purchases of souvenir
cards of the hotel. All told, some 300
sat down to Mr.. Miller's great meal.


During the late afternoon trains came
thick and fast, and the several depots
became rallying points for most of the
townspeople, who threw in their own
work with that of the regular commit
tees.


No arrivals were permitted to pass
on without abundance of blossoms and
fruit. and in every possible case visit
was made to the Mission inn, whose
fame seems to have extended to the
uttermost corners Of the Shriners' do
main.


Pamphlets and descriptive matter
about Riverside were placed on all
trains, and everyone who stopped was
fully informed both by actual vision
and by reading, about the city and its
chief attractions. The same course
will be pursued all day tomorrow, and
as long as the specials come, and the
attention will be resumed when the
trains begin to return east.

PORTSMOUTH, England, Aug. 3.-The
200 ships of war constituting Great Brit
aims fleet paraded before King Edward
and Queen Alexandra today on the So
lent, and incidentally furnished mag
nificent pageant for the opening of the
annual Cowes regatta week.


Spread out in seven long lines between
the Isle of Wight and the Hampshire
shore, this splendid array of vessels,
great and small formed a floating steel
city with a population of $1,000 officers
| and men.


Never before have so many British
men-of-war been seen together under the
control of single admiral. From the
battleship Dreadnaught down to the
smallest submarine, every vessel was
decked from stem to stern with flags.
The crews were assembled on deck, and
as the king and queen, on board the
royal yacht Victoria and Albert, passed
down the lines each ships company gave
a rousing cheer.


For eleven miles up and down the king
and queen steamed between steel walls.


This gathering of warships forms the
recently organized home guard section
of the British navy, and the government
and the admiralty are so proud of the
assemblage that they departed from the
usual rule about the visitors, and threw
the entire fleet open to the critical In
spection of the public. Dotted through
the lines were no fewer than six hagshlps'
headed by the Dreadnaught. The splen-
did naval panorama was completed by
scores of pleasure yachts clustered off the
Uncovered walls of the Royal Yacht
suuadron'S castle at Cowes.


Hosts of pleasure launches and excur-
sionists' steamers loaded with thousands
of the general public, each with its band
of music playing, helped to enliven the
unusually attractive scene. The weather,
which was gloomy early in the morning
cleared up before the departure of the
king from Portsmouth.

CHICAGO, May 9.-suburban 9. passen-
ger train No. ia on the Burlington
railroad, running between Aurora, ILL.,,
and Chicago, was wrecked today near
Lawdale, six miles from the city, and
twenty passengers were hurt and sew
eral are reported to have been killed.


The train was running at high speed
when the engine struck a broken rail
and leaped from the track. 1t dragged
the baggage car and one coach with
it and all three rolled down small
embankment. The other five coaches
remained on the track.


After leaving the rails the engine slid
along the track for fifty feet and turned
over. 1t rolled down the bank, drag
ging with it the first passenger coach
and the baggage car. The roof of the
first coach was smashed in and all the
passengers were injured more or less
severely.


The wreckage caught fire, but the
flames were quickly eXtinguished. The
steam from the engine burned some of
the passengers, but the injuries from
this cause were not severe. The pas
sengers in the first coach were hurled
into pile. They were rescued with
difficulty. The majority of the injured
were not seriously hurt. Those whose
injury was more severe were carried
away from the wreck and placed on
blankets on the ground. Then they
were carried by ambulances to hos
pitfalls and nearby drug stores.


Harry Newlands the engineer, was
badly scalded and cut, but he aided
in the rescue work. He was unable to
account for the accident, unless the
rails spread.


Mrs. Mary Miller, whose hips were
crushed. died on the way to a hospital
She was the widow of Thomas Miller
formerly freight traffic manager of the
Burlington. When the car overturned
Mrs. Miller was thrown between the
seats and the wreckage piled upon her.
She was conscious when taken from the
car and insisted that she was not badly
hurt She died, however, as she was
being carried into the hospital.

tackled her, had fed. Miss Lizzie Zehder, a

jures are not serious The girls arms and

enough to tell that Barton did the killing

paid to the matter until yesterday, when
neighbors discovered Barton's body lying
on the front porch and that of his wife on
the back porch. The children We're found

to have been responsible for the crime.

battered them down and began his work
of destruction.

after will come on January l., making a

after.

CASA BLANCA, Morocco, Aug. ia
large force of Moors suddenly descended
upon the French camp early yesterday,
but were driven off after sharp conflict.
The tribesmen advanced to within 800
Yards of the city, when Gen. Drude sent
against them under cover of the guns of
the warships detachment of fifty Alger-
ian spahis (Arab horsemen in the French
service).


The Moors permitted the small body Of
cavalry to advance for q half mile un-
molested, when they suddenly ambushed
them and in wild charge got right
among the spahis. The head of one spahi
was cut off with one sweep of big
Moorish sword. The French officer in
command of the spahis and several Of his
men were wounded, but the officer rallied
his forces and slowly retreated, fighting
until a large body of spahis from the town
came to the rescue of their comrades and
routed the Moors.


The fighting covered a front of about 16
miles and lasted from to IL a. m. The
French used field and machine guns with
deadly effect in repelling the attack of
the Moors, and shells from the cruiser
Gloire also rendered efficient service.
The spahis and sharpshooters each lost
one man killed and had several wounded,
including Capt. Coud of the spahis About
dozen horses were killed.


When groups of Moors were first dis
covered the French sharpshooters and
light cavalry were sent to the front and
were followed by the Algerian horsemen.
The engagement was begun at o'clock.
Threafter steady fire from the French
cleared the beach of the enemy, while the
French artillery were exploding shrapnell
shells further south, and at II o'clock the
Moors scattered in every direction. The
French officers believe that the main
body of the Moors remained behind the
ridge.

known.


After attending picnic at New Attn

something besides blood-poisoning, and
an x-ray examination which followed
showed that three ribs on the right side
near the shoulder had been fractured.


After being taken to the hospital and
pressed to make known the cause Of the
accident the young woman told her

young mans name before she died The

Five thousand Shriners, Shrineresses

grove in the valley.

PORTLAND. Ore, July 25.-Deeds of
valor were many among those who passed
through the trying experiences during the
wreck of the steamship Columbia off
Shelter Cove, and to the weaker sex
are accredited acts of surprising courage.


One is that of Miss Watson, who sup
ported Miss Griese for two hours before
being rescued.


The other and by all odds the most
extraordinary is the performance of
Ethel Johnson, IL years old, who saved
two lives-a child of IL and a man.


Buoyed by life preserver little Ethel
held to u-year-old Effie Gordon and later
cheerfully gave aid to Olaf Pearson Of
this city, who, all but exhausted from
his efforts, swan up to her.


Pearson had no life preserver, but by
placing his hand lightly on the childs
shoulder he kept his head above water
until rescue came.


Pearson says the child showed mar
velous presence of mind and remarkable
courage and helped him in every way
she could.


Tows Burdens to Raft


Eventually after much exposure, he
says, the little girl towed her burden to
life raft, upon which all three were
taken.


Her brother, C. Johnson, II years old,
kept hold of his mother, who had been
knocked senseless, and buoying her upon
his shoulders kept her afloat until they
were saved.


To A. Larsen and S. Peterson are
credited the saving of the lives of twen-
ty-siX passengers


During the time that interviewed be-
tween the collision and sinking of the
Columbia the sailors observed several
people vainly trying to clear a lifeboat.


Though the boat was almost a length
away they ran to their assistance and
with their knives cut away the lashings.
filled the boat with twenty-six people
and rowed the boat clear from the whirl-
pool the Columbia caused when she sank.
This was the boat which picked UP Pear
son, Ethel Johnson and Effie Gordon.

don to lay the case of the British colony

for the losses sustained. British interests

BALTIMORE, Aug. 30.-John Leitnerr

Twice within forty-eight hours Leitner
has slumbered peacefully on the top of
a pole, and on both occasions the police
have been called upon to take his sup
posed dead body from the wires.


A few minutes before IL o'clock today
the superintendent of Timanus' mills
telephoned to the Northern Pacific sta
ton that an employee of the Chesapeake
and Potomac Telephone company had
been stricken by electricity and that his
body was resting on the wires.


A moment later the Mount Vernon
mills, the Timanus mills and other indus
turtles in the neighborhood were emptied
of their workmen going to dinner, but
nearly all of them halted and with pity
ing chances and horror-stricken faces
leveled their eyes upon the still figure
on the top of the pole.


The man lay perfectly still. One leg
was thrown over a cross beam, the
other was wrapped around cable, and
his arms were extended and partly rest
ing his dropping head on the beam above
him. Just as the ambulance approached
the pole the supposed dead man awak-
ened, but lay down again.


The policemen recognized him as the
same individual who had fooled them
last Saturday and they ordered him down.
Leitner descended and when he reached
the foot of the pole he staggered SO per-
ceptibly and talked so vaguely Of the
wires being hot" that he was taken into
custody and charged with being drunk.

From the HOusekeeper.


1t was in Japanese kindergarten that I
received my first vivid impressions of what
the training of japanese women means
Twenty thirty butterfly babies sat about
the kindergarten table studying silk
worms. The ugly gray worms were nib
bling industriously in their boxes of green
leaves, and the tiny tots were chattering
about them excitedly. The teacher i'm
posed upon them a hard task, moving the
silk worms into other boxes of fresh leaves
and in order that the stale leaves should
not be put in the fresh boxes 1t was neces-
sary for the children to remove the worms
individually and by the aid of their own
small hands.


The little students understood their order
and knew but to obey, but the worms We're
very ugly and Gravity, and the baby hands
were not eager for their task. Intently l
watched their faces. First they gaZed long
at the worms then puckerng their brows
determinedly prepared to lift them to the
other box. Slowly, slowly, slowly the tiny
thumb and forefinger would draw nearer
to the worms and then when almost touch
ing, within quarter of an inch, there was in
variably little shiver, the hand was quick
ly drawn back and the babies. looking at
their teacher, laughed. Oh, precious Jap
anese babies, have you any idea how many
generations of the relentless training of
your mothers were required to produce your
involuntary instinct of obedience and your
brave laughter at your own fright?


The Japanese teacher laughed, too but
from different cause, and finally gave her
pupils chopsticks wherewith to lift them
With the o hashi the removal was indeed
easy, and not only was the transference of
the worms quickly effected, but they were
made to assume different positions, the
straight ones being made to curve and the
curled ones to lie straight, to the hugo
entertainment of the children.

fiume and wheels We're full of eels. The

to her assistance The rough sea pre-
vented her from approaching close,
but she managed to get line aboard.
This line parted in a short time and
another was spliced aboard, but 1t also
parted. The Santa Ana was powerless
to assist the disabled vessel in any way
and fearing that he would meet with
a similar fate, her master proceeded.


BY this time the Coquille River was
in waterlogged condition. with the
seas washing over her. A portion of
her deckload was thrown overheard
and the crew were put to work bailing
out the vessel Her pumps were clogged
and the crew strived to keep the yes
sci afioat bailing her with small cans.


1t was this morning before the bar
tug was able to cross out, and after
reaching her a heavy hawser was
placed aboard with much difficulty and
she was towed into port.

Vienna. Oct. 1S.-The Emperor passed a
quieter night His cough and fever have
diminished, but the catarrhal symptoms
are unchanged. His general condition is
brighter.


Late last night the report from the
bedside Of the Emperor was anything
but favorable. His physicians said that
the patients sleep was frequently dis
turbed by fits Of violent coughing, and,
though the fever at times. subsided. his
appetite was unsatisfactory, and that
they we're experiencing much difficulty in
pursuading the patient to take sufficient
nourishment.


An earlier report from the sick room
said that the Emperor's condition had
changed for the worse, and that his
physicians admitted his case was hope
less.


After having spent an unexpectedly
good night. the Emperor was able 10 rise
yesterday morning at an unusually early
hour. He coughed less and slept more
quietly The catarrhal inflammation,
however. has not diminished. and his ap-
petite continues bad.


An unsatisfactory symptom of the En-
perOr's condition is his recurring indif-
ference to what Is going on around him
and his own state Of health.


The report from Madrid that the visit
Of King Alfonso and Queen Victoria to
Vienna has been postponed Indefinitely S
confirmed.

lating pump. and could not be got out
again. Consequently 1t was necessary to
take out the blocked section of the pipe

any moral from the occurrence, but these
yarns seldom do contain any moral The
obvious moral would be that CAPTAINS
should never allow any but soft-shell crabs
to enter the circulating systems of the
steamers under their command BY care
fully observing this precaution they will
avoid danger of being called nature takers.

offered little resistance.


These operations were chiefly notable for
brilliant forced march of the French troops who
covered forty kilometres inside of twelve hours.
The expedition consisting of 1000 infantry.
with detachment of cavalry, artillery and
tive auxiliaries, left camp before dawn and
formed in two hollow squares. behind the
other. In this formation the troops marched
some distance under the cover of darkness, un-
observed by the tribesmen. \ heavy morning
sea fog came up at daybreak and forced a half
hours halt. during which shots fired by the ad
vance guards gave the alarm to the enemy The
tribesmen came up in large numbers. but
vigorous attack by the first square soon dis
persed them. No further stand was made by
the enemy during the march, although scat
tered groups Of horsemen harassed the French
fanks.


After the destruction of the camps had been
effected the tribesmen returned to the attack,
troop of cavalry repelling a spirited charge by
the Moorish horsemen. The French then aban-
doned their defensive formation and the column
returned to camp. Their losses were one killed
and ten wounded.

! The truest harbinger of the Easter

In fact Hamburgers have gathered

A certain lady riding a few days
ago on a street car. Its atmosphere being
even more fetid than usual she finally
asked the conductor whether he did not
realize that keeping all his ventilators tight
shut was very injurious to the health of
the passengers. He replied that there was
SO much pneumonia about that he dared
not keep the ventiators open for fear the
germs might get into the car through them


When the lady eXpla med to him that it
the passengers who brought the germs
into the car and that the closed ventilators
merely served to cage them in ever-increas-
ing multitudes inside the car he was as
tonished at the novelty of this theory.
Although he muttered that he could not
open anything anyway, because the pas
sengers would object, yet after he had
ruminated awhile over the original point
of view that had just been submitted to
him he furtively entered the car and sur
"reptitiously opened one ventilator.


This story draws its own conclusion. If
the powers that pack the street cars would
only realize that they cannot collect
nickels from microbes, and that, on the
other hand, microbes can collect passengers
from them, they would issue strict orders
to all their conductors to keep the ven
tilators open. Their passengers would soon
become educated out of the dread of fresh
air and great many of them would be
saved from pneumonia and the last long
transfer

BELFAST, July 6.-Before the eyes
of her father and brothers a German
girl trick cyclist, aged 16 was killed in
the Belfast hippodrome while perform
ing gratuitously in a Queens college
fete.


The family acted together in what is
known as the Aurora troupe, and the
girl had given expert cycling exhibi-
tions ever since she was 5. The climax
of the entertainment was as follows:
Four of the men cycling in one direc-
tion supported a platform upon which
the girl c. LED in the contrary direc-
ton. Somehow she lost her balance and
fell. Presumably she dislocated her
neck, for, though doctors were in the
audience and at once attended her, she
breathed her last behind the scenes
before the ambulance sent for arrived.


At once the curtain was rung down,
the manager announced the sad news
and the cancellation of the nights per-
formance, and the audience, which was
greatly shocked, passed out in silence.
The fathers grief was almost uncon-
trollable and the mother, who was at
their lodgings at the time, received a.
terrible blow. The college fete authori-
ties are to give all the proceeds of the
matinee to the family, which is taking
the body to Germany for burial. The
Dowager Lady Dufferin and others.
who were patrons of the fete, deeply
deplore the tragedy.

Aprons are by no means modern in

been fashions in aprons. as well as in
gowns, for at least 600 years, for in
Illuminated manuscripts Of the four
teenth century are obtained pictures
showing long. narrow aprons. gathered
at the TOP. These were more for utility
than for ornament. but beginning with
the reign of Queen Elizabeth the apron
became and remained an important ae-
cessory to the toilet until late IN the
last century.


1t was Queen Anne, or rather during
her reign. that lace aprons were fol-
lowed by satin creations marvelously
embroidered in colors. and bordered
with gold or silver fringe or lace.


The grande dame never wore a bib
upon her apron; only children and the
lower classes did this. The elaborate
aprons were very expensive, and were
often of Oriental workmanship.


They came into wear even for dress
occasions. these satin and gold lace
affairs. and IL was not until the shirt

LONG BEACH, Nov. 25.--To prevent the
destruction Of the Johnsor-Shields gar
age Thomas Mieklejohn last night cast
aside all thoughts OF his personal safety,
Jumped into car which was ablaze and,
though the flames leaped all about the
steering wheel, guided the auto out into
the middle Of Pacific avenue. A few
seconds later the gasoline tank exploded.


Mickeljohn was filling the tank with
gasoline wnen a spark struck the half
empty can in his hands and it exploded,
the burning oil flying over the auto, upon
the floor and upon his clothing.


He ran to a sandpile in the rear Of the
building and extinguished the flames by
rolling over and over.


Then he hurried back to the blazing
auto and despite the warnings Of men
gathered in front sprang to the seat,
wrapped an oilcloth apron about the
scorching steering wheel and ran the
car to the street.


His hands were severely burned.


The car belonged to William McGinnis.

text:
Let me show you something which
is more terrible than tragedy and
more hideous than vice. Itisa close
wedged procession of thousands of
happy but shabby men and women
and children passing at crawl be-
tween shop windows and costermon-
gers barrows on a Saturday night in
southeast London. The wind from
the Thames blows hither and thither
the flames and naphtha lamps and
makes them tug and hiss at the greasy
burners. 1t is bitterly cold. Wo-
men draw their gray shawls closer
over their heads; men turn up their
coat collars, hump their shoulders and
thrust their hands deeper in their
pockets, and the blue faced children,
squeezed between thelegs of the crawl
ing multitude, shiver and shuttle as
they creep so slowly forward with chat
tering teeth and purple lips, which
twitch and shudder, half from cold
and half from hunger.


Look at some of the faces. The
women have their hair dragged back
from their foreheads. The eyes are
hardly visible. The noses are short
and broad. The biubber lips reach
across their swollen faces. The men
have shifty eyes. Their underjaws
project. There is nothing in their
faces which suggests dignity or kind
ness. On all the faces you read sat-
isfaction and content. Even the starv-
ing children peep about with excite
ment.


On the top rail of stall, stuck upon
hooks and just high enough to grin
above the multitude, are the heads of
two sucking pigs. The eyes are half
open and wear CLASSY smile. Round
the rim of the ears and at the edge OF
the open grinning lips is a line of
blood. They seem to hang there like
the presiding deities of the market, the
gods of this sordid festival.


Butchers stand before their open
windows, calling loudlyand briskly for
customers and reaching down joints
of meat from steel hooks, which they
fling to man inside to be weighed.
Children, bareheaded and in rags,
thrust themselves among the crowd,
offering beet roots on pieces of dirty
newspaper. The street is filled with
cries. There is a smell of fish and
fusty garments. Into Our faces as we
90 forward foul, fat women with
hoarse voices shove handfuls of animal
matter-things all bloody and dread
ful-and tell us that the cost is only
two-pence. At another barrow an
old woman and her three daughters,
are selling for pennies, twopences,
threepences and fourpences the loath-
some oddments from their rag shop.
Blouses, stays, petticoats, nightdress-
es, trousers, waistcoats and caps-all
of them so sodden and musty that we
doubt if they would burn-are snatch
ed up from the wide stall, fourished
in the light of the naphtha lamps and
flung across to the highest bidder for
a few coppers.


And, while this marketing is going
on and while the air is filled with the
hoarse shouts of the hucksters, out
from the public houses, like bees dis
lodged from a swarm, drop men and
women, many of them carrying babies
In their arms, and slouch away into
the darkness of some neighboring
court. The gin shops are crammed-
crammed with men, women and chill
dren. The more careful housewives
are lingering bits of meat scarce fit for
dogs and haunting the stalls till they
have collected enough for Sundays
dinner, but when this is done they,
too, fight their way into the gin shops
and drink till closing time. In and
out of the pawnbrokers' shops pass
the mothers who wish to rescue their
best clothes for the Sunday. The
money lenders doors are never still.
And the crowd in the street grows
denser and noisier. The smell of it
fills the soul with nausea.


A young man, with child or two
in his arms, comes out of public
house. His wife and girl friend fol.
low after him mocking him for going
home so early. The wife carries a
baby of three or four months in her
arms. In the middle of the road the
girls begin to dance and sing. The
husband turns round and laughs.
The child in his arms, with dazed
eyes, watches her mother singing
and dancing. The dirty linen cap on
baby's head slips off as the mother
whirls about, and we see the poor lit
tie bald head going round and round
in the glare of the naphtha. How that
tiny brain must swim How 1t must
wonder at the shrill laughter of its
swaying mother The baby is nc
larger than skinned rabbit. Round
and round, round and round, to the
shrieked tune of sally, Sally, Was
In the Ballet" while the husband
stands grinning and the girl friend
suddenly reels and goes down behind
a barrow, chuckling and cursing.-
Detroit Meas.

And the car windows would have been

ed, and the dignity of Mayor Water
house of Pasadena would not have

Pasadena mayor and party of

ers warned them to walk more care

man, had long since taken his flight.

loss of 1900 killed. The fighting con-
tinued for long time and was conducted

struction of the buildings the disturbance

A number of enthusiasts took advantage
of the fine weather yesterday afternoon
and went to National Park and saw the
Fort Monroe foot ball team defeat the
All-Navy team by a score of IL to .. The
result of the contest was big surprise
to the Navy followers, as this same team
defeated the All-Army team Thanksgiving
day. and it was thought that the bog S
from the fort would not present as strong
a lineup against the Navy team, but they
sprung a surprise and played rings around
the sailor team.


Although the soldiers were lighter, they
were faster than the sailors and succeed
ed in pulling off several good gains on
end runs, while on the other hand the
Navy team made only a few gains and
they were small ones. The muddy condi-
ton of the field was a big handicap to
both teams. but the soldiers suffered
worse. as twice the runner fell while max

could regain his feet.


The star work of the game was done by
the two Army ends, James and Monroe,
and Douglass at right tackle. The two end
men got down the field on every punt and
tackled the Navy runner almost before
he could move out of his tracks. Doug
lass made several good runs through the
opposite tackles. James, who scored the
first touchdown. is about seven feet tall
and is considered the best foot ball player
enlisted in the ranks of the Army. Brill
at left halfback also did good work. For
the Navy team Gaskins. who played only
the second half, made several fine tackles.
Twice the Army runner had clear field
before him when this stockily-built sailor
downed him. Sherier made three good
runs through tackle near the close Of the

Army's Good Team Work.


The team work displayed by the Army

plays executed they showed that they de-
serve the title of being the best team in
the United States Army. Libby. at quar-
terback, ran the team in fine style and
took advantage of every weakness in the
Navy line. Time and time again he ran
Douglass through the Navy tackle and
on every down the runner made a good
gain. Bishop, who was at the helm for
Navy, used poor judgment on several
plays when he tried them through the
center position of the Army, as it could
be seen in the early stages of the game
that Swicegood was holding down his po-
sition in tip-top style.


The Navy center, Watson, and the two
guards, Anderson and Boche. also stopped
plunges through their positions. Brill.
who did the punting for Army, placed all
of his kicks, which were long and high,
and gave his ends time to get down the
field. while Bishop made only short kicks,
which resulted in a loss for his team.


The game was not so well played as
the Thanksgiving day game, as the Army
boys so far outclassed the sailors in team
work. Their strong point was in inter-
ference. The playing of both teams was
clean and the officials had little to. de pc
nalizing either.

Army won the toss and chose the south
goal. Erwin for Army kicked off to

yards. Army was held for downs.

SAN FRANCISCO Aug. 15.-The oil
steamer Santa Maria was saved from de-
struction on the rocks off Fort Point this
morning The Santa Maria is a $500,OOO
steel craft belinging to the Union Oil
company and recently laid up until $780,,
900 worth of work on her was completed.


Yesterday Captain Darling started to
take her on her initial voyage to Port
Hartford after her rest. She was just
off Fort Point, near the place the Ala
media was wrecked, when her oil burners
balked.


The Santa Maria began to drift rapidly
and would undoubtedly have heaved her
self upon the rocks had it not been for
the Sea Rover, which was just coming
through the heads after towing out the
ship w. H. Macy.


The captain of the Sea Rover saw the
distress of the big vessel and quickly
made for her, receiving line. The
Rover could not save the craft alone, and
word was sent to the city.


Superintendent Landell of the oil com
pany hurried out on the tug Sea Witch.
The two tugs stayed by for eleven hours
and at o'clock this morning they were
placed in service once more

ALBANY, Jan. Charles Evans
Hughes today took the oath of office as
Governor of the State of New York and
with his Democratic colleagues began
has two years term.


The retiring Governor, Frank w.
Higgins. formally surrendered the reins
of government to his successor and
left late this afternoon for his home,
a private citizen for the first time since
1898, when he was first elected Senator.


In his inaugural address Governor
Hughes paid marked tribute TO Gov
ernor Higgins. commencing his public
services and conscientious devotion to
the interests of the State. The inaug-
ural ceremonies were unusually bril-
liant and the attendance almost unpre-
cedented. Following them the new
Governor held reception in the execu-
tive chamber and in the afternoon he
and Mrs. Hughes received a cordial
welcome from very large humber of
people from Albany and elsewhere in
the usual public reception at the execu-
tive mansion.


The 130th session of the New York
State Legislature will convene tomor-
row and practically all of the newly
elected members of both houses attend
ed the inauguration today.

On the Ist of July, 1868, band of


$40 tall, lank Carolinians shouldered

Lee. Fresh from long furlough,


the bursting files of stalwart yeo-


manry, Zeb Vance's boys-tbe Twen-


ty.sixth regiment-marched cheeriiy


on to Gettysburg, "good food for


powder" old wardogs would say.


1t is an old story how the Confed-
crates under Heth clashed that day


with the Federal cavalry and infantry


under Buford and Reynolds. Heth's


leading brigade plunged across Will
loughby creek, dropped Reynolds
with chance shot and were them
selves quickly destroyed. Heth's
reserves, led by Pettigrew and Brock
enbrough, rushed to the rescue, and
the three days combat was begun.


The Twenty-sixth North Carolina
was on the left of Pettigrew's brigade
and crossed the creek abreast of Nc
Pherson's woods, where Sol Mere
dith's Iron brigade and Rowley's
Pennsylvanians were forming a line.
The continual shifting of the Federal
regiments from position to position
led the Confederates to look for an
easy victory, but every step of their
march revealed a new foe.


In the pathway of the Carolinians
Cooper's Pennsylvania battery was
posted, covering the interval between
Rowley's men and the Iron brigade.
Cooper's guns showered the butter
nut ranks with grape, and eleven
color bearers in the Twenty-sixth
were shot down during the struggle
with Meredith, Rowley and Cooper.
The Twenty.fourth Michigan of the
Iron brigade fought against the Car
olinians, and its loss that day was the
highest in the Federal army on the
field of Gettysburg. The One Hun
cred and Fifty-frst Pennsylvania,
also opposed to the Carolinians, lost
10 per cent. Of its men, killed and
wounded. After the battle the posi-
tions held by the Federal regiments
could be distinguished by the rowsof
dead who had fought till they fell in
defense of the roads to Gettysburg.
But the Twenty-sixth North Caro-
lima had got as good as it gave. At
roll call that night only 2I6 men
were shown to have come through
by bullets. Captain
Tuttle's company went into action
with three officers and eighty.four
men. All of the officers and eighty
three men were killed or wounded. |
The remnant of the Twenty-sixth |
.ook part in Pickett's charge and at
lacked the line of Smyth's brigade,
n Hancock's corps, near the Bloody |
Angle. It came out with only eighty |
men fit for duty.

OMAHA, Neb September 6.-The Rocky
Mountain Limited on the Rock Island was
raided this morning just before daylight
near Murdoch. Neb., by three masked men,
The robbers went through the chair car
robbing every passenger therein, securing
their pocketbooks and purses, covered the
train crew with revolvers and escaped by
leaping from the train. Railroad detectives
and sheriff posses are in pursuit. but the
robbers have several hour start on the
officers.


The robbers We're passengers on the
train. Shortly after leaving Murdoch the
men arose in their seats, their faces coy
cred with masks. and, with revolvers IN
each hand. covered the passengers Then
the leader ordered everybody to keep stu
and not to resist. else they would be shot.
Two men went down the aisle with mats
in hand, while the third kept he passen-
gers covered.


All passengers were ordered to throw
pocketbooks into the hats, and this was
done The conductor appeared in the car
with a pistol in his hand, but was promptly
covered with four guns and forced to drop
his revolver.


After getting all the money in the car
the robbers jumped from the train, which
had slowed down for grade An at
tempt was made to enter the sleeper sec
ton but the door was locked and the at
tempt was unsuccessful. The search and
pursuit is being prosecuted vigorously.


Bloodhounds in Pursuit.


City Detective Malone of Lincoln this
morning started two men with bloodhounds
In pursuit of bandits who looted Rock Is
land train No. s. 1t is known that the
three robbers were in Lincoln yesterday
One of the three joined the otner two here,
coming from Alvo. The trail OF the ROBBERS
was discovered this morning a snort dis
tance from AiVo.

LEXINGTON. Ky. January News
reached here tonight of a bloody battle in
Pike county mountains. which resulted in
Chris Doc and Drue Wright being killed.
and Isaac Wallace, George Birchett and
Columbus Colly were wounded Birchett
and Colly fatally. The battle occurred
near th> Pond post Office. in Pike county
The men gathered at a moonshine distil-
lery there and all got drunk, and a quarrel
arose.


All were armed with pistols, which they
began using. About twenty-five shots were
fired, and the fight ceased only when the
three Wright boys were dead. The men
fought Indian fashion. from behind rocks
and trees The three Wright brothers were
urged into battle by their father Samuel
Wright. who began firing first. He has
long been identified with mountain feuds


News also comes today of a fight at
Boone Fork. Letcher county. where Bill
Ellsworth was killed by Clark Vanover
This fight occurred at Vanover's moonshine
still. Ellsworth attacked Hanover with
knife and the latter defended himself with
an ak, killing Ellsworth.

Special Dispatch to The Star.


WOODS HOLE. Mass, August 14.-Here
and all throughout Cape Cod, Martha's Vine
yard and Nantucket all commercial tele-
graph business is practically suspended.


Ninety-five per cent of the wireless tele-
graph messages sent from steamships
bound to New York pass through the cable
Office at Woods Hole. This serviceNis sus-
pended. There are plenty Of operators at
this end of Cape Cod, Marthas Vineyard
and Nantucket, but they cannot get anybody
on the other end to receive the messages.


The slump in the stock market caused an
increase in the business between Nam
tucket and Martha's Vineyard where there
are many wealthy summer visitors from
Boston and New York. All the operators
on Cape Cod at Martha's Vineyard and
other places are still at work and refuse to
strike but are helpless. for they cannot
raise anybody on the other end. Tele
graphic orders to Boston from Nantucket
are relayed to Boston by long distance tele
phone.

afresh.

Angeles, especially among the visit

the sense of responsibility felt in Los

had lowered their flag and disarmed.

from the Richmond reunion and after
visiting the White House marched
down Pennsylvania avenue to the cap
itol The capitol police informed them
that they would be allowed admission
to the capitol only as private citizens
and not as an organized body. Con-
gressman John Wesley Gaines OF Ten
nessee, who accompanied the veterans,
entered protest.

must break rank and disarm before
entering the building. Finally this was
done and the old soldiers were shown
through the building.

DIES MONIES, Iowa, March 15.-Be-
cause her mother and father would not
consent to her marriage with the man
of her choice Miss Bessie Algrowes of
Prairie Center locked them in the cell
lar of their home and drove twenty
miles across country with Abe Gun
nells to Mason City, where they were
married yesterday.


Soon after dinner the girl called her
parents to come into the cellar, saying
she had something to show them. I'm
suspectingly they went. The daughter
climbed out, bolted the door behind her
and ran around the other exit and fas-
tened it.


Then, calmly sitting down, she asked
the angry pair if they would consent
to her marriage. She said she would
leave them there until they did.


After several hours, the father re-
naming inexorable, she placed some
food in a small window and went to
join her impatient sweetheart outside.
With the shouts of the father ringing
in her ears they drove away.


The old people were forced to remain
in the callar until morning, when a
passing neighbor released them.


The happy bride and groom returned
today. After much persuasion they
were forgiven.

Special Correspondence Of The Star.


OCEAN CITY. Md, August 81, 1907.


Among ths more inexpensive resorts along
the Atlantic coast where brain and body find
rest and relaxation from the daily grind,
Ocean City Is gaining more and more at
tention as its many attractions become bet
ter known. Forty years ago there was no
sign of hut or house on this Sinepuxent
Island-a narrow strip Of land fifty miles
long, lying between the ocean and Sine
puxent bay, its greatest width being
scarcely mile and half. In place Of
sand dune and hummock today has risen
beautiful little seaside city destined to
become one OF the rival resorts along the
coast.


With the broad Atlantic at ones very
door and the quiet waters Of the bay in the
rear. with boardwalk several miles in
length upon which borders a long line of at
tractiye hotels and cottages, with magnih-
cent bathing, boating, fishing and Grabbing.
with music and dancing and all the varied
amusements dear to the popular heart he
must indeed be cynical who cannot find
some pleasure best suited to his need


The broad sandy beach is perpetual para
disc for children, whose tanned and ruddy
faces bespeak the health-giving tonic Of the
sea. while their elders, less bronzed,
though less strenuous. gain new health and
vigor with every breath OF this nfe-gtving
ozone and salt-laden air.


AT the Sunday evening concert at tho At
lantic Hotel the Rev. DR.. Dudley rector
OF st. Stephens Church in Washington.
sang three magnificent solos. and the Bos-
ton Mountfort Orchestra Of five young
ladies rendered the instrumental numbers


The men Of the United States life saving
service gtve'a drill Mondays and Thurs
days, which affords a most interesting ex-
hibition for the early riser. Ocean City
has splendid water and sewerage system,
relying wholly for its drinking water upon
It's artesian wells. 1000 feet deep. the water
possessing medicinal properties and said to
be % per cent pure. This favored spot,
famed by the breezes of the gulf stream.
has an ideal temperature during the time
when less favored places are sweltering
with the torrid heat This fact and the
bathing, so free from treacherous undertow
or dangerous side currents, form combi-
nation hard to resist, and make this south
ern city by the sea haven of health for
the nervous wreck or the wearied brain.

NEW YORK, Jan. 9.-No tidings

steamship Ponce, which sailed from
Porto Rico for New York on December
26, and anxiety for her safety increases
as the hours pass without news of the
ship.


The Ponce, when she left Porto Rico,
carried seven passengers and a crew
of thirty men. Captain William Har-
vey, whose home is in Brooklyn, where
his wife and two daughters reside, was
in command. The agents of the steam
ship have not abandoned hope that the
vessel will return all right. They be-
lieve that the machinery became dis
abled and that she Is drifting about
the ocean while the engineers are en-
deavoring to effect repairs or that she
has been picked up by some passing
steamer and is now being towed to
some port.


The Ponce was equipped with good
life RATS and boats so that even If
she struck a derelict that caused her
to sink, as some seafaring men fear,
there Ia good chance that those on
board escaped.

dered Captain Swift of the battleship
Connecticut sailing from Hampton
Roads for Culebra, off the coast OF
Porto Rico. the winter rendezvous OF
the Atlantic fleet. to do everything pos.
stble to traceTthe missing Ponce.


None of the cutters, the Onondagc
from Porto Rico. the Seminole from
Charleston and the Mohawk from New
York dispatched to find her, have yet
reported.


Still another ship was ordered yes
terday to search for the Ponce. Gen
eral Manager Mooney of the New
York and Porto Rico Steamship COM
pany cabled the liner San Juan, a sis
ter ship of the Ponce, sailing yesterday
from Mayaguez to veer from her usual
track and rake the southern water
ways.

The truest harbinger of the Easter
time is the display of the new spring
goods, and Hamburger's has surpassed
itself this year in gathering together all
that is new, chic and beautiful.
Yesterday was the first day of their
Easter opening, and it will continue to-
day and tomorrow. They are featuring
the $50 French hats, and yesterday
morning they had 240 original Partisan
dreams.


Yellow seems to be the predominating
color although blue is claiming its
share of popularity. Some of the most
beautiful hats that Hamburger's are
showing have the new willow plumes.
These are the regular ostrich feather,
but the tendrils are twice as long and
fall over the straw or lace in soft,
curly shower that gives the hat an
added charm and distinction.


The ostrich plumes are still holding
their own, and the lingerie hat, trimmed
with flowers instead of ribbon, has also
been brought over from across the
water. The greater part of the hats
shown are miniature flower gardens.
Wisteria seems to be greatly used in
the trimming, although all kinds of
blossoms are favorites Some of the
hats are loaded down with 81 small
novelty fruits, such as crab apples,
loquats, and so forth. Other hats which
Hamburgers are showing and which,
from their general air of style and
beauty, will probably prove favorites,
are those trimmed with the cassowary
plume, something entirely new The
plumes are long with quantities of short
tendrils tipped with a darker and more
wide-spreading feather. The natural
colored leghorns trimmed with black
are being sold extensively to lovers Of
the stylish hat. Quantities of grasses
and ferns are also a new departure in
the art of trimming.


Hamburger's new gowns, which were
imported directly from Paris, London
and Berlin, are mostly made in the
princess and bodice styles. Their line
this year contains some of the most
beautiful creations that famous Euro
pean artists could conceive. Butter,
ecru and azure blue are the colors
shown, and light fluffy silks are in the
greatest demand. All their newest cos
tunes are fancy, every available inch
being covered with lace or embroidery.
Even the tailor gowns are heavily
trimmed. Many of the costumes are IN
three pieces, and all have the short
sleeves, but made looser than last year.
The jackets are made Eton and the
bodice gowns are among the most ex-
pensive. The long coats are pongee or
all over lace. A great many of, the
new waists are made of net over Dres-
den silk and almost entirely of ruffles.
The gowns in the leather shades are
new, and most of the lingerie dresses
are made princess and elaborately
trimmed.


The beautiful line of silk underskirte
that Hamburgers are showing attracted
the attention yesterday of all the lovers
of dainty clothes. They are in all the
shades to match the gowns and are
hand embroidered.


In fact Hamburger's have gathered
together all that is stylish and dainty
and yesterday crowds of people testified
their appreciation by thronging al
parts of the store, admiring and buying
While the millinery cloaks and suits
were the center of attraction there We're
many other novelties that drew then
share of attention.


Peeping into the future this is prob
ably the last Opening" Hamburger S
will hold in their present location, fol-
they are building what, when finished
win be the 'grandest store I'm America
IA store which will be devoted to the
shopping interests of all California.
With perfect weather conditions the
forces of workmen will be doubled and
the immense task Of building this great
store will be rushed forward without
cessation until completed, They are
exerting every possible effort to the
end that their annual fall opening may
be in the new store at Eighth ano
! Broadway.

est fire that devastated the south enc

The Aimee is owned by Innis Kin

The party left here a week ago Satur-

Adverse winds added to their discom-

The vessel was quickly anchored and

morning sun.


A fire was hastily made and after
not breakfast the flames were covered

other campers appeared to be, intending
to inquire the distance to Avalon.

Scarcely had they reached the neigh
boring camp. however, when their atten-
ton was attracted to huge clouds OF
smoke arising from where they had left
their belongings, and with all possible
speed they dashed back to the scene


AS they reached the summit OF nil
overlooking their camp the youths were
confronted with a spectacle that ma1e
their hearts sink.


The fire they had left smoldering had
been started afresh by a party OF young
people who had taken possession OF the
camp and had gotten beyond control.


The flames were travelling rapidly in
land, swept by wind from the ocean,
and We're last gaining headway notwith-
standing the efforts of a half dozen attn
letic young men who were members OF
the intruding party.


With two bronzed youths who had been
mountain climbing. the local party quickly
Joined the fire fighters. For more than
three hours the battle against the flames
was waged before they were put under
control All of those who took part In
extinguishing the fire were utterly ex-
hausted when the last fickering ember
had been beaten out, and 1t was not un-
til late in the afternoon that they felt
sufficiently recovered to show any signs
of activity.


The fire swept large portion Of land
known as Emerald cove and its smoke
was visible for a distance of ten miles.
Young Kinney is planning a second
yachting-campin expedition to San Gle
mente island next Saturday.

enty-five feet of it.

SALINAS, March 25.-The situation
here is growing worse hourly. Traffic
on the Southern Pacific main line north
Is entirely suspended beyond Castro
vile. Heaviest rain ever known in this
section has been falling at intervals
during the past twenty-four hours.


Alisal creek broke from it's banks and
flooded the country just outside of the
city limits and the water is rapidly ex-
tending toward the city. Chinatown,
situated near the railroad track, inside
the city limits, is partially flooded.


At Sand Cut, Logans, Chittenden,
New Ria and Sargents new landslides
are reported. The Pajaro river cut
through banks above Watsonville and
rushed down Second street of that
town.


The tracks between Pajaro and Cas-
troville are covered with water several
feet deep. The San Lorenzo river is
over it's banks and is flooding all the
low-lying districts. huge jam Of
logs occurred at the bridge between
Santa Cruz and Watsonville and no ore
is allowed to cross. Salinas has had
no newspapers or mails from anywhere
since Friday afternoon, and is COM
pletely isolated. Snow now covers
both the Santa Lucia and Gabiian
ranges.
