Today marks the second week of the
poultry show for Los Angeles and the
first day of the Los Angeles County
Poultry associations exhibition. Almost
$500 birds will shine in the coming fowl
meet, birds which have been brought
from the best poultry farms in the
United States and England.


One of the gratifying features of last
weeks show was the fact that in sew
eral cases native California birds took
the blue ribbons away from fowls which
had won the first prizes at the large
eastern exhibits.


In the show opening today the native
birds will have another opportunity to
prove their superiority over the foreign
breeds, for among the bipeds to be ex-
hibited are some that took the blue at
the London and birmingham shows.
Others held down first place at large
poultry shows in New York, Chicago,
Boston, indianapolis, Cincinnati and
San Francisco.


Some of the birds which have been
entered at the Panorama rink show are
highly valued by their owners. For
four high bred Orpington cocks one of
the exhibitors is said to have paid $4,000.


Several of the other exhibits are
scarcely less valuable.


In point of novelties introduced the
show will be far in advance of any
previous attempt made in this city.
Pheasants, turkeys, pigeons of many
breeds, rare imported bantams, pea
fowls, ostriches, and lastly, several
jungle fowls, birds which are the pro-
genitors of the present day hen, biped
known for it's savory eggs which it lays
only when eggs are cheap.


The prizes offered are said to be
more numerous and finer than the
premiums offered in the large Boston
and New York shows. Eighty-five cups,
valued at hundreds of dollars, will be
competed for, in addition to the regular
ribbons without which no show could
succeed. A special offer of medals for
the best chicken in each class has also
been made, and even, barring the asso-
Citations connected with such affairs,
the pecuniary value of the trophies will
make them worth competing for.


The show will be in progress till
January IL at the Panorama rink, which
had been fitted up with pens and deco
rated for the occasion.

A hunting expedition that promised a day
of pleasure for Harry Crabbs and his son,
Ernest, fourteen years old of 233 14th street
southeast yesterday had a sad termination
about $50 o'clock yesterday morning, when
the gun used by Ernest was accidentally
discharged, killing him instantly. The ac-
cdent happened on the farm of George
Rhinefelt, about two miles from Marshall
Hall, in Charles county, Md. The body was
brought 10 this city last night by the father
on steamer from Marshall Hall and was
turned to local undertaking estab-
lishment.


No definite arrangements for the funeral
have been made, but 1t will be held either
tomorrow afternoon or Thursday morning
from the family home, at 233 l4th street
southeast.


Planning to enjoy Labor day in Charles
county yesterday, Ernest and his father
left their home Sunday evening, each armed
with dou5le-barreled shotgun. They made
their headquarters at the farm of MIR.
Rhinefelt Arising early yesterday morn
ing, they went out looking for game before
breakfast. About 8 O'Clock they returned
to the farmhouse for something to eat.


Gun Slips From Chair.


Ernest put his gun against a chair that
was under tree in the yard and was talk
ing with his father and George Rhinefelt
when the gun suddenly slipped from the
chair and fell TO the ground. The trigger
evidently caught on part of the chair and
the gun was discharged. The load pene-
tTated Ernests stomach and inflicted ter
rlble wound. The boy fell to the ground in
an instant and it is believed that he was
dead before his father could reach him.


Mr.. Crat5s picked up the limp body and
carried II inside the house and a doctor
was summoned But it was soon realized
that the boy was dead and that the doctor
could do nothing.


a justice of the peace for Charles county
was notified of the sudden death, and made
an investigation of the circumstances. He
decided that death was due entirely to
accident.


About O'Clock yesterday afternoon word
reached his home here that Ernest had been
Killed. Mrs. Crabhs nearly prostrated
oy the sudden shock. She embarked on the
boat for Marshall Hall and soon joined her
husband. They returned with the body late
last night.


Ernest had two sisters, Annie and Myrtle,
and one brother, John, who survive him,
besides his parents. They were in great
grief when Star reporter called at the
home.

threatens to bury Scott streets twenty-five

and Lake Erie Railroad Company recently
started to make cut for additional tracks

on which the houses stand is underlai id

mass is slowly slipping toward the cut

street for 100 yards. with its houses, dropped
10 feet below Its original level. bursting
gas and water mains and leaving half the
village without light or fire protection

vainly endeavoring 10 check the landslide
while crowds of hystericaI women and chill
dren watch the widea,ng assures.

NEW YORK, July 2S.-An explosion, ac-
companied by fire shattered an east side
tenement late tonight, and with the
crumbling walls fourteen persons, per-
haps more went down to death, while
twice as many were probably fatally in
jured.


The wrecked building tonight was at
222 Christie street, where six-story tene-
ment rose above the grocery store base
ment.


The explosion is as yet unaccounted for

The fire that followed caught the twenty
families, numbering about 100 persons,
while most of them were sound asleep.

Fire which threatened the entire up

volunteer firemen and rangers.


Several ranch houses in the line of prog

flames, hedged in by the hills which sur


round the canyon, worked up the narrow
valley with incredible rapidity, and al
most before the alarm had been sounded

fighting brigades, had swept over nearly


mile of territory. A strong breeze car


ried the fire in a northerly direction, but
fortunately toward point where the land
is cultivated and cleared of thick under


brush and timber.


Under the direction of Chief Ranger


Phil Bigue and two of his assistants the
farmers for miles around gathered to re-
pei the flames, and with wet sacks and
frequent back-firing kept them from
spreading into the hills which lie between
the San Fernando valley and La Cres-


centa. Had the flames penetrated these
hills the loss would undoubtedly have


amounted to considerable, as numerous


bee ranches and small farms dot their
slopes on both sides.


Wild animals and birds would also have
suffered, as the small mountains in the


region are pientifully stocked with wild


cats, foxes, doves, quail and also with


few deer. Rabbits abound and song birds


of all kinds are to be found in large num-


bers. The principal damage dore by the


flames was the destroying of beautiful


groves of oak and sycamore trees, and


also an abandoned orchard in the vicinity


of the La Crescenta schoolhouse.

SAN FRANCISCO, Nov. S.-Five women
and one man were injured in street car
accident this morning when a Hayes VAL
ley car of the United Railroads was
switching back on Devisadero street at
Eddy street. The car slid back on the
Eddy street track, got beyond control of
the motorman and rushed down the hill
to Fillmore street.


Early in the dash the crew, powerless
to stop the car jumped off, leaving a
dozen terror stricken and screaming pas
sengers on the runaway.


AT Fillmore street the car, which had
gained terrific speed in its dash down
the steep hill from Devisadero street.
smashed into an Eddy street car bound
west with a crash that was heard for
blocks, and which telescoped both cars
for a distance of two feet beyond the
platforms. Those injured are:


Miss Mabel Marshall, rib fractured:
Mrs. Mary B. McGlade, bruises and cuts;
Mrs. James Keefe, skull probably frac-
tured; Mrs B. Macouilliard, bruises and
cuts; Mrs. K. Oestrick Oakland, bruises
and shock; Samuel King. Lyon street,
bruised.


James Lenole, motorman, and Gustave
Mattheson. conductor, of the Hayes VAL
ley car. which caused the crash, were

| The following statement has been made
public at the Department of Justice:
| THE petition filed by the government
in the United States circuit court at
Philadelphia is aimed at the anthracite
| coal monopoly. The Reading company. a
holding corporation: the Philadelphia and
Reading Railway Company, the Lehigh
Valley Railroad Company, the Delaware.
Lackawanna and Western Railroad Com
pany. the Central Railroad Of New Jersey.
the Erie Railroad Company and the New

(Which last does not extend to tidewater),

connect the three last named railroads with
the alleged unlawful combination and
! monopoly has been found Should such
evidence be forthcoming in the progress OF
the trial they may. and of course will, be
joined with the other defendants.


In brief the petition recites that the de-
PENDANT railroads control all the means Of
transportation between the anthracite
mines and tidewater except the lines of
the Pennsylvania railroad and the New
York. Ontario and Western railway, which
reach only limited number of collieries;
that they transport annually about IS per

panieS whose capital stock they own they

thracite deposits and produce about Is per
cent of the annual supply; that independ-
ent operators. although owning probably
little more than per cent of the anthra-
cite deposits. yet produce about 20 per cent
Of the annual supply. which would be sold
in competition with the output of the de-
PENDANTS were it not for the restraints i'm
posed by the latter.


The petition then charges that the de-

petition among themselves In the transport
sale Of the Independent output in COMPETE
ton with their own. thereby establishing a
monopoly. and in support Of this general
allegation 1t specifies


"ta) That the defendant railroads agreed
among themselves upon uniform contract
to be entered into by them or their coal
companies with the Independent operators
along their respective lines under which
the railroads would be able to control the
sale of the independent output, and that by
virtue of their control Of all the means Of
transportation from the anthracite mines to
tidewater save the lines of the Pennsyl-
vania Railroad Company and the New
York. Ontario and Western Railway Com
pany. the defendant railroads were able
to force and practically did force the indie
pendent operators along their lines into
making these contracts.


"lb) That, the Erie Railroad Company
has exchanged shares of its own capital
stock for a majority OF the shares or the
New York Susquehanna and Western Rail-
road Company competing line, thereby
uniting under common source OF con-
troll the two competing railroad companies
and their subsidiary coal companies.


''(c) That the Reading company, which
already held all the shares of the Philadel-
phia and Reading Railway Company. has

ma jority of the shares OF the Central Rail-
road Company of New Jersey, competing

'"CdD That twice in recent years the de-

dent operators to be sold in the markets In

Persia, after the latters conquest by

wed Statiro, daughter of the conquered

sian and Medean families. He further

erected, the pillars being 60 feet high.

Joined this for the 100 noble bridegrooms.

court was inclosed. Outside of this tables
were spread for the multitude.

selves in seni-circle round the royal
throne. AS 1t would have taken several
weeks for the few priests to have mar
ried this vast number of couples had the
ceremony been performed in the ordinary
way. Alexander invented a simple way
out of the difficulty. He gave his hand
to Statiro and kissed her, and all the
remaining bridegrooms did the same to
the women beside them; and thus ended
the ceremony that united the greatest
number of people at one time ever known.


Then occurred a five days festival which
for grandeur and magnificence never has
been equaled.

man was installed In her new position.

One thousand school children and
700 of their elders yelled their throats
hoarse yesterday afternoon when the
Los Angeles city school officials in
augurated the first annual kite flying
contest at Stephenson and Lorena
streets yesterday afternoon, which
Euclid school won. A wind that
seemed just made for kites dotted the
blue with hundreds of quaint and ar
tistic shapes, all the product of young
Americas cunning fingers. From the
two score schools represented almost
200 kites of all stages of beauty and
novel design were flown by the young
contestants for championship honors.


Field Divided Into Tracts


The big field had been divided into
tracts 100 feet square, one tract being
allotted to each school. In the center
of each the school occupying 1t had
placed it's banner made of the school
coIors and bearing the school name.
Around this as a nucleus gathered the
dozens of contestants and rooters, who
had come to cheer their warriors in
the fray. Red and white, green and
blue, red and yellow. The field was a
sight more gay than the kite-dotted
sky above. Organized bands of root
ers proclaimed in loud and insistent
tones the merits of their respective col
ors and institutions of learning.


The program included quarter mile
dashes for boys and girls; best deco
rated kite; most artistic; strongest
puller; best tetrahedral; highest flyer,
yacht race, quarter mile and return:
parachute contest; curious messenger
and display of flags. BY the time
the first six events had been pulled off
the wind had become so strong that
the others were declared off.


Eight Girls in Contest


Hoover street, besides taking a first
in the contests, showed up strong in
it's school spirit. Led by Captain
Arthur Fischer, a gang of the young
sters, resplendent in red caps and red
and white pennants, marched on the
field, giving vent to the calculating
yell quoted above. This was followed
by the following effort:

This school had the largest entry

the various events.

cry victory till it was an assured thing
and then T. remained for the girls to
uphold the honor of their school. Pull
